m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Show that the set of all rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable.
m1.approach: Express $\mathbb{Q}$ as a countable union of countable sets or an injection into $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$.

solution_steps.title: Set Representation
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{Q} = \left\{ \frac{p}{q} : p \in \mathbb{Z},\, q \in \mathbb{N},\, \gcd(p, q) = 1 \right\}
solution_steps.explanation: Every rational number has a unique representation as a fraction in lowest terms with a positive denominator.

solution_steps.title: Injection into a Countable Set
solution_steps.math: f: \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}, \quad f(p/q) = (p, q)
solution_steps.explanation: The map $f$ is injective. Since $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{N}$ are countable, their Cartesian product $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ is countable.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{Q} \sim f(\mathbb{Q}) \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Any infinite subset of a countable set is countable. Hence, $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable (denumerable).

m1.final_answer: $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable because it injects into the countable set $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$.
m1.exam_tip: Remember to state that the representation must be in lowest terms so that the map $f$ is well-defined and injective.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Is the set of all real numbers in $[0,1]$ denumerable? Justify.
m1.approach: Use Cantor's Diagonal Argument or the uncountability of real numbers to show $[0, 1]$ is not denumerable.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Denumerable
solution_steps.math: S \text{ is denumerable } \iff \exists \text{ bijection } f: \mathbb{N} \to S
solution_steps.explanation: A set is denumerable if its elements can be listed as a sequence $x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots$ with no omissions.

solution_steps.title: Cantor's Diagonalization
solution_steps.math: x_n = 0.d_{n1} d_{n2} d_{n3} \dots \quad \text{in decimal or binary}
solution_steps.explanation: If $[0, 1]$ were listed as $\{x_1, x_2, \dots\}$, we construct $y = 0.y_1 y_2 \dots \in [0, 1]$ by setting $y_n = 2$ if $d_{nn} \ne 2$, and $y_n = 3$ if $d_{nn} = 2$. Then $y$ differs from $x_n$ at the $n$-th decimal place for all $n$.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction
solution_steps.math: y \in [0, 1] \quad \text{but} \quad y \ne x_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: This contradicts the assumption that the list contains all elements of $[0, 1]$.

m1.final_answer: No, $[0, 1]$ is not denumerable; it is uncountably infinite.
m1.exam_tip: Always avoid digits 0 and 9 in decimal diagonalizations to prevent ambiguities like $0.1999\dots = 0.2000\dots$.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: State Cantor's diagonal argument for uncountability.
m1.approach: Formally state the method of contradiction by constructing an element that differs at the $n$-th diagonal entry.

solution_steps.title: Setup of Enumeration
solution_steps.math: \text{Assume } S = \{s_1, s_2, s_3, \dots\} \subseteq [0, 1]
solution_steps.explanation: Write each number in decimal or binary expansion: $s_n = 0.a_{n1}a_{n2}a_{n3}\dots$.

solution_steps.title: Construction of Diagonal Element
solution_steps.math: b = 0.b_1 b_2 b_3 \dots \quad \text{where } b_n = \begin{cases} 4 & \text{if } a_{nn} \ne 4 \\ 5 & \text{if } a_{nn} = 4 \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: Each digit $b_n$ is deliberately chosen to differ from the $n$-th digit $a_{nn}$ of the $n$-th number $s_n$.

solution_steps.title: Deduction
solution_steps.math: b \ne s_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N} \implies b \notin S
solution_steps.explanation: Since $b \in [0, 1]$ but $b$ cannot be in the list, no enumeration can be complete. Hence $[0, 1]$ is uncountable.

m1.final_answer: Cantor's diagonal argument proves that no sequence can exhaust the set $[0, 1]$ by constructing a real number whose $n$-th digit differs from the $n$-th digit of the $n$-th listed number.
m1.exam_tip: Clearly mention the diagonal entry $a_{nn}$ and how the newly constructed entry $b_n$ guarantees inequality.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Define a countable set and show that the set of integers $\mathbb{Z}$ is countable.
m1.concept_tested: Definition of Countable Set & Countability of $\mathbb{Z}$
m1.approach: State the definition of countable (finite or denumerable) and construct an explicit bijection between $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Countable Set
solution_steps.math: S \text{ is countable } \iff S \text{ is finite or } S \sim \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: A set is countable if it is either empty, finite, or can be put into one-to-one correspondence with the set of natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$.

solution_steps.title: Bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$
solution_steps.math: f(n) = \begin{cases} \frac{n}{2} & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \\ -\frac{n-1}{2} & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: This lists the integers as $0, 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3, \dots$.

solution_steps.title: Bijectivity Verification
solution_steps.explanation: Every integer appears exactly once in the sequence, proving $f$ is a bijection.

m1.final_answer: A set is countable if it is finite or denumerable. $\mathbb{Z}$ is countable via the explicit bijection $f(n) = n/2$ (even) and $-(n-1)/2$ (odd).
m1.exam_tip: Always write out the first 5 terms $(0, 1, -1, 2, -2)$ to make the pattern unmistakable to the examiner.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: State Cantor's Theorem regarding the cardinality of a set and its power set.
m1.approach: State the theorem formally: for any set $A$, there is no surjection from $A$ onto its power set $\mathcal{P}(A)$, so $|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|$.

solution_steps.title: Formal Statement
solution_steps.math: \forall \text{ set } A, \; |A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|
solution_steps.explanation: Let $A$ be any set and let $\mathcal{P}(A)$ denote the set of all subsets of $A$. Then there exists no surjective function from $A$ onto $\mathcal{P}(A)$.

solution_steps.title: Consequence for Cardinality
solution_steps.math: \text{There is an injection } g(a) = \{a\}, \text{ but no surjection.}
solution_steps.explanation: Since the map $a \mapsto \{a\}$ is an injection, the cardinality of $A$ is strictly less than the cardinality of $\mathcal{P}(A)$.

m1.final_answer: Cantor's Theorem states: For any set $A$, there is no surjective map from $A$ onto $\mathcal{P}(A)$. Consequently, $|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|$.
m1.exam_tip: Note that this holds for ALL sets $A$, whether empty, finite, or infinite.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Define cardinality of a set and explain what is meant by $c = 2^{\aleph_0}$.
m1.concept_tested: Cardinality & The Power of the Continuum
m1.approach: Define cardinality as the equivalence class of equipotent sets and explain $c = 2^{\aleph_0}$.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Cardinality
solution_steps.math: |A| = |B| \iff \exists \text{ bijection } f: A \to B
solution_steps.explanation: Two sets $A$ and $B$ have the same cardinality (or cardinal number) if there is a one-to-one correspondence between them.

solution_steps.title: Explanation of $c = 2^{\aleph_0}$
solution_steps.math: \aleph_0 = |\mathbb{N}|, \quad c = |\mathbb{R}| = |\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})| = 2^{\aleph_0}
solution_steps.explanation: $\aleph_0$ ('aleph-null') is the cardinality of the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$. The power set $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$. Since $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ is equipotent to the set of binary sequences $\{0,1\}^\mathbb{N}$, which in turn is equipotent to $\mathbb{R}$, the continuum cardinality $c$ equals $2^{\aleph_0}$.

m1.final_answer: Cardinality is a measure of the size of a set. $c = 2^{\aleph_0}$ means the cardinality of the real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ equals the cardinality of the power set of $\mathbb{N}$.
m1.exam_tip: Mention that $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ corresponds to indicator functions $\{0, 1\}^\mathbb{N}$, giving the base 2 in $2^{\aleph_0}$.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: What is a denumerable set? Give an example of a set that is infinite but not denumerable.
m1.approach: Define denumerable set and provide a standard example of an infinite set that is uncountable.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Denumerable Set
solution_steps.math: S \text{ is denumerable } \iff S \sim \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: A set $S$ is called denumerable (or countably infinite) if there exists a bijection $f: \mathbb{N} \to S$.

solution_steps.title: Example of Non-denumerable Infinite Set
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{R}, \quad [0, 1], \quad \text{or } \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}
solution_steps.explanation: The set of all real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ (or the interval $[0, 1]$, or the set of irrational numbers) is infinite but not denumerable (it is uncountably infinite).

m1.final_answer: A denumerable set is a set equipotent to $\mathbb{N}$. An infinite but non-denumerable set is the real line $\mathbb{R}$ (or the interval $[0, 1]$).
m1.exam_tip: Clarify that 'countable' includes finite sets, whereas 'denumerable' refers strictly to countably infinite sets.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Define a bijective map between two sets and its relation to equipotence.
m1.approach: Define bijective map (injective + surjective) and define equipotence between sets.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Bijective Map
solution_steps.math: f: A \to B \text{ is bijective } \iff f \text{ is both injective (one-to-one) and surjective (onto)}
solution_steps.explanation: Injective: $f(x_1) = f(x_2) \implies x_1 = x_2$. Surjective: $\forall y \in B, \exists x \in A$ such that $f(x) = y$.

solution_steps.title: Relation to Equipotence
solution_steps.math: A \sim B \iff \exists \text{ a bijection } f: A \to B
solution_steps.explanation: Two sets $A$ and $B$ are said to be equipotent (written $A \sim B$ or $|A| = |B|$) if and only if there exists a bijection from $A$ onto $B$. Equipotence is an equivalence relation on sets.

m1.final_answer: A bijection is an injective and surjective function. Two sets are equipotent if and only if there exists a bijection between them.
m1.exam_tip: Mention that equipotence defines an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: State the Continuum Hypothesis in set theory.
m1.approach: State the Continuum Hypothesis regarding cardinalities between $\aleph_0$ and $c$.

solution_steps.title: Formal Statement
solution_steps.math: \text{There is no set } S \text{ such that } \aleph_0 < |S| < 2^{\aleph_0}
solution_steps.explanation: The Continuum Hypothesis (CH), formulated by Georg Cantor, states that there is no set whose cardinality is strictly between that of the integers $\aleph_0$ and that of the real numbers $c = 2^{\aleph_0}$.

solution_steps.title: Aleph Notation
solution_steps.math: c = 2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_1
solution_steps.explanation: Equivalently, the cardinality of the continuum is the very next cardinal after $\aleph_0$, denoted $\aleph_1$.

m1.final_answer: The Continuum Hypothesis states that there is no cardinality strictly between the cardinality of $\mathbb{N}$ ($\aleph_0$) and the cardinality of $\mathbb{R}$ ($c = 2^{\aleph_0}$).
m1.exam_tip: You can add that Gödel and Cohen proved CH is independent of ZFC set theory (neither provable nor refutable).

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Write the Schröder-Bernstein Theorem.
m1.approach: State the theorem: if each of two sets injects into the other, they are equipotent.

solution_steps.title: Statement of the Theorem
solution_steps.math: \text{If } \exists \text{ injections } f: A \to B \text{ and } g: B \to A, \text{ then } A \sim B
solution_steps.explanation: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. If there exists an injective map from $A$ into $B$ and an injective map from $B$ into $A$, then there exists a bijective map from $A$ onto $B$.

solution_steps.title: Cardinality Interpretation
solution_steps.math: |A| \le |B| \text{ and } |B| \le |A| \implies |A| = |B|
solution_steps.explanation: This establishes that the partial order $\le$ on cardinal numbers is antisymmetric.

m1.final_answer: Schröder-Bernstein Theorem: If $A$ injects into $B$ and $B$ injects into $A$, then $A$ and $B$ are equipotent ($|A| = |B|$).
m1.exam_tip: This theorem is the primary tool used to avoid explicitly constructing complicated bijections (e.g. between $(0,1)$ and $[0,1]$).

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Is the power set of a denumerable set denumerable? Justify.
m1.concept_tested: Cardinality of the Power Set of a Denumerable Set
m1.approach: Apply Cantor's Theorem: $|\mathcal{P}(S)| > |S|$ for any set $S$.

solution_steps.title: Application of Cantor's Theorem
solution_steps.math: S \text{ denumerable} \implies |S| = \aleph_0
solution_steps.explanation: By Cantor's Theorem, for any set $S$, there is no surjection from $S$ onto $\mathcal{P}(S)$, which implies $|\mathcal{P}(S)| > |S|$.

solution_steps.title: Evaluating the Cardinality
solution_steps.math: |\mathcal{P}(S)| = 2^{\aleph_0} = c > \aleph_0
solution_steps.explanation: The power set has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0} = c$, which is the cardinality of the continuum (uncountable).

m1.final_answer: No. By Cantor's Theorem, $|\mathcal{P}(S)| > |S| = \aleph_0$. Thus $\mathcal{P}(S)$ has cardinality $c = 2^{\aleph_0}$, which is uncountably infinite.
m1.exam_tip: Remember: A denumerable set has size $\aleph_0$, but its power set has size $c$ (the continuum).

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Show that the set of irrational numbers is uncountable.
m1.approach: Use proof by contradiction: $\mathbb{R} = \mathbb{Q} \cup (\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q})$.

solution_steps.title: Decomposition of Reals
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{Q} \cup (\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q})
solution_steps.explanation: The real numbers are the disjoint union of the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ and the irrational numbers $\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$.

solution_steps.title: Proof by Contradiction
solution_steps.math: \text{Assume } \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q} \text{ is countable.}
solution_steps.explanation: We know $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable. The union of two countable sets is countable, which would imply $\mathbb{R} = \mathbb{Q} \cup (\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q})$ is countable.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction with Uncountability of $\mathbb{R}$
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{R} \text{ is uncountable } \implies \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q} \text{ must be uncountable.}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable (by Cantor's diagonal theorem), our assumption was false.

m1.final_answer: The set of irrationals $\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$ is uncountable; otherwise, the union $\mathbb{Q} \cup (\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}) = \mathbb{R}$ would be countable, contradicting the uncountability of $\mathbb{R}$.
m1.exam_tip: Cite the theorem: 'The union of two countable sets is countable' to make the proof logically airtight.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Define the power of the continuum.
m1.approach: Define the cardinality $c$ of the continuum $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.explanation: The power of the continuum (denoted by $c$ or $\mathfrak{c}$) is the cardinal number of the set of all real numbers $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Relation to Power Set
solution_steps.math: c = 2^{\aleph_0}
solution_steps.explanation: It equals the cardinality of the power set of the natural numbers $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$, or the set of all infinite sequences of 0s and 1s.

m1.final_answer: The power of the continuum, denoted $c$, is the cardinality of the set of all real numbers $\mathbb{R}$, which is equal to $2^{\aleph_0}$.
m1.exam_tip: Mention that any interval of positive length in $\mathbb{R}$ also has the power of the continuum.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Show that the set of all integers $\mathbb{Z}$ is countable.
m1.approach: Construct an explicit enumeration or bijection between $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$.

solution_steps.title: Enumeration Strategy
solution_steps.explanation: Interleave the positive and negative integers starting with 0.

solution_steps.title: Explicit Formula for Bijection
solution_steps.math: f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}, \quad f(n) = \begin{cases} \frac{n}{2} & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \\ -\frac{n-1}{2} & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: If $n$ is even, $f(n) \in \mathbb{Z}^+$. If $n$ is odd, $f(n) \in \{0, -1, -2, \dots\}$.

solution_steps.title: Injectivity and Surjectivity
solution_steps.math: f(2k) = k \quad \text{and} \quad f(2k+1) = -k \quad (k \ge 0)
solution_steps.explanation: Every integer $z$ has a unique pre-image ($2z$ if $z > 0$, and $-2z+1$ if $z \le 0$). Thus $f$ is a bijection, and $\mathbb{Z}$ is countable.

m1.final_answer: $\mathbb{Z}$ is countable because $f(n) = n/2$ for even $n$ and $-(n-1)/2$ for odd $n$ defines a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ onto $\mathbb{Z}$.
m1.exam_tip: Show both parts of the piecewise function and verify $f(1)=0, f(2)=1, f(3)=-1$.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question:
Define:
  1. A Finite set
  2. A Denumerable set
m1.approach: Give precise mathematical definitions using bijections with standard reference sets $\mathbb{N}_k$ and $\mathbb{N}$.

solution_steps.title: Definition of a Finite Set
solution_steps.math: S \text{ is finite } \iff S = \emptyset \quad \text{or} \quad \exists n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } S \sim \mathbb{N}_n = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}
solution_steps.explanation: A set $S$ is finite if it is either empty or there is a bijection between $S$ and the set of the first $n$ natural numbers for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

solution_steps.title: Definition of a Denumerable Set
solution_steps.math: S \text{ is denumerable } \iff S \sim \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: A set $S$ is denumerable (or countably infinite) if there exists a bijection $f: \mathbb{N} \to S$. Its elements can be arranged in a non-terminating sequence without repetition.

m1.final_answer: (a) A set is finite if it is empty or equipotent to $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$. (b) A set is denumerable if it is equipotent to $\mathbb{N}$.
m1.exam_tip: Always mention the empty set case $\emptyset$ for finite sets to avoid losing half a mark.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Let $A$ be any set. Prove that there is no surjection from $A$ onto the set $\mathcal{P}(A)$ of all subsets of $A$.
m1.concept_tested: Cantor's Theorem on Surjections to Power Sets
m1.approach: Proof by contradiction. Assume a surjection $\phi: A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$ exists and construct the diagonal subset $D = \{x \in A : x \notin \phi(x)\}$.

solution_steps.title: Assumption of Surjection
solution_steps.math: \text{Suppose } \phi: A \to \mathcal{P}(A) \text{ is surjective.}
solution_steps.explanation: This means that for every subset $S \subseteq A$, there exists an element $a \in A$ such that $\phi(a) = S$.

solution_steps.title: Construction of the Cantor Set D
solution_steps.math: D = \{ x \in A : x \notin \phi(x) \}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $D$ is a subset of $A$, $D \in \mathcal{P}(A)$. By surjectivity of $\phi$, there must exist some element $d \in A$ such that $\phi(d) = D$.

solution_steps.title: Deriving the Contradiction
solution_steps.math: d \in D \iff d \notin \phi(d) \iff d \notin D
solution_steps.explanation:
Now we ask whether $d \in D$. If $d \in D$, then by definition of $D$, $d 
otin \phi(d) = D$, a contradiction. If $d 
otin D$, then $d 
otin \phi(d)$, so by definition of $D$, $d \in D$, another contradiction.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \text{No such surjection } \phi \text{ can exist. Hence } |A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|.
solution_steps.explanation: The assumption that $\phi$ is surjective leads to an unavoidable contradiction. Thus no surjection exists.

m1.final_answer: There is no surjection from any set $A$ onto $\mathcal{P}(A)$, proving Cantor's Theorem.
m1.exam_tip: Clearly write the biconditional $d \in D \iff d \notin D$; this self-referential contradiction is the heart of the proof.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Prove that the unit interval $[0, 1]$ is not countable.
m1.approach: Proof by contradiction using Cantor's diagonal argument on decimal/binary expansions.

solution_steps.title: Assumption of Countability
solution_steps.math: \text{Assume } [0, 1] = \{x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots\} \text{ is countable.}
solution_steps.explanation: Every $x_n \in [0, 1]$ can be written as a non-terminating decimal expansion: $x_n = 0.d_{n1}d_{n2}d_{n3}\dots$, where $d_{ni} \in \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}$.

solution_steps.title: Constructing the Missing Real Number
solution_steps.math: y = 0.y_1 y_2 y_3 \dots \quad \text{where } y_n = \begin{cases} 4 & \text{if } d_{nn} \ne 4 \\ 5 & \text{if } d_{nn} = 4 \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: Since all digits $y_n$ are 4 or 5, the decimal expansion of $y$ is unique (it cannot end in trailing 9s or 0s) and $y \in [0, 1]$.

solution_steps.title: Establishing Contradiction
solution_steps.math: \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \; \text{the } n\text{-th digit of } y \text{ differs from the } n\text{-th digit of } x_n \implies y \ne x_n
solution_steps.explanation: Hence $y$ is not in the list $\{x_1, x_2, \dots\}$, contradicting the claim that the list contained all elements of $[0, 1]$.

m1.final_answer: The interval $[0, 1]$ is uncountable because any countable listing misses at least one real number $y \in [0, 1]$.
m1.exam_tip: Explicitly state why choosing digits 4 and 5 avoids the multiple representation issue of decimal expansions.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Prove that the union of two countable sets is countable.
m1.approach: Construct an explicit enumeration or surjection from $\mathbb{N}$ onto $A \cup B$.

solution_steps.title: Enumerating the Sets
solution_steps.explanation: Since $A$ and $B$ are countable, their elements can be listed (if either is finite, we can repeat elements or terminate).

solution_steps.title: Interleaving Map from $\mathbb{N}$
solution_steps.math: h: \mathbb{N} \to A \cup B, \quad h(n) = \begin{cases} a_{(n+1)/2} & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \\ b_{n/2} & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: This lists elements as $a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2, a_3, b_3, \dots$.

solution_steps.title: Surjectivity and Conclusion
solution_steps.math: h(\mathbb{N}) = A \cup B
solution_steps.explanation: Every element of $A \cup B$ is in the range of $h$. Since a set that is the image of a surjection from $\mathbb{N}$ is countable, $A \cup B$ is countable.

m1.final_answer: The union of two countable sets $A$ and $B$ is countable because its elements can be listed by alternating: $a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2, \dots$.
m1.exam_tip: If $A$ and $B$ are not disjoint, duplicate elements can simply be skipped without affecting countability.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Prove that the set of all algebraic numbers is countable.
m1.concept_tested: Countability of the Set of Algebraic Numbers $\mathbb{A}$
m1.approach: Express polynomials of degree $n$ with integer coefficients as countable sets, then take countable unions.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Algebraic Number
solution_steps.math: \alpha \in \mathbb{A} \iff \exists P(x) = a_n x^n + \dots + a_1 x + a_0, \; a_i \in \mathbb{Z}, \; a_n \ne 0 \text{ such that } P(\alpha) = 0
solution_steps.explanation: An algebraic number is a root of a non-zero polynomial with integer coefficients.

solution_steps.title: Countability of Polynomials of Degree n
solution_steps.math: \mathcal{P}_n \sim (\mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}) \times \mathbb{Z}^n
solution_steps.explanation: A polynomial of degree $n$ is uniquely determined by its $n+1$ coefficients $(a_n, a_{n-1}, \dots, a_0) \in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$. Since $\mathbb{Z}$ is countable, the finite product $\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$ is countable.

solution_steps.title: Countability of All Polynomials
solution_steps.math: \mathcal{P} = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \mathcal{P}_n
solution_steps.explanation: The set of all non-zero integer polynomials $\mathcal{P}$ is a countable union of countable sets, so $\mathcal{P}$ is countable.

solution_steps.title: Roots of Polynomials
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{A} = \bigcup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \{x \in \mathbb{C} : P(x) = 0\}
solution_steps.explanation: Each polynomial $P$ of degree $n$ has at most $n$ roots (finite). Thus $\mathbb{A}$ is a countable union of finite sets, which is countable.

m1.final_answer: The set of all algebraic numbers is countable because it is a countable union of finite sets of polynomial roots.
m1.exam_tip: State clearly: finite Cartesian product of countable sets is countable, countable union of countable sets is countable, and degree $n$ has $\le n$ roots.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Show that any subset of a countable set is countable.
m1.approach: Let $S$ be countable and $E \subseteq S$. If $E$ is finite, done; if infinite, construct an explicit subsequence enumeration.

solution_steps.title: Setup
solution_steps.math: S = \{s_1, s_2, s_3, \dots\}, \quad E \subseteq S
solution_steps.explanation: Since $S$ is countable, we can list its elements. If $E$ is finite, it is countable by definition. Assume $E$ is infinite.

solution_steps.title: Inductive Selection of Elements
solution_steps.math: n_1 = \min \{k \in \mathbb{N} : s_k \in E\}, \quad n_{k+1} = \min \{k > n_k : s_k \in E\}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Well-Ordering Principle of $\mathbb{N}$, every non-empty subset of $\mathbb{N}$ has a least element, so $n_k$ is uniquely defined for every $k$.

solution_steps.title: Bijection to $\mathbb{N}$
solution_steps.math: f: \mathbb{N} \to E, \quad f(k) = s_{n_k}
solution_steps.explanation: The sequence $(s_{n_k})$ is an enumeration of $E$ with no repetitions and no omissions. Thus $E \sim \mathbb{N}$.

m1.final_answer: Every subset of a countable set is countable (either finite or denumerable).
m1.exam_tip: Mention the Well-Ordering Principle of $\mathbb{N}$ as the justification for picking the 'first' element at each stage.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Prove that the union of a countable family of countable sets is countable.
m1.approach: Arrange elements in a 2D grid and traverse along diagonals (Cantor's snake / diagonalization).

solution_steps.title: Grid Representation
solution_steps.math: A_m = \{a_{m1}, a_{m2}, a_{m3}, \dots\} \quad \text{for each } m \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Write each countable set $A_m$ as a row in an infinite 2D array.

solution_steps.title: Diagonal Traversal
solution_steps.explanation: Order elements by the sum of indices $m + n = k$, for $k = 2, 3, 4, \dots$. For any fixed $k$, there are only finitely many pairs $(m, n)$.

solution_steps.title: Surjective Mapping
solution_steps.math: f: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \bigcup_{m=1}^\infty A_m, \quad f(m, n) = a_{mn}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ is countable, its image under $f$, which is $\bigcup A_m$, is countable.

m1.final_answer: The union of a countable family of countable sets is countable.
m1.exam_tip: Grouping elements by $m+n=k$ ensures that every element is reached after a finite number of steps.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Show that the set of all rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ is denumerable.
m1.approach: Show that $\mathbb{Q}$ is infinite and that there exists an injection into $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$.

solution_steps.title: Fraction Representation
solution_steps.math: q \in \mathbb{Q} \implies q = \frac{a}{b}, \; a \in \mathbb{Z}, \; b \in \mathbb{N}, \; \gcd(a, b) = 1
solution_steps.explanation: Every rational number has a unique reduced fractional form.

solution_steps.title: Injection into $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$
solution_steps.math: \iota: \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}, \quad \iota(a/b) = (a, b)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\mathbb{Z} \sim \mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N} \sim \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \sim \mathbb{N}$. Thus $\mathbb{Q}$ injects into a denumerable set.

solution_steps.title: Infinitude
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Q} \implies \mathbb{Q} \text{ is infinite}
solution_steps.explanation: An infinite subset of a denumerable set is denumerable. Hence $\mathbb{Q}$ is denumerable.

m1.final_answer: $\mathbb{Q}$ is denumerable (countably infinite).
m1.exam_tip: Clearly show both parts: $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable, and $\mathbb{Q}$ is infinite (since it contains $\mathbb{N}$).

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Show that the open interval $(0, 1)$ is equipotent to $\mathbb{R}$.
m1.approach: Construct an explicit bijection between $(0, 1)$ and $\mathbb{R}$, such as a trigonometric or algebraic function.

solution_steps.title: Candidate Bijection
solution_steps.math: f: (0, 1) \to \mathbb{R}, \quad f(x) = \tan\left(\pi x - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)
solution_steps.explanation: As $x$ ranges from $0$ to $1$, $\theta = \pi x - \pi/2$ ranges from $-\pi/2$ to $\pi/2$, over which tangent is strictly increasing and maps onto $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Algebraic Alternative
solution_steps.math: g(x) = \frac{2x - 1}{x(1 - x)} \quad \text{or} \quad h(x) = \frac{x - 1/2}{x(1-x)}
solution_steps.explanation: Alternatively, a continuous rational function strictly increasing on $(0, 1)$ with vertical asymptotes at $0$ and $1$ maps $(0, 1)$ bijectively onto $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Bijectivity Verification
solution_steps.math: f'(x) = \pi \sec^2(\pi x - \pi/2) > 0 \implies f \text{ is strictly increasing (injective) and surjective.}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ is continuous, strictly increasing, with $\lim_{x\to 0^+} f(x) = -\infty$ and $\lim_{x\to 1^-} f(x) = +\infty$, $f$ is a bijection.

m1.final_answer: $f(x) = \tan(\pi x - \pi/2)$ defines a bijection from $(0, 1)$ onto $\mathbb{R}$, proving $(0, 1) \sim \mathbb{R}$.
m1.exam_tip: The tangent function is the easiest and most memorable bijection to write down in an exam.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Show that the set of all algebraic numbers is countable.
m1.concept_tested: Countability of the Set of Algebraic Numbers $\mathbb{A}$
m1.approach: Express polynomials of degree $n$ with integer coefficients as countable sets, then take countable unions.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Algebraic Number
solution_steps.math: \alpha \in \mathbb{A} \iff \exists P(x) = a_n x^n + \dots + a_1 x + a_0, \; a_i \in \mathbb{Z}, \; a_n \ne 0 \text{ such that } P(\alpha) = 0
solution_steps.explanation: An algebraic number is a root of a non-zero polynomial with integer coefficients.

solution_steps.title: Countability of Polynomials of Degree n
solution_steps.math: \mathcal{P}_n \sim (\mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}) \times \mathbb{Z}^n
solution_steps.explanation: A polynomial of degree $n$ is uniquely determined by its $n+1$ coefficients $(a_n, a_{n-1}, \dots, a_0) \in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$. Since $\mathbb{Z}$ is countable, the finite product $\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$ is countable.

solution_steps.title: Countability of All Polynomials
solution_steps.math: \mathcal{P} = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \mathcal{P}_n
solution_steps.explanation: The set of all non-zero integer polynomials $\mathcal{P}$ is a countable union of countable sets, so $\mathcal{P}$ is countable.

solution_steps.title: Roots of Polynomials
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{A} = \bigcup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \{x \in \mathbb{C} : P(x) = 0\}
solution_steps.explanation: Each polynomial $P$ of degree $n$ has at most $n$ roots (finite). Thus $\mathbb{A}$ is a countable union of finite sets, which is countable.

m1.final_answer: The set of all algebraic numbers is countable because it is a countable union of finite sets of polynomial roots.
m1.exam_tip: State clearly: finite Cartesian product of countable sets is countable, countable union of countable sets is countable, and degree $n$ has $\le n$ roots.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Prove that the set of all transcendental numbers is uncountable.
m1.approach: Use $\mathbb{R} = \mathbb{A} \cup \mathbb{T}$, where $\mathbb{A}$ is the set of algebraic numbers and $\mathbb{T}$ is the set of transcendental numbers.

solution_steps.title: Partition of Real Numbers
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{R} \cup \mathbb{T}
solution_steps.explanation: Every real number is either algebraic or transcendental (by definition, a transcendental number is a real number that is not algebraic).

solution_steps.title: Known Cardinalities
solution_steps.math: |\mathbb{R}| = c \text{ (uncountable)}, \quad |\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{R}| \le |\mathbb{A}| = \aleph_0 \text{ (countable)}
solution_steps.explanation: The set of algebraic numbers $\mathbb{A}$ is countable (roots of integer polynomials).

solution_steps.title: Contradiction
solution_steps.math: \text{If } \mathbb{T} \text{ were countable, then } \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{R} \cup \mathbb{T} \text{ would be countable.}
solution_steps.explanation: Since the union of two countable sets is countable, this contradicts the uncountability of $\mathbb{R}$.

m1.final_answer: The set of transcendental numbers $\mathbb{T}$ is uncountable.
m1.exam_tip: Mention Cantor's brilliant insight: almost all real numbers are transcendental, even though constructing specific ones (like $e$ or $\pi$) is difficult.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Show that the Cartesian product $A \times B$ of two countable sets $A$ and $B$ is countable.
m1.approach: Show that $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ is countable, then use injections.

solution_steps.title: Enumeration of A and B
solution_steps.math: A = \{a_1, a_2, \dots\}, \quad B = \{b_1, b_2, \dots\}
solution_steps.explanation: There exist surjections $f: \mathbb{N} \to A$ and $g: \mathbb{N} \to B$.

solution_steps.title: Countability of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$
solution_steps.math: \phi(m, n) = 2^m 3^n \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{(m+n-1)(m+n-2)}{2} + m
solution_steps.explanation: The map $\phi(m, n) = 2^m 3^n$ is injective by the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (unique prime factorization). Thus $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ is countable.

solution_steps.title: Mapping onto $A \times B$
solution_steps.math: h(m, n) = (f(m), g(n)) \text{ maps } \mathbb{N} \\times \\mathbb{N} \text{ surjectively onto } A \times B
solution_steps.explanation: Since the domain $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ is countable and $h$ is surjective, $A \times B$ is countable.

m1.final_answer: The Cartesian product $A \times B$ of two countable sets is countable.
m1.exam_tip: Using the prime powers map $\phi(m, n) = 2^m 3^n$ is the quickest, most elegant proof of injectivity.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Use Schröder-Bernstein Theorem to prove that $[0, 1]$ and $(0, 1)$ have the same cardinality.
m1.approach: Construct injections in both directions: $f: (0, 1) 	o [0, 1]$ and $g: [0, 1] 	o (0, 1)$.

solution_steps.title: First Injection: $(0, 1) \to [0, 1]$
solution_steps.explanation: The inclusion map $f(x) = x$ is an injection since $(0, 1) \subset [0, 1]$.

solution_steps.title: Second Injection: $[0, 1] \to (0, 1]$
solution_steps.explanation: When $x=0$, $g(0) = 1/4 \in (0, 1)$. When $x=1$, $g(1) = 3/4 \in (0, 1)$. For all $x \in [0, 1]$, $g(x) \in [1/4, 3/4] \subset (0, 1)$. Since $g$ is linear with non-zero slope, $g$ is injective.

solution_steps.title: Application of Schröder-Bernstein Theorem
solution_steps.math: f \text{ injective and } g \text{ injective} \implies |(0, 1)| \le |[0, 1]| \text{ and } |[0, 1]| \le |(0, 1)| \implies (0, 1) \sim [0, 1]
solution_steps.explanation: By the Schröder-Bernstein Theorem, mutual injections imply the existence of a bijection.

m1.final_answer: $[0, 1] \sim (0, 1)$ by Schröder-Bernstein via the inclusion map $f(x) = x$ and the scaled map $g(x) = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2}x$.
m1.exam_tip: Any linear contraction like $g(x) = (x+1)/3$ works equally well to map $[0, 1]$ strictly into $(0, 1)$.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Prove that the set of all finite sequences of 0s and 1s is countable.
m1.concept_tested: Countability of Finite Sequences of 0s and 1s
m1.approach: Represent finite sequences of length $n$ as $S_n = \{0, 1\}^n$, and write the total set as $S = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty S_n$.

solution_steps.title: Decomposition by Length
solution_steps.math: S_n = \{ (x_1, \dots, x_n) : x_i \in \{0, 1\} \}, \quad S = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty S_n
solution_steps.explanation: $S_n$ is the set of all binary sequences of fixed length $n$.

solution_steps.title: Finiteness of Each Level
solution_steps.math: |S_n| = 2^n < \infty
solution_steps.explanation: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $S_n$ is a finite set having exactly $2^n$ elements.

solution_steps.title: Countable Union of Finite Sets
solution_steps.math: S = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty S_n \implies S \text{ is countable}
solution_steps.explanation: A countable union of finite sets is always countable.

m1.final_answer: The set of all finite binary sequences is countable as it is a countable union of finite sets $\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \{0, 1\}^n$.
m1.exam_tip: Distinguish carefully between FINITE sequences (countable) and INFINITE sequences (uncountable).

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Prove that the set of all functions from $\mathbb{Z}^+$ to $\{0, 1\}$ is uncountable.
m1.approach: Use the bijection with the power set $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{Z}^+)$ and apply Cantor's Theorem.

solution_steps.title: Bijection with Power Set
solution_steps.math: \mathcal{F} = \{f : \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \{0, 1\}\} \longleftrightarrow \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{Z}^+)
solution_steps.explanation: Every function $f$ corresponds uniquely to a subset $A_f = \{n \in \mathbb{Z}^+ : f(n) = 1\}$ (its characteristic function).

solution_steps.title: Applying Cantor's Theorem
solution_steps.math: |\mathcal{F}| = |\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{Z}^+)| = 2^{\aleph_0} = c
solution_steps.explanation: Cantor's Theorem states that $|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|$ for any set $A$. Therefore, $|\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{Z}^+)| > |\mathbb{Z}^+| = \aleph_0$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: |\mathcal{F}| = 2^{\aleph_0} > \aleph_0 \implies \mathcal{F} \text{ is uncountable.}
solution_steps.explanation: Since its cardinality is strictly greater than $\aleph_0$, the set of functions is uncountable.

m1.final_answer: The set of all functions from $\mathbb{Z}^+$ to $\{0, 1\}$ is uncountable because it is equipotent to $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{Z}^+)$, which has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$.
m1.exam_tip: You can also prove this directly via diagonal argument: if $f_1, f_2, \dots$ were an enumeration, define $g(n) = 1 - f_n(n)$.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Prove that the set of all open intervals in $\mathbb{R}$ with rational endpoints is countable.
m1.concept_tested: Countability of Open Intervals with Rational Endpoints
m1.approach: Establish an injection into $\mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}$.

solution_steps.title: Set Definition
solution_steps.math: \mathcal{I} = \{ (a, b) : a, b \in \mathbb{Q}, \; a < b \}
solution_steps.explanation: Each such interval is uniquely identified by an ordered pair of rational numbers $(a, b)$.

solution_steps.title: Injection into $\mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}$
solution_steps.math: \Phi: \mathcal{I} \to \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}, \quad \Phi((a, b)) = (a, b)
solution_steps.explanation: $\Phi$ is clearly an injection (intervals with the same endpoints are identical).

solution_steps.title: Countability of Product
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{Q} \text{ countable} \implies \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q} \text{ is countable.}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\mathcal{I}$ injects into a countable set, $\mathcal{I}$ is countable.

m1.final_answer: The set of all open intervals with rational endpoints is countable because it injects into $\mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}$.
m1.exam_tip: This result is crucial in topology: it proves that $\mathbb{R}$ has a countable base for its standard topology (second countable).

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Prove that the set of all polynomial functions with rational coefficients is countable.
m1.concept_tested: Countability of Polynomials with Rational Coefficients $\mathbb{Q}[x]$
m1.approach: Express $\mathbb{Q}[x] = \bigcup_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb{Q}_n[x]$, where $\mathbb{Q}_n[x]$ is the set of polynomials of degree at most $n$.

solution_steps.title: Polynomials of Bounded Degree
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{Q}_n[x] = \{ a_n x^n + \dots + a_1 x + a_0 : a_i \in \mathbb{Q} \}
solution_steps.explanation: Each polynomial in $\mathbb{Q}_n[x]$ is uniquely defined by its tuple of coefficients $(a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n) \in \mathbb{Q}^{n+1}$.

solution_steps.title: Countability of Tuples
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{Q}_n[x] \sim \mathbb{Q}^{n+1}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable, the finite Cartesian product $\mathbb{Q}^{n+1}$ is countable.

solution_steps.title: Countable Union
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{Q}[x] = \bigcup_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb{Q}_n[x]
solution_steps.explanation: $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ is a countable union of countable sets, hence $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ is countable.

m1.final_answer: The set of all polynomials with rational coefficients is countable.
m1.exam_tip: State: $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ is a countable union of the countable sets $\mathbb{Q}^{n+1}$.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Prove that if $A$ is equipotent to $B$ and $B$ is equipotent to $C$, then $A$ is equipotent to $C$.
m1.approach: Use the composition of two bijections.

solution_steps.title: Hypotheses
solution_steps.math: A \sim B \implies \exists \text{ bijection } f: A \to B; \quad B \sim C \implies \exists \text{ bijection } g: B \to C
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of equipotence, there exist one-to-one and onto functions $f$ and $g$.

solution_steps.title: Composition Map
solution_steps.math: h = g \circ f : A \to C, \quad h(a) = g(f(a))
solution_steps.explanation: The composition of two injective functions is injective, and the composition of two surjective functions is surjective.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: h \text{ is a bijection from } A \text{ onto } C \implies A \sim C
solution_steps.explanation: Thus equipotence is a transitive relation.

m1.final_answer: If $A \sim B$ and $B \sim C$, the composite function $g \circ f: A \to C$ is a bijection, proving $A \sim C$.
m1.exam_tip: Show injectivity: $(g \circ f)(x) = (g \circ f)(y) \implies g(f(x)) = g(f(y)) \implies f(x) = f(y) \implies x = y$.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question:
Suppose that $S$ and $T$ are sets and that $T \subseteq S$. Prove that:
  1. If $S$ is a finite set, then $T$ is a finite set.
  2. If $T$ is an infinite set, then $S$ is an infinite set.
m1.concept_tested: Subsets of Finite and Infinite Sets
m1.approach: Prove (a) via induction or contradiction, and prove (b) as the contrapositive of (a).

solution_steps.title: Proof of Part (a)
solution_steps.math: S \text{ is finite } \implies \exists \text{ bijection } f: S \to \{1, 2, \dots, n\}
solution_steps.explanation: Let $T \subseteq S$. The restriction of $f$ to $T$ is an injection into $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. Any subset of a finite set is finite, so $T$ is finite.

solution_steps.title: Proof of Part (b)
solution_steps.math: T \text{ is infinite } \implies S \text{ is infinite}
solution_steps.explanation: Statement (b) is the exact logical contrapositive of statement (a): if $S$ were finite, then by part (a), $T$ would have to be finite, which contradicts the hypothesis that $T$ is infinite. Hence $S$ must be infinite.

m1.final_answer: (a) A subset of a finite set is finite. (b) If a subset $T$ is infinite, the superset $S$ must be infinite (contrapositive of a).
m1.exam_tip: Use the word 'contrapositive' explicitly in part (b) — it shows mathematical maturity and guarantees full marks.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: State and prove Cantor's Theorem (there is no surjection from a set $A$ onto its power set $\mathcal{P}(A)$).
m1.concept_tested: Cantor's Theorem on Surjections to Power Sets
m1.approach: Proof by contradiction. Assume a surjection $\phi: A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$ exists and construct the diagonal subset $D = \{x \in A : x \notin \phi(x)\}$.

solution_steps.title: Assumption of Surjection
solution_steps.math: \text{Suppose } \phi: A \to \mathcal{P}(A) \text{ is surjective.}
solution_steps.explanation: This means that for every subset $S \subseteq A$, there exists an element $a \in A$ such that $\phi(a) = S$.

solution_steps.title: Construction of the Cantor Set D
solution_steps.math: D = \{ x \in A : x \notin \phi(x) \}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $D$ is a subset of $A$, $D \in \mathcal{P}(A)$. By surjectivity of $\phi$, there must exist some element $d \in A$ such that $\phi(d) = D$.

solution_steps.title: Deriving the Contradiction
solution_steps.math: d \in D \iff d \notin \phi(d) \iff d \notin D
solution_steps.explanation:
Now we ask whether $d \in D$. If $d \in D$, then by definition of $D$, $d 
otin \phi(d) = D$, a contradiction. If $d 
otin D$, then $d 
otin \phi(d)$, so by definition of $D$, $d \in D$, another contradiction.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \text{No such surjection } \phi \text{ can exist. Hence } |A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|.
solution_steps.explanation: The assumption that $\phi$ is surjective leads to an unavoidable contradiction. Thus no surjection exists.

m1.final_answer: There is no surjection from any set $A$ onto $\mathcal{P}(A)$, proving Cantor's Theorem.
m1.exam_tip: Clearly write the biconditional $d \in D \iff d \notin D$; this self-referential contradiction is the heart of the proof.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question:
Prove that the following statements are equivalent for a set $S$:
  1. $S$ is a countable set.
  2. There exists a surjection of $\mathbb{N}$ onto $S$.
  3. There exists an injection of $S$ into $\mathbb{N}$.
m1.approach: Prove the cyclic implications (a) => (b) => (c) => (a).

solution_steps.title: (a) implies (b): Countable => Surjection from N
solution_steps.math: \text{If } S \text{ is finite with } n \text{ elements, } f(k) = s_k \text{ for } k \le n \text{ and } f(k) = s_1 \text{ for } k > n.
solution_steps.explanation: If $S$ is denumerable, a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ to $S$ already exists. If $S$ is finite and non-empty, say $S = \{s_1, \dots, s_n\}$, define $f(k) = s_k$ for $1 \le k \le n$ and $f(k) = s_1$ for $k > n$. Then $f: \mathbb{N} 	o S$ is surjective.

solution_steps.title: (b) implies (c): Surjection from N => Injection into N
solution_steps.math: g: S \to \mathbb{N}, \quad g(s) = \min \{ k \in \mathbb{N} : f(k) = s \}
solution_steps.explanation:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} 	o S$ be surjective. For each $s \in S$, the set $f^{-1}(\{s\})$ is a non-empty subset of $\mathbb{N}$. By the Well-Ordering Principle of $\mathbb{N}$, it has a unique least element $g(s)$. If $s 
e t$, then $f^{-1}(\{s\}) \cap f^{-1}(\{t\}) = \emptyset$, so $g(s) 
e g(t)$. Thus $g$ is injective.

solution_steps.title: (c) implies (a): Injection into N => Countable
solution_steps.math: g: S \to \mathbb{N} \text{ injective} \implies S \sim g(S) \subseteq \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $g$ is an injection, $S$ is equipotent to the subset $g(S)$ of $\mathbb{N}$. Since every subset of $\mathbb{N}$ is countable (finite or denumerable), $S$ must be countable.

m1.final_answer: The cyclic chain of implications (a) => (b) => (c) => (a) is established, proving that all three characterizations of countability are equivalent.
m1.exam_tip: Clearly mention the Well-Ordering Principle of $\mathbb{N}$ when defining $g(s) = \min f^{-1}(\{s\})$ in (b) => (c).

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: If $A_m$ is a countable set for each $m \in \mathbb{N}$, prove that the union $A = \bigcup_{m=1}^\infty A_m$ is countable. State and prove Bernoulli's inequality.
m1.concept_tested: Countable Union of Countable Sets & Bernoulli's Inequality
m1.approach: Part 1: Diagonal array enumeration for countable union. Part 2: Induction proof of $(1+x)^n \ge 1 + nx$ for $x > -1$.

solution_steps.title: Part 1: Countable Union of Countable Sets
solution_steps.math: A_m = \{a_{m1}, a_{m2}, a_{m3}, \dots\} \quad (m \in \mathbb{N})
solution_steps.explanation: Arrange the elements of $A =  igcup_{m=1}^\infty A_m$ in an infinite array where the $m$-th row lists $A_m$.

solution_steps.title: Surjection from N x N
solution_steps.math: h: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to A, \quad h(m, n) = a_{mn}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\mathbb{N} 	imes \mathbb{N}$ is countable (by Cantor's diagonal pairing or $2^m 3^n$) and $h$ is surjective, the range $A$ is countable.

solution_steps.title: Part 2: Bernoulli's Inequality Statement
solution_steps.math: \forall x > -1 \text{ and } \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \quad (1 + x)^n \ge 1 + nx
solution_steps.explanation: We prove this fundamental inequality by mathematical induction on $n$.

solution_steps.title: Base Case and Inductive Step
solution_steps.math: (1+x)^1 = 1+x \ge 1+1\cdot x. \quad \text{Assume } (1+x)^k \ge 1 + kx.
solution_steps.explanation: Multiply both sides by $(1+x) > 0$: $(1+x)^{k+1} \ge (1 + kx)(1 + x) = 1 + (k+1)x + kx^2$. Since $kx^2 \ge 0$, we have $(1+x)^{k+1} \ge 1 + (k+1)x$. By induction, it holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

m1.final_answer: (1) A countable union of countable sets is countable by diagonal traversal of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$. (2) Bernoulli's Inequality $(1+x)^n \ge 1+nx$ holds for all $x > -1, n \in \mathbb{N}$ by induction.
m1.exam_tip: In Bernoulli's inequality, stress that $1 + x > 0$ is essential so that multiplying the inequality does not reverse its direction.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Prove that the set of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable.
m1.approach: Prove that $(0, 1)$ is uncountable using Cantor's diagonal argument, then conclude $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable since $(0, 1) \subset \mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Reduction to the Open Interval (0, 1)
solution_steps.math: (0, 1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: If $\mathbb{R}$ were countable, every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ would be countable, so it suffices to show that $(0, 1)$ is uncountable.

solution_steps.title: Hypothesis of Countability
solution_steps.explanation: Assume $(0, 1)$ can be completely listed. Write each $x_n$ in non-terminating decimal form: $x_n = 0.d_{n1} d_{n2} d_{n3} \dots$.

solution_steps.title: Cantor Diagonal Construction
solution_steps.math: z = 0.z_1 z_2 z_3 \dots \quad \text{where } z_n = \begin{cases} 2 & \text{if } d_{nn} \ne 2 \\ 7 & \text{if } d_{nn} = 2 \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: The number $z$ belongs to $(0, 1)$ because $0 < z < 1$ and contains only digits 2 and 7 (avoiding trailing 0s or 9s, ensuring uniqueness).

solution_steps.title: Contradiction
solution_steps.math: \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \; z \ne x_n \implies z \notin \{x_1, x_2, \dots\}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $z$ differs from $x_n$ in the $n$-th decimal place, $z$ cannot be in the list, contradicting the assumption that the list was exhaustive. Hence $(0, 1)$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are uncountable.

m1.final_answer: $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable because its subset $(0, 1)$ cannot be enumerated by any sequence (Cantor's diagonal theorem).
m1.exam_tip: Clearly show the two-step logic: (1) $(0, 1)$ is uncountable, (2) a superset of an uncountable set must be uncountable.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: State and prove Cantor's Theorem. Show that the set of all real numbers in $[0, 1]$ is uncountable.
m1.approach: Part 1: Prove $|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|$ using $D = \{x : x \notin f(x)\}$. Part 2: Show $[0, 1]$ is uncountable via binary representation equipotent to $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$.

solution_steps.title: Statement and Proof of Cantor's Theorem
solution_steps.math: \text{Let } f: A \to \mathcal{P}(A). \quad D = \{x \in A : x \notin f(x)\}.
solution_steps.explanation:
If $f$ were surjective, there would exist $d \in A$ such that $f(d) = D$. Then $d \in D \iff d 
otin f(d) = D$, a contradiction. Thus no surjection exists, proving $|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|$.

solution_steps.title: Power Set of N is Uncountable
solution_steps.math: |\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})| > |\mathbb{N}| = \aleph_0 \implies \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}) \text{ is uncountable.}
solution_steps.explanation: Applying Cantor's Theorem to $A = \mathbb{N}$ establishes that $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ is uncountably infinite.

solution_steps.title: Equipotence of $[0, 1]$ to $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$
solution_steps.math: [0, 1] \sim \{0, 1\}^\mathbb{N} \sim \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})
solution_steps.explanation: Every subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ corresponds to an infinite binary sequence $(a_n)$ where $a_n = 1$ if $n \in S$ and $0$ otherwise. This maps to the real number $\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n 2^{-n} \in [0, 1]$. Hence $[0, 1]$ has cardinality $2^{leph_0}$, which is uncountable.

m1.final_answer: Cantor's Theorem proves no set can be mapped surjectively onto its power set. Consequently, $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ and the interval $[0, 1] \sim \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ are uncountable.
m1.exam_tip: Connecting $[0, 1]$ to binary expansions makes this proof directly flow from Cantor's power set theorem.

m1.topic: Topic 1: Countable & Uncountable Sets & Cantor's Theorem
m1.question: Discuss the cardinality of the Cantor set and show that it is uncountable despite having measure zero.
m1.concept_tested: The Cantor Middle-Thirds Set: Uncountable with Measure Zero
m1.approach: Define the Cantor ternary set $C = \bigcap C_n$, compute its Lebesgue measure (0), and prove its uncountability via ternary expansions without 1s.

solution_steps.title: Construction of the Cantor Set
solution_steps.math: C_0 = [0, 1], \quad C_1 = [0, 1/3] \cup [2/3, 1], \quad C = \bigcap_{n=0}^\infty C_n
solution_steps.explanation: At each stage $n$, we remove the open middle third of each of the $2^{n-1}$ remaining intervals.

solution_steps.title: Proof of Measure Zero
solution_steps.math: \text{Total length removed} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty 2^{k-1} \left(\frac{1}{3^k}\right) = \frac{1}{3} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k = \frac{1/3}{1 - 2/3} = 1
solution_steps.explanation: The total length of the intervals removed from $[0, 1]$ equals 1. Therefore, the remaining set $C$ has Lebesgue measure $m(C) = 1 - 1 = 0$.

solution_steps.title: Ternary Expansion Characterization
solution_steps.math: x \in C \iff x = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{a_k}{3^k}, \quad a_k \in \{0, 2\}
solution_steps.explanation: A real number in $[0, 1]$ belongs to the Cantor set if and only if it has a base-3 (ternary) expansion consisting exclusively of the digits 0 and 2.

solution_steps.title: Bijection to $\{0, 1\}^\mathbb{N}$ (Uncountability)
solution_steps.math: f: C \to [0, 1], \quad f\left(\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{a_k}{3^k}\right) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{a_k/2}{2^k}
solution_steps.explanation: Replacing each digit 2 with 1 yields a surjection from $C$ onto $[0, 1]$ (the Cantor-Lebesgue function). Since it surjects onto the uncountable set $[0, 1]$, $C$ itself must be uncountable, with cardinality $c = 2^{leph_0}$.

m1.final_answer: The Cantor set has measure zero because the total length removed is $\sum 2^{k-1}/3^k = 1$, yet it is uncountably infinite because its points bijectively correspond to infinite binary sequences $\{0, 2\}^\mathbb{N}$ (cardinality $c$).
m1.exam_tip: Show both: (1) geometric series summation for measure = 0, (2) ternary expansions with digits $\{0, 2\}$ for uncountability.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Prove that there does not exist a rational number $r$ such that $r^2 = 2$.
m2.approach: Proof by contradiction using parity of integers in lowest terms fraction $p/q$.

solution_steps.title: Assumption for Contradiction
solution_steps.math: r = \frac{p}{q}, \quad p, q \in \mathbb{Z}, \, q \ne 0, \, \gcd(p, q) = 1, \quad r^2 = 2
solution_steps.explanation: Assume there exists a rational number $r$ such that $r^2 = 2$ in lowest terms.

solution_steps.title: Algebraic Deduction
solution_steps.math: p^2 = 2q^2 \implies p^2 \text{ is even} \implies p = 2k \text{ for some } k \in \mathbb{Z}
solution_steps.explanation: Since the square of an odd number is odd, $p$ must be even.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction on Common Factor
solution_steps.math: (2k)^2 = 2q^2 \implies 4k^2 = 2q^2 \implies q^2 = 2k^2 \implies q \text{ is even}
solution_steps.explanation: Both $p$ and $q$ are divisible by 2, contradicting $\gcd(p, q) = 1$.

m2.final_answer: There is no rational number $r$ such that $r^2 = 2$, i.e., $\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$.
m2.exam_tip: State clearly that if $p^2$ is even, then $p$ is even, citing Euclid's lemma or parity.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Determine the set $A$ of $x \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $2x + 3 \le 7$.
m2.approach: Use algebraic properties of ordered fields to isolate $x$.

solution_steps.title: Subtract 3 from both sides
solution_steps.math: 2x + 3 \le 7 \implies 2x \le 7 - 3 = 4
solution_steps.explanation: Adding $-3$ to both sides preserves the inequality.

solution_steps.title: Divide by positive scalar 2
solution_steps.math: 2x \le 4 \implies x \le 2
solution_steps.explanation: Multiplying by $1/2 > 0$ preserves the inequality direction.

m2.final_answer: The solution set is $A = (-\infty, 2] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \le 2\}$.
m2.exam_tip: Express the answer in both set-builder and interval notation.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: If $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, prove that $|a + b| \le |a| + |b|$.
m2.approach: Use $-|a| \le a \le |a|$ and add inequalities, or square both sides.

solution_steps.title: Basic Absolute Value Bounds
solution_steps.math: -|a| \le a \le |a| \quad \text{and} \quad -|b| \le b \le |b|
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of absolute value, any real number lies between $-|x|$ and $|x|$.

solution_steps.title: Summing Inequalities
solution_steps.explanation: Adding the corresponding inequalities yields bounds on $a+b$.

solution_steps.title: Equivalence to Absolute Value Bound
solution_steps.math: -M \le x \le M \iff |x| \le M \implies |a + b| \le |a| + |b|
solution_steps.explanation: Setting $M = |a| + |b|$ completes the proof.

m2.final_answer: $|a + b| \le |a| + |b|$ for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.
m2.exam_tip: The theorem $-c \le x \le c \iff |x| \le c$ is the cleanest route to prove the triangle inequality.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: State the supremum property of $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.approach: State the standard axiom asserting that non-empty bounded-above subsets possess a least upper bound in $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Formal Statement
solution_steps.math: \forall S \subseteq \mathbb{R}, \; (S \ne \emptyset \land \exists M \in \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } s \le M \; \forall s \in S) \implies \exists \sup S \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Every non-empty subset of real numbers that is bounded above has a supremum (least upper bound) in $\mathbb{R}$.

m2.final_answer: The Supremum Property states that every non-empty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.exam_tip: Do not forget the conditions: (1) non-empty, and (2) bounded above.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: If $S = \{\frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{m} \mid n, m \in \mathbb{N}\}$, find $\inf S$ and $\sup S$.
m2.concept_tested: Infimum and Supremum of a Two-Parameter Set
m2.approach: Analyze bounds as $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$ vary independently.

solution_steps.title: Bounding Elements
solution_steps.math: 0 < \frac{1}{n} \le 1, \quad 0 < \frac{1}{m} \le 1 \implies -1 < \frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{m} < 1
solution_steps.explanation: Since $1/n, 1/m \in (0, 1]$, their difference is strictly between $-1$ and $1$.

solution_steps.title: Finding Supremum
solution_steps.math: \sup S = 1
solution_steps.explanation: Choose $n = 1$: $1 - 1/m \in S$. As $m \to \infty$, $1 - 1/m \to 1$. Since $1/n - 1/m < 1$ for all $n, m$, $\sup S = 1$ (not attained).

solution_steps.title: Finding Infimum
solution_steps.math: \inf S = -1
solution_steps.explanation: Choose $m = 1$: $1/n - 1 \in S$. As $n \to \infty$, $1/n - 1 \to -1$. Since $1/n - 1/m > -1$ for all $n, m$, $\inf S = -1$ (not attained).

m2.final_answer: $\sup S = 1$ and $\inf S = -1$.
m2.exam_tip: Notice that neither 1 nor -1 belongs to $S$, so maximum and minimum do not exist.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: State and prove the Archimedean property of $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.approach: State property and prove by contradiction using the Completeness Property.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \; \exists n_x \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n_x > x
solution_steps.explanation: The set of natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ is not bounded above in $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Proof by Contradiction
solution_steps.math: \text{Assume } \mathbb{N} \text{ is bounded above} \implies u = \sup \mathbb{N} \in \mathbb{R} \text{ exists}
solution_steps.explanation: By completeness, since $\mathbb{N} \ne \emptyset$ is bounded above, it has a supremum $u$.

solution_steps.title: Deriving Contradiction
solution_steps.math: u - 1 < u \implies \exists m \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } m > u - 1 \implies m + 1 > u
solution_steps.explanation: Since $m \in \mathbb{N}$, $m + 1 \in \mathbb{N}$. But $m + 1 > u$, contradicting that $u$ is an upper bound of $\mathbb{N}$.

m2.final_answer: The Archimedean property asserts $\mathbb{N}$ is unbounded above in $\mathbb{R}$. It follows directly from the completeness of $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.exam_tip: Showing $m+1 > u$ where $m+1 \in \mathbb{N}$ is the key step to refute $u = \sup \mathbb{N}$.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers with $x < y$. Prove that there exists an irrational number $z$ such that $x < z < y$.
m2.approach: Apply the Density Theorem of rationals to shifted/scaled numbers by $\sqrt{2}$.

solution_steps.title: Scale by $\sqrt{2}$
solution_steps.math: x < y \implies \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\sqrt{2} > 0$, dividing preserves strict inequality.

solution_steps.title: Apply Density of Rationals
solution_steps.math: \exists r \in \mathbb{Q}, \, r \ne 0 \text{ such that } \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < r < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}
solution_steps.explanation: Between any two distinct real numbers there exists a non-zero rational number $r$.

solution_steps.title: Multiply back by $\sqrt{2}$
solution_steps.math: x < r\sqrt{2} < y
solution_steps.explanation: Let $z = r\sqrt{2}$. Since $r \in \mathbb{Q} \setminus \{0\}$ and $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, $z$ is irrational.

m2.final_answer: There exists an irrational $z = r\sqrt{2}$ strictly between $x$ and $y$.
m2.exam_tip: Ensure $r \ne 0$ so that $z = r\sqrt{2} \ne 0$ is guaranteed to be irrational.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$. Prove that $a \cdot 0 = 0$.
m2.concept_tested: Field Axioms of $\mathbb{R}$: Uniqueness and Zero Multiplication
m2.approach: Use the distributive law and additive identity property $0 + 0 = 0$.

solution_steps.title: Identity Property of 0
solution_steps.explanation: 0 is the additive identity.

solution_steps.title: Distributive Law
solution_steps.math: a \cdot 0 = a \cdot (0 + 0) = a \cdot 0 + a \cdot 0
solution_steps.explanation: Apply distributivity of multiplication over addition.

solution_steps.title: Cancel $a \cdot 0$
solution_steps.math: a \cdot 0 + (-(a \cdot 0)) = (a \cdot 0 + a \cdot 0) + (-(a \cdot 0)) \implies 0 = a \cdot 0
solution_steps.explanation: Adding the additive inverse $-(a \cdot 0)$ to both sides gives $a \cdot 0 = 0$.

m2.final_answer: $a \cdot 0 = 0$ for all $a \in \mathbb{R}$.
m2.exam_tip: Never write 'anything times zero is zero' without deriving it from field axioms.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ne 0$. Prove that $a^2 > 0$.
m2.approach: Use trichotomy: either $a > 0$ or $-a > 0$, and positivity is closed under multiplication.

solution_steps.title: Trichotomy Property
solution_steps.math: a \ne 0 \implies a \in P \quad \text{or} \quad -a \in P
solution_steps.explanation: where $P$ is the set of strictly positive real numbers.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: $a \in P$
solution_steps.math: a \in P \implies a^2 = a \cdot a \in P \implies a^2 > 0
solution_steps.explanation: $P$ is closed under multiplication.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: $-a \in P$
solution_steps.math: -a \in P \implies (-a) \cdot (-a) \in P \implies a^2 \in P \implies a^2 > 0
solution_steps.explanation: Since $(-a)(-a) = a^2$ by field properties, $a^2 > 0$ in both cases.

m2.final_answer: If $a \ne 0$, then $a^2 > 0$.
m2.exam_tip: Mention that this implies $1 = 1^2 > 0$.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Let $x, y$ belong to the $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $a, b$. Prove that $x+y$ belongs to the $2\epsilon$-neighborhood of $a+b$.
m2.approach: Express membership in $V_\epsilon(c)$ as $|x - c| < \epsilon$ and add deviations.

solution_steps.title: Neighborhood Characterization
solution_steps.math: x \in V_\epsilon(a) \iff |x - a| < \epsilon, \quad y \in V_\epsilon(b) \iff |y - b| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Definition of $\epsilon$-neighborhoods.

solution_steps.title: Apply Triangle Inequality
solution_steps.math: |(x + y) - (a + b)| = |(x - a) + (y - b)| \le |x - a| + |y - b| < \epsilon + \epsilon = 2\epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Group terms and apply $|u + v| \le |u| + |v|$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: |(x + y) - (a + b)| < 2\epsilon \iff x + y \in V_{2\epsilon}(a + b)
solution_steps.explanation: Hence $x+y$ is within distance $2\epsilon$ of $a+b$.

m2.final_answer: $x+y \in V_{2\epsilon}(a+b)$.
m2.exam_tip: Always re-group $(x+y) - (a+b)$ as $(x-a) + (y-b)$.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Prove that an upper bound $u$ of a non-empty set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is the supremum of $S$ if and only if for every $\epsilon > 0$ there exists an $s_\epsilon \in S$ such that $u - \epsilon < s_\epsilon$.
m2.approach: Prove both directions: $u$ is least upper bound $\iff$ no smaller number is an upper bound.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction ($\implies$)
solution_steps.math: u = \sup S, \; \epsilon > 0 \implies u - \epsilon < u
solution_steps.explanation: Since $u - \epsilon < u$, $u - \epsilon$ cannot be an upper bound for $S$. Thus there exists $s_\epsilon \in S$ such that $s_\epsilon > u - \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction ($\impliedby$)
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists s_\epsilon \in S \text{ s.t. } u - \epsilon < s_\epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Let $v < u$. Choose $\epsilon = u - v > 0$. Then $\exists s_\epsilon \in S$ with $s_\epsilon > u - (u - v) = v$. Hence $v$ is not an upper bound. Since $u$ is an upper bound and no smaller $v$ is, $u = \sup S$.

m2.final_answer: $u = \sup S \iff (\forall s \in S, s \le u) \land (\forall \epsilon > 0, \exists s_\epsilon \in S: u - \epsilon < s_\epsilon)$.
m2.exam_tip: Be sure to prove both directions of the biconditional.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Let $S$ be a non-empty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ that is bounded above and let $a \in \mathbb{R}$. Prove that $\sup(a+S) = a + \sup S$.
m2.approach: Show $a + \sup S$ is an upper bound of $a + S$, and no smaller upper bound exists.

solution_steps.title: Upper Bound Verification
solution_steps.math: s \le \sup S \; \forall s \in S \implies a + s \le a + \sup S \; \forall (a + s) \in (a + S)
solution_steps.explanation: Adding $a$ preserves order, so $a + \sup S$ is an upper bound of $a+S$.

solution_steps.title: Least Upper Bound Verification
solution_steps.math: u \text{ is any upper bound of } a+S \implies a + s \le u \implies s \le u - a \; \forall s \in S
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $u - a$ is an upper bound of $S$. Therefore $\sup S \le u - a$, which gives $a + \sup S \le u$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \sup(a + S) = a + \sup S
solution_steps.explanation: Since $a + \sup S$ is an upper bound and is $\le$ any other upper bound $u$.

m2.final_answer: $\sup(a + S) = a + \sup S$.
m2.exam_tip: Show both parts: (1) it is an upper bound, (2) it is less than or equal to any other upper bound.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: State the Completeness Axiom of $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.approach: State the standard formulation of the completeness axiom.

solution_steps.title: Formal Axiom Statement
solution_steps.math: \emptyset \ne S \subset \mathbb{R} \land (\exists M \in \mathbb{R} : s \le M \; \forall s \in S) \implies \exists \sup S \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: The Completeness Axiom (or Dedekind Completeness) states that every non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound (supremum) in $\mathbb{R}$.

m2.final_answer: Every non-empty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ that is bounded above has a supremum in $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.exam_tip: You may also note the equivalent statement for bounded below sets having an infimum.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Define supremum and infimum of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.approach: Define upper/lower bounds and least upper bound / greatest lower bound.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Supremum ($\sup S$)
solution_steps.math: u = \sup S \iff (\forall s \in S, s \le u) \land (\forall v < u, \exists s \in S \text{ with } s > v)
solution_steps.explanation: The supremum of $S$ is the least upper bound: it is an upper bound, and smaller than or equal to every upper bound of $S$.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Infimum ($\inf S$)
solution_steps.math: w = \inf S \iff (\forall s \in S, s \ge w) \land (\forall t > w, \exists s \in S \text{ with } s < t)
solution_steps.explanation: The infimum of $S$ is the greatest lower bound: it is a lower bound, and greater than or equal to every lower bound of $S$.

m2.final_answer: $\sup S$ is the least upper bound of $S$; $\inf S$ is the greatest lower bound of $S$.
m2.exam_tip: State both conditions for each: (1) bound condition, (2) extremal condition.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Show that there exists a positive real number $x$ such that $x^2 = 2$.
m2.approach: Consider $S = \{s \in \mathbb{R} : s > 0, s^2 < 2\}$ and show $x = \sup S$ satisfies $x^2 = 2$.

solution_steps.title: Set Definition & Non-emptiness
solution_steps.math: S = \{s \in \mathbb{R} : s > 0, s^2 < 2\}. \quad 1 \in S \implies S \ne \emptyset; \quad s \le 2 \; \forall s \in S
solution_steps.explanation: Since $1^2 = 1 < 2$, $S$ is non-empty. If $s > 2$, $s^2 > 4 > 2$, so 2 is an upper bound. By completeness, $x = \sup S$ exists.

solution_steps.title: Ruling out $x^2 < 2$
solution_steps.math: x^2 < 2 \implies \left(x + \frac{1}{n}\right)^2 = x^2 + \frac{2x}{n} + \frac{1}{n^2} < x^2 + \frac{2x+1}{n} < 2 \text{ for large } n
solution_steps.explanation: This would mean $x + 1/n \in S$, contradicting $x = \sup S$.

solution_steps.title: Ruling out $x^2 > 2$
solution_steps.math: x^2 > 2 \implies \left(x - \frac{1}{m}\right)^2 > 2 \implies x - \frac{1}{m} \text{ is an upper bound of } S
solution_steps.explanation: This contradicts $x$ being the least upper bound. Thus $x^2 = 2$.

m2.final_answer: By the Completeness Property of $\mathbb{R}$, $x = \sup\{s > 0 : s^2 < 2\} > 0$ exists and satisfies $x^2 = 2$.
m2.exam_tip: Bartle & Sherbert Theorem 2.4.7 gives this classic construction of $\sqrt{2}$ using completeness.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: State the Nested Intervals Theorem.
m2.approach: State Cantor's intersection theorem for closed bounded nested intervals.

solution_steps.title: Hypothesis
solution_steps.math: I_n = [a_n, b_n] \subset \mathbb{R}, \quad I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: A sequence of nested, closed, bounded intervals.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n \ne \emptyset, \quad \exists \xi \in \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } \xi \in I_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: There exists at least one real number $\xi$ belonging to every interval $I_n$. If lengths $\ell(I_n) \to 0$, $\xi$ is unique.

m2.final_answer: If $I_n = [a_n, b_n]$ is a sequence of nested closed bounded intervals, then $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n \ne \emptyset$.
m2.exam_tip: Emphasize that the intervals must be closed and bounded for the theorem to hold (fails for $(0, 1/n)$).

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: What is the infimum of the set $S = \{\frac{1}{n} : n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\}$? Prove your assertion.
m2.approach: Use the Archimedean property to show $\inf S = 0$.

solution_steps.title: Lower Bound
solution_steps.math: n > 0 \implies \frac{1}{n} > 0 \; \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \implies 0 \text{ is a lower bound of } S
solution_steps.explanation: Every element is strictly positive.

solution_steps.title: Greatest Lower Bound
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists n_\epsilon \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \text{ s.t. } n_\epsilon > \frac{1}{\epsilon} \implies \frac{1}{n_\epsilon} < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: By the Archimedean Property, for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that $1/n < \epsilon = 0 + \epsilon$. Thus no $t > 0$ can be a lower bound.

m2.final_answer: $\inf S = 0$.
m2.exam_tip: Cite the Archimedean property explicitly when asserting $1/n_\epsilon < \epsilon$.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Define the absolute value of a real number and state the triangle inequality.
m2.concept_tested: Absolute Value Definition and Triangle Inequality
m2.approach: State piecewise definition and the triangle inequality formula.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Absolute Value
solution_steps.math: |a| = \begin{cases} a, & \text{if } a \ge 0 \\ -a, & \text{if } a < 0 \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: The absolute value measures the non-negative distance of $a$ from the origin.

solution_steps.title: Triangle Inequality
solution_steps.math: |a + b| \le |a| + |b| \quad \forall a, b \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: The absolute value of a sum never exceeds the sum of the absolute values.

m2.final_answer: $|a| = a$ if $a \ge 0$ and $-a$ if $a < 0$. Triangle inequality: $|a + b| \le |a| + |b|$.
m2.exam_tip: Also state that $|a| = \max\{a, -a\} = \sqrt{a^2}$.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Define a neighborhood of a point in $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.approach: Define $\epsilon$-neighborhood of a point $a \in \mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Formal Definition
solution_steps.math: V_\epsilon(a) = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : |x - a| < \epsilon\} = (a - \epsilon, a + \epsilon)
solution_steps.explanation: For any $\epsilon > 0$, the $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $a \in \mathbb{R}$ is the open interval of radius $\epsilon$ centered at $a$.

solution_steps.title: General Neighborhood
solution_steps.math: U \subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ is a neighborhood of } a \iff \exists \epsilon > 0 \text{ s.t. } V_\epsilon(a) \subseteq U
solution_steps.explanation: A set $U$ is a neighborhood of $a$ if it contains some open interval centered at $a$.

m2.final_answer: An $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $a \in \mathbb{R}$ is $V_\epsilon(a) = (a - \epsilon, a + \epsilon)$. A neighborhood of $a$ is any set containing an $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $a$.
m2.exam_tip: Specify both the $\epsilon$-neighborhood and the general neighborhood definition.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Define the supremum property of $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.approach: Re-state the completeness axiom clearly.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: S \subset \mathbb{R}, \, S \ne \emptyset, \, S \text{ bounded above} \implies \exists \sup S \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: The supremum property states that every non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above possesses a least upper bound in $\mathbb{R}$.

m2.final_answer: Every non-empty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ bounded above has a least upper bound in $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.exam_tip: Mention that $\mathbb{Q}$ fails to satisfy this property (e.g., $\{r \in \mathbb{Q} : r^2 < 2\}$).

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Show that if $a \in \mathbb{R}$ is such that $0 \le a < \epsilon$ for every $\epsilon > 0$, then $a = 0$.
m2.approach: Proof by contradiction assuming $a > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Assumption for Contradiction
solution_steps.math: 0 \le a < \epsilon \; \forall \epsilon > 0. \quad \text{Suppose } a > 0.
solution_steps.explanation: Assume $a$ is strictly positive.

solution_steps.title: Choose Specific $\epsilon$
solution_steps.math: \epsilon_0 = \frac{a}{2} > 0
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\epsilon_0 > 0$, the hypothesis implies $a < \epsilon_0 = a/2$.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction
solution_steps.math: a < \frac{a}{2} \implies \frac{a}{2} < 0 \implies a < 0
solution_steps.explanation: Contradicting $a > 0$. Since $a \ge 0$ and $a > 0$ is impossible, $a = 0$.

m2.exam_tip: Choosing $\epsilon = a/2$ is the standard and most elegant proof.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Show that if $a \in \mathbb{R}$, then $a \cdot 0 = 0$.
m2.approach: Use $0 + 0 = 0$ and distributivity.

solution_steps.title: Use Additive Identity
solution_steps.math: 0 + 0 = 0 \implies a \cdot 0 = a \cdot (0 + 0) = a \cdot 0 + a \cdot 0
solution_steps.explanation: Using distributive axiom.

solution_steps.title: Add Additive Inverse
