solution_steps.math: a \cdot 0 + (-(a \cdot 0)) = (a \cdot 0 + a \cdot 0) + (-(a \cdot 0)) \implies 0 = a \cdot 0
solution_steps.explanation: Using associativity and inverse axiom.

m2.final_answer: $a \cdot 0 = 0$.
m2.exam_tip: Always specify which field axiom is used at each step (distributivity, additive inverse).

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Find all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the inequality $|4x - 5| \le 13$.
m2.approach: Use $|u| \le c \iff -c \le u \le c$.

solution_steps.title: Convert to Double Inequality
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of absolute value inequality.

solution_steps.title: Add 5 to All Parts
solution_steps.explanation: Adding 5 throughout.

solution_steps.title: Divide by 4
solution_steps.explanation: Dividing by positive scalar 4.

m2.final_answer: $x \in \left[-2, \frac{9}{2}\right]$.
m2.exam_tip: Write the final answer in interval notation $[-2, 9/2]$.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $\sqrt{ab} \le \frac{a+b}{2}$, and show that equality holds if and only if $a=b$.
m2.approach: Expand $(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^2 \ge 0$ and analyze equality conditions.

solution_steps.title: Non-negativity of Squares
solution_steps.math: (\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^2 \ge 0 \quad \forall a, b > 0
solution_steps.explanation: Since every square of a real number is non-negative, $(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^2 \ge 0$.

solution_steps.title: Expansion and Rearrangement
solution_steps.math: (\sqrt{a})^2 - 2\sqrt{a}\sqrt{b} + (\sqrt{b})^2 \ge 0 \implies a - 2\sqrt{ab} + b \ge 0 \implies a + b \ge 2\sqrt{ab}
solution_steps.explanation: Expand the binomial square and move $2\sqrt{ab}$ to the right-hand side.

solution_steps.title: Division by 2
solution_steps.math: \frac{a + b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab} \iff \sqrt{ab} \le \frac{a+b}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: Dividing both sides by 2 proves the inequality.

solution_steps.title: Condition for Equality
solution_steps.math: \sqrt{ab} = \frac{a+b}{2} \iff (\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^2 = 0 \iff \sqrt{a} = \sqrt{b} \iff a = b
solution_steps.explanation: Equality holds if and only if the squared difference is 0, which occurs precisely when $a = b$.

m2.final_answer: $\sqrt{ab} \le \frac{a+b}{2}$, with equality holding if and only if $a = b$.
m2.exam_tip: Do not skip the 'if and only if' biconditional demonstration for the equality case.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: State and prove the Density Theorem for real numbers.
m2.concept_tested: Density Theorem for Rational Numbers in $\mathbb{R}$
m2.approach: Use the Archimedean Property to find an integer denominator $n$ such that $1/n < y - x$, then select the appropriate numerator $m$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R} \text{ with } x < y, \; \exists r \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ such that } x < r < y
solution_steps.explanation: Between any two distinct real numbers, there exists at least one rational number.

solution_steps.title: Step 1: Choose Denominator $n$
solution_steps.math: y - x > 0 \implies \exists n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } n > \frac{1}{y - x} \iff ny - nx > 1
solution_steps.explanation: By the Archimedean Property, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ large enough so that the interval $(nx, ny)$ has length strictly greater than 1.

solution_steps.title: Step 2: Choose Numerator $m$
solution_steps.math: \exists m \in \mathbb{Z} \text{ such that } m - 1 \le nx < m
solution_steps.explanation: Every real number $nx$ lies between two consecutive integers. Hence $nx < m$ and $m \le nx + 1$.

solution_steps.title: Step 3: Verification of Bounds
solution_steps.math: nx < m \le nx + 1 < ny \implies nx < m < ny \implies x < \frac{m}{n} < y
solution_steps.explanation: Dividing through by $n > 0$ yields $r = m/n \in \mathbb{Q}$ strictly between $x$ and $y$.

m2.final_answer: The rational number $r = m/n$ satisfies $x < r < y$.
m2.exam_tip: Clearly show how $ny - nx > 1$ ensures an integer $m$ falls strictly inside $(nx, ny)$.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. Prove that (i) $|ab| = |a||b|$, (ii) $|a+b| \le |a| + |b|$.
m2.concept_tested: Properties of Absolute Value: Multiplicative and Subadditive
m2.approach: Prove (i) using sign cases or squaring, and (ii) using $-|a| \le a \le |a|$.

solution_steps.title: Proof of (i) $|ab| = |a||b|$
solution_steps.explanation: Since $|x|^2 = x^2$ for all real numbers and both sides are non-negative, taking the positive square root gives $|ab| = |a||b|$.

solution_steps.title: Proof of (ii) $|a+b| \le |a| + |b|$
solution_steps.math: -|a| \le a \le |a| \quad \text{and} \quad -|b| \le b \le |b|
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of absolute value, $-|x| \le x \le |x|$.

solution_steps.title: Adding Inequalities
solution_steps.math: -(|a| + |b|) \le a + b \le |a| + |b| \iff |a + b| \le |a| + |b|
solution_steps.explanation: Since $-c \le u \le c \iff |u| \le c$, this proves the triangle inequality.

m2.final_answer: (i) $|ab| = |a||b|$, and (ii) $|a+b| \le |a| + |b|$ hold for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.
m2.exam_tip: The squaring method for $|ab| = |a||b|$ is much shorter and avoids checking 4 separate sign cases.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ with $x < y$. Prove that there exists an irrational number $z$ such that $x < z < y$.
m2.approach: Scale the interval $(x, y)$ by $1/\sqrt{2}$ and invoke the density of rationals.

solution_steps.title: Transformation by Scaling
solution_steps.math: x < y \implies \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\sqrt{2} > 0$, dividing by $\sqrt{2}$ preserves strict order.

solution_steps.title: Application of Density Theorem
solution_steps.math: \exists r \in \mathbb{Q}, \, r \ne 0 \text{ such that } \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < r < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Density Theorem, between any two reals there is a rational; since $(x/\sqrt{2}, y/\sqrt{2})$ contains infinitely many rationals, choose a non-zero one.

solution_steps.title: Return to Original Variable
solution_steps.math: x < r\sqrt{2} < y, \quad z = r\sqrt{2} \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}
solution_steps.explanation: Multiplying through by $\sqrt{2} > 0$. Since $r \ne 0$ is rational and $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, $z = r\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

m2.final_answer: $z = r\sqrt{2}$ is an irrational number satisfying $x < z < y$.
m2.exam_tip: Make sure to explicitly mention $r \ne 0$; if $r=0$, $z=0$ which is rational!

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: State and prove the Archimedean Property of $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.approach: State the property and prove it using the Supremum Property (Completeness).

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \; \exists n_x \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n_x > x
solution_steps.explanation: Equivalently: if $y > 0$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $ny > x$.

solution_steps.title: Proof by Contradiction
solution_steps.math: \text{Suppose } \exists x \in \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } n \le x \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Then the set $\mathbb{N}$ is bounded above by $x$. Since $\mathbb{N} \ne \emptyset$ ($1 \in \mathbb{N}$), $\mathbb{N}$ is a non-empty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ bounded above.

solution_steps.title: Existence of Supremum
solution_steps.math: u = \sup \mathbb{N} \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Property of $\mathbb{R}$, the supremum $u$ exists.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction via Supremum Characterization
solution_steps.math: u - 1 < u \implies \exists m \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } m > u - 1 \implies m + 1 > u
solution_steps.explanation: Since $m \in \mathbb{N}$, $m + 1 \in \mathbb{N}$. But $m + 1 > u$, contradicting that $u$ is an upper bound of $\mathbb{N}$.

m2.final_answer: Hence $\mathbb{N}$ is unbounded above in $\mathbb{R}$, proving the Archimedean Property.
m2.exam_tip: List the two corollaries often asked: (1) $\inf\{1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} = 0$, (2) $\exists n$ with $1/n < \epsilon$ for any $\epsilon > 0$.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: State and prove the Density Theorem for rational numbers in $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.approach: Rigorous full proof with all cases ($x > 0$, $x = 0$, $x < 0$).

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R} \text{ with } x < y, \; \exists q \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ such that } x < q < y
solution_steps.explanation: Between any two distinct real numbers lies a rational number.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: $x > 0$
solution_steps.math: y - x > 0 \implies \exists n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } n(y - x) > 1 \iff ny - nx > 1
solution_steps.explanation: By the Archimedean Property, such an $n \in \mathbb{N}$ exists.

solution_steps.title: Selecting the Integer $m$
solution_steps.math: A = \{k \in \mathbb{N} : k > nx\} \ne \emptyset \implies m = \min A \implies m - 1 \le nx < m
solution_steps.explanation: By Well-Ordering Principle of $\mathbb{N}$, $A$ has a least element $m$.

solution_steps.title: Establishing the Inequality
solution_steps.math: nx < m \le nx + 1 < ny \implies nx < m < ny \implies x < \frac{m}{n} < y
solution_steps.explanation: Dividing by $n$ produces $q = m/n \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $x < q < y$.

solution_steps.title: General Cases ($x \le 0$)
solution_steps.math: \text{If } x \le 0, \text{ choose } k \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } x + k > 0, \text{ find } q' \in (x+k, y+k), \text{ then } q = q' - k \in (x, y)
solution_steps.explanation: Shifting by an integer $k$ reduces the general case to the positive case.

m2.final_answer: There exists a rational number $q \in (x, y)$ for any $x < y$.
m2.exam_tip: Showing how the case $x \le 0$ reduces to $x > 0$ via integer shift earns full marks.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Let $S$ be a non-empty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ that is bounded below. Prove that $\inf(S) = -\sup(\{-x : x \in S\})$.
m2.approach: Show that $-\sup(-S)$ is a lower bound of $S$ and is greater than or equal to every lower bound.

solution_steps.title: Define $-S$ and verify bounds
solution_steps.math: -S = \{-x : x \in S\}. \quad S \text{ bounded below by } w \implies x \ge w \; \forall x \in S \implies -x \le -w \; \forall -x \in -S
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $-S$ is non-empty and bounded above by $-w$. Hence $u = \sup(-S)$ exists by completeness.

solution_steps.title: Show $-u$ is a lower bound of $S$
solution_steps.math: -x \le u \; \forall x \in S \implies x \ge -u \; \forall x \in S
solution_steps.explanation: Multiplying by $-1$ reverses inequality, so $-u$ is a lower bound of $S$.

solution_steps.title: Show $-u$ is the greatest lower bound
solution_steps.math: t \le x \; \forall x \in S \implies -x \le -t \; \forall -x \in -S \implies u = \sup(-S) \le -t \implies -u \ge t
solution_steps.explanation: If $t$ is any lower bound of $S$, then $-t$ is an upper bound of $-S$, so $u \le -t$, which gives $-u \ge t$.

m2.final_answer: $\inf(S) = -\sup(-S) = -\sup(\{-x : x \in S\})$.
m2.exam_tip: This duality allows every theorem about suprema to be immediately converted to a theorem about infima.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Prove that if $I_n = [a_n, b_n]$ is a nested sequence of closed bounded intervals, then there exists a point $\xi \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$.
m2.approach: Define $S = \{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and use $\xi = \sup S$ to prove $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n$.

solution_steps.title: Nested Condition
solution_steps.math: I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n \iff a_n \le a_{n+1} \le b_{n+1} \le b_n \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}^+
solution_steps.explanation: The left endpoints $(a_n)$ form an increasing sequence and the right endpoints $(b_n)$ form a decreasing sequence.

solution_steps.title: Every $b_m$ is an Upper Bound for $S = \{a_n\}$
solution_steps.math: \forall n, m \in \mathbb{Z}^+, \quad a_n \le a_{\max(n, m)} \le b_{\max(n, m)} \le b_m \implies a_n \le b_m
solution_steps.explanation: Every right endpoint $b_m$ is greater than or equal to every left endpoint $a_n$.

solution_steps.title: Supremum Existence
solution_steps.math: S = \{a_n : n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\} \ne \emptyset \text{ is bounded above by } b_1 \implies \xi = \sup S \in \mathbb{R} \text{ exists}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Axiom of $\mathbb{R}$, $\xi = \sup S$ exists.

solution_steps.title: Verification that $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n$
solution_steps.math: a_n \le \xi \; \forall n \quad \text{and} \quad \xi \le b_n \; \forall n \implies a_n \le \xi \le b_n \iff \xi \in [a_n, b_n] = I_n
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\xi = \sup S$, $a_n \le \xi$. Since each $b_n$ is an upper bound of $S$, $\xi \le b_n$. Thus $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n$.

m2.final_answer: $\xi = \sup\{a_n : n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\} \in \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n$, so the intersection is non-empty.
m2.exam_tip: If the problem also asks for uniqueness, note that $\inf\{b_n - a_n\} = 0 \implies \xi$ is unique.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Prove that if $x$ and $y$ are real numbers with $x < y$, then there exists an irrational number $z$ such that $x < z < y$.
m2.approach: Use the existence of rationals in $(x/\sqrt{2}, y/\sqrt{2})$.

solution_steps.title: Scale by $\sqrt{2}$
solution_steps.math: x < y \implies \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\sqrt{2} > 0$, order is preserved.

solution_steps.title: Find Non-zero Rational
solution_steps.math: \exists r \in \mathbb{Q} \setminus \{0\} \text{ such that } \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < r < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}
solution_steps.explanation: Density of rationals provides a non-zero rational $r$ in this open interval.

solution_steps.title: Form Irrational Number
solution_steps.math: z = r\sqrt{2} \implies x < z < y, \quad z \notin \mathbb{Q}
solution_steps.explanation: Product of a non-zero rational and an irrational is irrational.

m2.final_answer: $z = r\sqrt{2}$ is irrational and satisfies $x < z < y$.
m2.exam_tip: Alternatively, you can use $z = x + \frac{y-x}{\sqrt{2} + n}$ for sufficiently large $n$.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Prove the triangle inequality: $|x+y| \le |x| + |y|$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.
m2.approach: Use algebraic properties of absolute values and $-|x| \le x \le |x|$.

solution_steps.title: Inequalities for components
solution_steps.math: -|x| \le x \le |x| \quad \text{and} \quad -|y| \le y \le |y|
solution_steps.explanation: Valid for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ by definition of $|\cdot|$.

solution_steps.title: Adding inequalities
solution_steps.explanation: Summing the two inequalities maintains the order.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion via Lemma
solution_steps.math: -c \le u \le c \iff |u| \le c \implies |x + y| \le |x| + |y|
solution_steps.explanation: Applying the lemma with $c = |x| + |y|$ and $u = x+y$ completes the proof.

m2.final_answer: $|x + y| \le |x| + |y|$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.
m2.exam_tip: Mention the corollary: $||x| - |y|| \le |x - y|$ (Reverse Triangle Inequality).

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Show that the set of real numbers has no upper bound.
m2.approach: Proof using the Archimedean Property or contradiction via Supremum Property.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Bounded Above
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{R} \text{ is bounded above } \iff \exists M \in \mathbb{R} \text{ such that } x \le M \; \forall x \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: An upper bound must exceed every single real number.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction
solution_steps.math: \text{Take } x_0 = M + 1 \in \mathbb{R}. \quad x_0 = M + 1 > M
solution_steps.explanation: Since $1 > 0$, $M + 1 > M$. But $M + 1 \in \mathbb{R}$, which contradicts that $x \le M$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Alternative via Archimedean Property
solution_steps.math: \forall M \in \mathbb{R}, \; \exists n \in \mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{R} \text{ such that } n > M
solution_steps.explanation: Since natural numbers are unbounded above in $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{R}$ itself cannot be bounded above.

m2.final_answer: The set of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ has no upper bound.
m2.exam_tip: The simple element $M+1$ immediately refutes any candidate upper bound $M$.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Let $A$ and $B$ be bounded subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. Prove that $\sup(A + B) = \sup(A) + \sup(B)$ where $A + B = \{a+b : a \in A, b \in B\}$.
m2.concept_tested: Supremum of Sum of Sets: $\sup(A + B) = \sup(A) + \sup(B)$
m2.approach: Show that $\sup A + \sup B$ is an upper bound, and then show that for every $\epsilon > 0$, an element exceeds $\sup A + \sup B - \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Step 1: Upper Bound Property
solution_steps.math: a \le \sup A \; (\forall a \in A), \quad b \le \sup B \; (\forall b \in B) \implies a + b \le \sup A + \sup B \; (\forall a+b \in A+B)
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $\sup A + \sup B$ is an upper bound of $A+B$, so $\sup(A+B) \le \sup A + \sup B$.

solution_steps.title: Step 2: Least Upper Bound Property
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists a_\epsilon \in A \text{ s.t. } a_\epsilon > \sup A - \frac{\epsilon}{2}, \quad \exists b_\epsilon \in B \text{ s.t. } b_\epsilon > \sup B - \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By the $\epsilon$-characterization of the supremum for sets $A$ and $B$.

solution_steps.title: Summing Elements
solution_steps.math: a_\epsilon + b_\epsilon \in A + B, \quad a_\epsilon + b_\epsilon > (\sup A + \sup B) - \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: This shows no number smaller than $\sup A + \sup B$ can be an upper bound of $A+B$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \sup(A+B) \ge \sup A + \sup B \implies \sup(A + B) = \sup A + \sup B
solution_steps.explanation: Combining the two inequalities gives exact equality.

m2.final_answer: $\sup(A + B) = \sup(A) + \sup(B)$.
m2.exam_tip: Splitting $\epsilon$ into $\epsilon/2 + \epsilon/2$ is the standard technique here.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Show that the set $S = \{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 3\}$ has no supremum in $\mathbb{Q}$.
m2.approach: Show that the least upper bound of $S = \{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 3\}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ is $\sqrt{3}$, which is not rational.

solution_steps.title: Properties of $S$
solution_steps.math: S = \{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 3\} \subset \mathbb{Q}. \quad 1 \in S \implies S \ne \emptyset; \quad x < 2 \; \forall x \in S
solution_steps.explanation: $S$ is non-empty and bounded above in $\mathbb{Q}$ (e.g. by 2).

solution_steps.title: Supremum in $\mathbb{R}$
solution_steps.math: \sup_\mathbb{R}(S) = \sqrt{3}
solution_steps.explanation: In $\mathbb{R}$, $S$ has supremum $\sqrt{3}$.

solution_steps.title: Irrationality of $\sqrt{3}$
solution_steps.math: \sqrt{3} \notin \mathbb{Q}
solution_steps.explanation: If $\sqrt{3} = p/q$ in lowest terms, $p^2 = 3q^2 \implies 3|p \implies 9|p^2 \implies 3|q$, contradicting $\gcd(p, q) = 1$.

solution_steps.title: Non-existence in $\mathbb{Q}$
solution_steps.math: \forall q \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ with } q > 0: \quad q^2 < 3 \implies \exists q' \in S \text{ with } q' > q; \quad q^2 > 3 \implies \exists q'' \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ upper bound with } q'' < q
solution_steps.explanation: Hence no rational number can serve as the least upper bound of $S$ inside $\mathbb{Q}$.

m2.final_answer: The set $S = \{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 3\}$ has no supremum in $\mathbb{Q}$.
m2.exam_tip: State clearly that this proves $\mathbb{Q}$ fails the Completeness Axiom.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Prove that if $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a non-empty bounded set, and $c \ge 0$, then $\sup(cS) = c \sup(S)$.
m2.concept_tested: Homogeneity of Supremum for Non-negative Scaling
m2.approach: Consider cases $c = 0$ and $c > 0$, using order preservation of multiplication by positive numbers.

solution_steps.title: Case $c = 0$
solution_steps.math: cS = \{0 \cdot s : s \in S\} = \{0\} \implies \sup(cS) = 0 = 0 \cdot \sup S
solution_steps.explanation: Trivial case when $c = 0$.

solution_steps.title: Case $c > 0$: Upper Bound
solution_steps.math: s \le \sup S \; \forall s \in S \implies cs \le c \sup S \; \forall cs \in cS
solution_steps.explanation: Multiplying by $c > 0$ preserves inequality, so $c \sup S$ is an upper bound of $cS$.

solution_steps.title: Case $c > 0$: Least Upper Bound
solution_steps.math: u \text{ is any upper bound of } cS \implies cs \le u \implies s \le \frac{u}{c} \; \forall s \in S \implies \sup S \le \frac{u}{c} \implies c \sup S \le u
solution_steps.explanation: Since $c > 0$, dividing by $c$ gives $u/c$ as an upper bound of $S$. Therefore $\sup S \le u/c$, so $c \sup S \le u$.

m2.final_answer: $\sup(cS) = c \sup(S)$ for all $c \ge 0$.
m2.exam_tip: Remember to address the case $c = 0$ separately.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Prove that there does not exist a rational number $r$ such that $r^2 = 2$.
m2.approach: Assume $r = p/q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $\gcd(p, q) = 1$, square both sides and show both $p$ and $q$ must be even.

solution_steps.title: Hypothesis for Contradiction
solution_steps.math: r = \frac{p}{q} \in \mathbb{Q}, \quad p, q \in \mathbb{Z}, \, q \ne 0, \, \gcd(p, q) = 1, \quad r^2 = 2
solution_steps.explanation: Assume $r$ is rational in lowest terms.

solution_steps.title: Parity of $p$
solution_steps.math: \frac{p^2}{q^2} = 2 \implies p^2 = 2q^2 \implies p^2 \text{ is even} \implies p \text{ is even}
solution_steps.explanation: The square of an odd number $(2k+1)^2 = 4k^2+4k+1$ is odd. Thus $p$ must be even, so $p = 2k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

solution_steps.title: Parity of $q$
solution_steps.math: (2k)^2 = 2q^2 \implies 4k^2 = 2q^2 \implies q^2 = 2k^2 \implies q^2 \text{ is even} \implies q \text{ is even}
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $q$ must also be even.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction
solution_steps.math: 2 | p \quad \text{and} \quad 2 | q \implies \gcd(p, q) \ge 2
solution_steps.explanation: Contradicts the assumption that $\gcd(p, q) = 1$.

m2.final_answer: There is no rational number $r$ such that $r^2 = 2$.
m2.exam_tip: State clearly the lemma: 'If $p^2$ is even, then $p$ is even'.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: Find all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the equation $|x + 1| + |x - 2| = 7$.
m2.approach: Partition $\mathbb{R}$ into intervals determined by critical points $x = -1$ and $x = 2$.

solution_steps.title: Critical Points and Intervals
solution_steps.math: \text{Critical points: } x = -1, \, x = 2. \quad \text{Intervals: } (-\infty, -1), \; [-1, 2], \; (2, \infty)
solution_steps.explanation: The behavior of $|x+1|$ and $|x-2|$ changes at $x = -1$ and $x = 2$.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: $x < -1$
solution_steps.math: -(x+1) - (x-2) = 7 \implies -2x + 1 = 7 \implies -2x = 6 \implies x = -3
solution_steps.explanation: Check: $-3 < -1$, so $x = -3$ is a valid solution.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: $-1 \le x \le 2$
solution_steps.math: (x+1) - (x-2) = 7 \implies x + 1 - x + 2 = 7 \implies 3 = 7 \quad (\text{No solution})
solution_steps.explanation: In this interval the sum of distances is constant and equals 3, which cannot equal 7.

solution_steps.title: Case 3: $x > 2$
solution_steps.math: (x+1) + (x-2) = 7 \implies 2x - 1 = 7 \implies 2x = 8 \implies x = 4
solution_steps.explanation: Check: $4 > 2$, so $x = 4$ is a valid solution.

m2.final_answer: The solutions are $x = -3$ and $x = 4$.
m2.exam_tip: Always verify candidate solutions against the interval condition for that case.

m2.topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
m2.question: State and prove the Density Theorem for rational numbers in $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.concept_tested: Density Theorem for Rational Numbers and Irrationals in $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete Essay)
m2.approach: State the theorem, use the Archimedean Property to establish existence of denominator $n$, apply the well-ordering principle / integer bounds for numerator $m$, handle all sign cases, and prove the corollary on density of irrational numbers.

solution_steps.title: Statement of the Density Theorem
solution_steps.math: \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R} \text{ with } x < y, \; \exists q \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ such that } x < q < y
solution_steps.explanation: Every non-empty open interval $(x, y) \subset \mathbb{R}$ contains at least one (and hence infinitely many) rational numbers.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: $x > 0$ — Choosing the Denominator $n$
solution_steps.math: y - x > 0 \implies \exists n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n > \frac{1}{y - x} \iff ny - nx > 1
solution_steps.explanation: By the Archimedean Property of $\mathbb{R}$, since $y - x > 0$, there exists a natural number $n$ whose reciprocal is less than $y-x$.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: Choosing the Numerator $m$
solution_steps.math: S = \{k \in \mathbb{N} : k > nx\} \ne \emptyset \implies m = \min S \implies m - 1 \le nx < m
solution_steps.explanation: By the Archimedean Property, $S$ is non-empty. By the Well-Ordering Principle of $\mathbb{N}$, $S$ has a least element $m$. Then $m-1 \notin S$, meaning $m-1 \le nx$, and $m \in S$, meaning $nx < m$.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: Enclosing $m$ in $(nx, ny)$
solution_steps.math: m \le nx + 1 < ny \implies nx < m < ny \implies x < \frac{m}{n} < y
solution_steps.explanation: Since $ny - nx > 1$, we have $nx + 1 < ny$. Dividing through by $n > 0$ yields the rational number $q = m/n$ satisfying $x < q < y$.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: General Case ($x \le 0$)
solution_steps.math: \text{If } x \le 0, \text{ by Archimedean Property } \exists k \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } k > |x| \implies x + k > 0
solution_steps.explanation: Now $0 < x + k < y + k$. By Case 1, there exists $q' \in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $x + k < q' < y + k$. Subtracting integer $k$ gives $q = q' - k \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $x < q < y$.

solution_steps.title: Corollary: Density of Irrational Numbers
solution_steps.math: \exists r \in \mathbb{Q} \setminus \{0\} \text{ s.t. } \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < r < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}} \implies x < r\sqrt{2} < y
solution_steps.explanation: Since $r$ is a non-zero rational and $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, the product $z = r\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, proving that irrationals are also dense in $\mathbb{R}$.

m2.final_answer: Every open interval $(x, y)$ contains a rational number $q = m/n$ and an irrational number $z = r\sqrt{2}$. Thus both $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$ are dense in $\mathbb{R}$.
m2.exam_tip: In a 10-mark essay, always state the Archimedean property explicitly, detail both the positive and negative cases, and include the irrational density corollary.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: State and prove the Squeeze Theorem for sequences of real numbers.
m3.approach: Use the definition of sequence convergence with $\epsilon$ bounds to trap $(y_n)$ between $(x_n)$ and $(z_n)$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: x_n \le y_n \le z_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \quad \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} z_n = L \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} y_n = L
solution_steps.explanation: If a sequence is trapped between two sequences converging to the same limit, it must also converge to that limit.

solution_steps.title: Proof using $\epsilon$-definition
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K_1, K_2 \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } n \ge K_1 \implies L - \epsilon < x_n < L + \epsilon, \quad n \ge K_2 \implies L - \epsilon < z_n < L + \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Convergence of $x_n$ and $z_n$ implies they eventually stay within an $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $L$.

solution_steps.title: Trapping $y_n$
solution_steps.math: n \ge K = \max(K_1, K_2) \implies L - \epsilon < x_n \le y_n \le z_n < L + \epsilon \implies |y_n - L| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $y_n$ satisfies the definition of convergence to $L$.

m3.final_answer: $\lim_{n \to \infty} y_n = L$.
m3.exam_tip: Remember to specify $K = \max(K_1, K_2)$ so both bounds hold simultaneously.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: If a sequence $(x_n)$ of real numbers converges to $x$, prove that any subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ of $(x_n)$ also converges to $x$.
m3.approach: Use the strictly increasing property of index sequence $n_k \ge k$.

solution_steps.title: Index Property
solution_steps.math: n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \dots < n_k < \dots \implies n_k \ge k \quad \forall k \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: By induction, the subsequence indices satisfy $n_k \ge k$.

solution_steps.title: Apply Sequence Convergence
solution_steps.math: \lim x_n = x \implies \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } n \ge K \implies |x_n - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Definition of limit for the parent sequence.

solution_steps.title: Subsequence Bound
solution_steps.math: k \ge K \implies n_k \ge k \ge K \implies |x_{n_k} - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Hence the subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ converges to the same limit $x$.

m3.final_answer: Every subsequence of a convergent sequence converges to the same limit: $\lim x_{n_k} = x$.
m3.exam_tip: Mention $n_k \ge k$ as the crucial lemma in the proof.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Prove that every Cauchy sequence of real numbers is bounded.
m3.approach: Set $\epsilon = 1$, bound terms after index $H$, and take max/min of the finite initial terms.

solution_steps.title: Cauchy Definition for $\epsilon = 1$
solution_steps.math: \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n, m \ge H \implies |x_n - x_m| < 1
solution_steps.explanation: Choosing $\epsilon = 1$ in the Cauchy definition.

solution_steps.title: Fix $m = H$
solution_steps.math: n \ge H \implies |x_n - x_H| < 1 \implies |x_n| < |x_H| + 1
solution_steps.explanation: By reverse triangle inequality, all terms after index $H$ are bounded by $|x_H| + 1$.

solution_steps.title: Global Bound $M$
solution_steps.math: M = \max\{|x_1|, |x_2|, \dots, |x_{H-1}|, |x_H| + 1\} \implies |x_n| \le M \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Since the set of preceding terms is finite, its maximum exists, bounding the entire sequence.

m3.final_answer: Every Cauchy sequence is bounded by $M = \max\{|x_1|, \dots, |x_{H-1}|, |x_H| + 1\}$.
m3.exam_tip: Choosing $\epsilon = 1$ is the canonical choice; any fixed positive constant works.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be two sequences of real numbers with $x_n \le y_n$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. If $\lim x_n = +\infty$, prove that $\lim y_n = +\infty$.
m3.approach: Use the definition: $\forall M > 0$, terms eventually exceed $M$.

solution_steps.title: Definition of $\lim x_n = +\infty$
solution_steps.math: \forall M > 0, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n \ge K \implies x_n > M
solution_steps.explanation: Terms of $(x_n)$ eventually exceed any positive real number $M$.

solution_steps.title: Comparison with $y_n$
solution_steps.math: x_n \le y_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N} \implies \text{for } n \ge K, \quad y_n \ge x_n > M \implies y_n > M
solution_steps.explanation: Since $y_n \ge x_n$, $y_n$ also exceeds $M$ for all $n \ge K$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} y_n = +\infty
solution_steps.explanation: By definition, $(y_n)$ properly diverges to $+\infty$.

m3.final_answer: $\lim y_n = +\infty$.
m3.exam_tip: This is often called the Comparison Theorem for properly divergent sequences.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Consider the sequences $X = (2, 4, 6, \dots, 2n, \dots)$ and $Y = (1, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{8}, \dots)$. Find $XY$ and $X/Y$.
m3.approach: Identify $n$-th terms: $x_n = 2n$ and $y_n = (1/2)^{n-1}$ (or geometric terms), then multiply and divide termwise.

solution_steps.title: General terms of $X$ and $Y$
solution_steps.math: x_n = 2n, \quad y_n = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{(n-1)n}{2}} \text{ or } y_n = 2^{-(n-1)} \quad (\text{with } y_1=1, y_2=1/2, y_3=1/8 = (1/2)^3)
solution_steps.explanation: Notice the exponents of $1/2$ are $0, 1, 3, \dots$, which is $T_{n-1} = \frac{(n-1)n}{2}$.

solution_steps.title: Product Sequence $XY$
solution_steps.math: (XY)_n = x_n y_n = 2n \cdot 2^{-\frac{n(n-1)}{2}} = n \cdot 2^{1 - \frac{n(n-1)}{2}}
solution_steps.explanation: First few terms: $XY = \left(2 \cdot 1, \; 4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}, \; 6 \cdot \frac{1}{8}, \dots\right) = \left(2, \; 2, \; \frac{3}{4}, \dots\right)$.

solution_steps.title: Quotient Sequence $X/Y$
solution_steps.explanation: First few terms: $X/Y = \left(\frac{2}{1}, \; \frac{4}{1/2}, \; \frac{6}{1/8}, \dots\right) = (2, \; 8, \; 48, \dots)$.

m3.final_answer: $XY = \left(2, 2, \frac{3}{4}, \dots\right)$ and $X/Y = (2, 8, 48, \dots)$.
m3.exam_tip: Show both the termwise values for the first 3 terms and the general formula.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Let $(x_n)$ be a sequence of real numbers that converges to $x$. Prove that $(|x_n|)$ converges to $|x|$.
m3.concept_tested: Continuity of Absolute Value / Reverse Triangle Inequality
m3.approach: Apply the reverse triangle inequality $||x_n| - |x|| \le |x_n - x|$.

solution_steps.title: Reverse Triangle Inequality
solution_steps.math: ||x_n| - |x|| \le |x_n - x| \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: A direct consequence of $|a - b| \ge ||a| - |b||$.

solution_steps.title: Apply Definition of Limit
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } n \ge K \implies |x_n - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\lim x_n = x$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: n \ge K \implies ||x_n| - |x|| \le |x_n - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $(|x_n|)$ converges to $|x|$.

m3.final_answer: $\lim_{n \to \infty} |x_n| = |x|$. Note the converse is false unless $x = 0$.
m3.exam_tip: Mention that the converse is generally false (counterexample: $x_n = (-1)^n$).

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Determine if the sequence $(1 + (-1)^n)$ is a Cauchy sequence. Justify your answer.
m3.concept_tested: Cauchy Criterion / Divergence of Alternating Sequences
m3.approach: Evaluate consecutive terms and show $|x_{n} - x_{n+1}| = 2$ for all $n$.

solution_steps.title: Sequence Terms
solution_steps.math: x_n = 1 + (-1)^n = \begin{cases} 2, & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \\ 0, & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: The sequence alternates: $(0, 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, \dots)$.

solution_steps.title: Check Cauchy Condition
solution_steps.explanation: For any index $H$, we can pick $n = 2H$ and $m = 2H+1 > H$.

solution_steps.title: Violation for $\epsilon = 1$
solution_steps.math: |x_n - x_m| = 2 > 1 = \epsilon_0
solution_steps.explanation: Hence there is no $H$ such that $|x_n - x_m| < 1$ for all $n, m \ge H$.

m3.final_answer: No, $(1 + (-1)^n)$ is NOT a Cauchy sequence because it oscillates between 0 and 2 and does not converge.
m3.exam_tip: Since $\mathbb{R}$ is complete, a sequence is Cauchy iff it converges; since this diverges, it cannot be Cauchy.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Let $c > 1$. Find the limit $\lim(c^n)$.
m3.approach: Write $c = 1 + b$ with $b > 0$ and apply Bernoulli's Inequality.

solution_steps.title: Substitution
solution_steps.math: c > 1 \implies c = 1 + b \quad \text{where } b = c - 1 > 0
solution_steps.explanation: Express $c$ as 1 plus a positive increment.

solution_steps.title: Bernoulli's Inequality
solution_steps.math: c^n = (1 + b)^n \ge 1 + nb \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: By Bernoulli's Inequality for $b > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Archimedean Limit
solution_steps.math: \forall M > 0, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } K > \frac{M - 1}{b} \implies c^n \ge 1 + nb > M \; (\forall n \ge K)
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $c^n \to +\infty$ as $n \to \infty$.

m3.final_answer: $\lim_{n \to \infty} c^n = +\infty$ (properly diverges to $+\infty$).
m3.exam_tip: Bernoulli's inequality $(1+b)^n \ge 1 + nb$ is the standard and expected tool here.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Define a Cauchy sequence in a general metric space.
m3.approach: State the metric definition using metric distance $d(x_n, x_m)$.

solution_steps.title: Formal Definition
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \text{ is Cauchy in } (X, d) \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n, m \ge H \implies d(x_n, x_m) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Terms of the sequence become arbitrarily close to each other with respect to the metric $d$ as the indices grow.

m3.final_answer: A sequence $(x_n)$ in $(X, d)$ is Cauchy if $\forall \epsilon > 0, \exists H \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $d(x_n, x_m) < \epsilon$ whenever $n, m \ge H$.
m3.exam_tip: Note that both indices $n$ and $m$ must be $\ge H$ independently.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Define a Cauchy sequence of real numbers.
m3.approach: State definition for real numbers using the standard Euclidean distance $|x_n - x_m|$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ is a Cauchy sequence} \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } \forall n, m \ge H, \; |x_n - x_m| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: In $\mathbb{R}$, terms get arbitrarily close under the absolute value difference.

m3.final_answer: A real sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy if $\forall \epsilon > 0, \exists H(\epsilon) \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $|x_n - x_m| < \epsilon$ for all $n, m \ge H(\epsilon)$.
m3.exam_tip: State that in $\mathbb{R}$, Cauchy sequences and convergent sequences are identical (Cauchy Completeness).

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: State the definition of the limit of a sequence.
m3.concept_tested: Definition of Limit of a Sequence
m3.approach: State the $\epsilon-K$ definition of convergence.

solution_steps.title: Formal $\epsilon-K$ Definition
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } \forall n \ge K, \; |x_n - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: For every positive tolerance $\epsilon$, all terms after some index $K$ lie in the open interval $(x - \epsilon, x + \epsilon)$.

m3.final_answer: A sequence $(x_n)$ converges to $x$ if for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists an integer $K \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $|x_n - x| < \epsilon$ for all $n \ge K$.
m3.exam_tip: Also mention the neighborhood formulation: for every neighborhood $V_\epsilon(x)$, all but finitely many terms belong to $V_\epsilon(x)$.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Find the limit of the sequence $(\frac{2n}{3n+1})$ as $n \to \infty$.
m3.approach: Divide numerator and denominator by highest power $n$.

solution_steps.title: Algebraic Simplification
solution_steps.explanation: Divide top and bottom by $n$.

solution_steps.title: Apply Limit Laws
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} = 0 \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{2}{3 + \frac{1}{n}} = \frac{2}{3 + 0} = \frac{2}{3}
solution_steps.explanation: By the quotient rule for limits.

m3.final_answer: $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{2n}{3n+1} = \frac{2}{3}$.
m3.exam_tip: For full marks on a 2-mark question, also show the $\epsilon-K$ verification: $|\frac{2n}{3n+1} - \frac{2}{3}| = \frac{2}{3(3n+1)} < \frac{2}{9n} < \epsilon \implies n > \frac{2}{9\epsilon}$.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Define subsequential limit of a sequence.
m3.approach: Define cluster point / limit of a subsequence.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: L \in \mathbb{R} \text{ is a subsequential limit of } (x_n) \iff \exists \text{ subsequence } (x_{n_k}) \text{ such that } \lim_{k \to \infty} x_{n_k} = L
solution_steps.explanation: A real number $L$ is a subsequential limit if there exists a subsequence of $(x_n)$ converging to $L$.

m3.final_answer: A subsequential limit of $(x_n)$ is any real number $L$ that is the limit of some subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ of $(x_n)$.
m3.exam_tip: Example: For $x_n = (-1)^n$, the subsequential limits are $-1$ and $+1$.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Prove that a sequence of real numbers in $\mathbb{R}$ can have at most one limit.
m3.concept_tested: Uniqueness of Limit of a Sequence
m3.approach: Proof by contradiction: assume two distinct limits $x$ and $x'$, choose $\epsilon = |x - x'|/2$.

solution_steps.title: Assumption for Contradiction
solution_steps.math: \lim x_n = x \quad \text{and} \quad \lim x_n = x', \quad x \ne x'
solution_steps.explanation: Assume $(x_n)$ has two distinct limits.

solution_steps.title: Choose $\epsilon$
solution_steps.math: \epsilon = \frac{|x - x'|}{2} > 0
solution_steps.explanation: Half the positive distance between the two candidate limits.

solution_steps.title: Derive Contradiction via Triangle Inequality
solution_steps.math: \exists K_1, K_2 : n \ge K_1 \implies |x_n - x| < \epsilon, \; n \ge K_2 \implies |x_n - x'| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: For $n \ge \max(K_1, K_2)$: $|x - x'| \le |x - x_n| + |x_n - x'| < \epsilon + \epsilon = |x - x'|$, which is $|x - x'| < |x - x'|$, a contradiction.

m3.final_answer: A sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ can have at most one limit.
m3.exam_tip: The triangle inequality $|x - x'| \le |x - x_n| + |x_n - x'|$ produces the crisp contradiction.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question:
Give an example of two divergent sequences $X$ and $Y$ such that:
  1. Their sum $X + Y$ converges
  2. Their product $XY$ converges
m3.concept_tested: Non-preservation of Divergence under Algebraic Operations
m3.approach: Use oscillating sequences like $x_n = (-1)^n$ and $y_n = (-1)^{n+1}$ or $y_n = (-1)^n$.

solution_steps.title: Part (a): Convergent Sum
solution_steps.explanation: Both $X$ and $Y$ diverge. But $X + Y = (0, 0, 0, \dots) \to 0$, which converges.

solution_steps.title: Part (b): Convergent Product
solution_steps.explanation: Both $X$ and $Y$ diverge, but their product is the constant sequence 1, which converges.

m3.exam_tip: Alternating sequences $(-1)^n$ are the best counterexamples for sequence algebra.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Give an example of an unbounded sequence that has a convergent subsequence.
m3.approach: Interleave an unbounded sequence with a convergent one.

solution_steps.title: Construction
solution_steps.math: x_n = \begin{cases} n, & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \\ 0, & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: The sequence is $(1, 0, 3, 0, 5, 0, 7, 0, \dots)$.

solution_steps.title: Verification of Unboundedness
solution_steps.math: \sup\{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} = +\infty \implies (x_n) \text{ is unbounded}
solution_steps.explanation: Odd terms grow without bound.

solution_steps.title: Convergent Subsequence
solution_steps.math: x_{2k} = 0 \; \forall k \in \mathbb{N} \implies \lim_{k \to \infty} x_{2k} = 0
solution_steps.explanation: The even subsequence $(x_{2k}) = (0, 0, 0, \dots)$ is constant and converges to 0.

m3.final_answer: $x_n = (1 - (-1)^n) \frac{n}{2}$ gives $(1, 0, 3, 0, 5, 0, \dots)$, which is unbounded, but the even subsequence converges to 0.
m3.exam_tip: Another classic example: $x_n = n \sin(n\pi/2)$.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Write a short note on Properly Divergent Sequences.
m3.approach: Define divergence to $+\infty$ and $-\infty$, contrast with oscillatory divergence.

solution_steps.title: Definition of $\lim x_n = +\infty$
solution_steps.math: \forall M \in \mathbb{R}, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n \ge K \implies x_n > M
solution_steps.explanation: The terms eventually exceed any real bound $M$.

solution_steps.title: Definition of $\lim x_n = -\infty$
solution_steps.math: \forall M \in \mathbb{R}, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n \ge K \implies x_n < M
solution_steps.explanation: The terms eventually fall below any real bound $M$.

solution_steps.title: Contrast with Oscillatory Divergence
solution_steps.math: x_n = (-1)^n \text{ or } x_n = (-1)^n n
solution_steps.explanation: A sequence that does not converge and does not tend to $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ is said to diverge by oscillation.

m3.final_answer: A sequence $(x_n)$ is properly divergent if $\lim x_n = +\infty$ or $\lim x_n = -\infty$. Unlike oscillatory divergent sequences, it tends toward infinity in a definite direction.
m3.exam_tip: Include examples: $x_n = n^2$ (properly divergent) vs $x_n = (-1)^n n$ (improperly/oscillatory divergent).

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Define Euler's number $e$ as the limit of a sequence.
m3.concept_tested: Euler's Number $e$ as a Sequence Limit
m3.approach: Define $e = \lim (1 + 1/n)^n$ and state its monotonicity and boundedness.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Sequence $e_n$
solution_steps.math: e_n = \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n \quad \text{for } n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: The standard sequence defining Euler's constant.

solution_steps.title: Monotonicity and Bound
solution_steps.math: e_n < e_{n+1} \; (\text{strictly increasing}) \quad \text{and} \quad 2 \le e_n < 3 \; (\text{bounded above})
solution_steps.explanation: Using binomial expansion, each term is shown to increase with $n$ and remain bounded above by $1 + 1 + 1/2! + 1/3! + \dots = 3$.

solution_steps.title: Definition of $e$
solution_steps.math: e = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n \approx 2.718281828459\dots
solution_steps.explanation: By the Monotone Convergence Theorem, this limit exists and defines $e$.

m3.final_answer: $e = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{1}{k!} \approx 2.71828$.
m3.exam_tip: Mention that existence of the limit is guaranteed by the Monotone Convergence Theorem.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: State and prove Cantor's Nested Intervals Theorem.
m3.approach: Define the set of left endpoints, take its supremum $\xi$, and prove $\xi \in [a_n, b_n]$ for all $n$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: I_n = [a_n, b_n], \quad I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N} \implies \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n \ne \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: If $I_n$ is a nested sequence of closed bounded intervals, there exists at least one real number $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n$.

solution_steps.title: Properties of Endpoints
solution_steps.math: a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_n \le \dots \le b_m \le \dots \le b_2 \le b_1
solution_steps.explanation: For any $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, $a_n \le a_{\max(n,m)} \le b_{\max(n,m)} \le b_m$. Thus every $b_m$ is an upper bound for $A = \{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$.

solution_steps.title: Existence of Supremum
solution_steps.math: A = \{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \ne \emptyset \text{ is bounded above} \implies \xi = \sup A \in \mathbb{R} \text{ exists}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Property of $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Verification that $\xi \in I_n$
solution_steps.math: a_n \le \xi \; (\forall n) \quad \text{and} \quad \xi \le b_n \; (\forall n) \implies a_n \le \xi \le b_n \implies \xi \in [a_n, b_n] = I_n \; (\forall n)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\xi$ is the supremum of $A$, $a_n \le \xi$. Since each $b_n$ is an upper bound for $A$, $\xi \le b_n$. Hence $\xi \in \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n$.

m3.final_answer: $\xi = \sup\{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \in \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n$, so the intersection is non-empty.
m3.exam_tip: If the problem also mentions length tending to zero: $\inf\{b_n - a_n\} = 0 \implies \xi$ is unique.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: State and prove the Monotone Convergence Theorem for bounded sequences.
m3.concept_tested: Monotone Convergence Theorem for Bounded Sequences
m3.approach: State the theorem and prove the increasing case using $x = \sup\{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \text{A monotone sequence of real numbers is convergent if and only if it is bounded.}
solution_steps.explanation: Specifically: an increasing sequence bounded above converges to its supremum; a decreasing sequence bounded below converges to its infimum.

solution_steps.title: Setting up the Supremum
solution_steps.math: S = \{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}. \quad S \ne \emptyset \text{ and bounded above} \implies x = \sup S \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Property of $\mathbb{R}$, $x = \sup S$ exists.

solution_steps.title: Applying the $\epsilon$-characterization
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; x - \epsilon < x \implies \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } x_K > x - \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x - \epsilon$ is not an upper bound of $S$.

solution_steps.title: Monotonicity and Conclusion
solution_steps.math: n \ge K \implies x - \epsilon < x_K \le x_n \le x < x + \epsilon \implies |x_n - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Because $(x_n)$ is increasing, $x_n \ge x_K$. Since $x$ is an upper bound, $x_n \le x$. Thus $|x_n - x| < \epsilon$ for all $n \ge K$, so $\lim x_n = x$.

m3.final_answer: Every bounded monotone sequence converges. For an increasing sequence, $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = \sup\{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$.
m3.exam_tip: Clearly show the two bounds: $x - \epsilon < x_K \le x_n$ (from monotonicity) and $x_n \le x < x + \epsilon$ (from upper bound).

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Let $X = (x_n)$ be a sequence of real numbers that converges to $x$ and $Z = (z_n)$ be a sequence of non-zero real numbers that converges to $z \ne 0$. Prove that $X/Z$ converges to $x/z$.
m3.concept_tested: Quotient Rule for Limits of Sequences
m3.approach: Show that $1/z_n \to 1/z$ using a lower bound for $|z_n|$, then apply the product limit theorem.

solution_steps.title: Bound on $|z_n|$ away from 0
solution_steps.math: \lim z_n = z \ne 0. \quad \text{Set } \epsilon_0 = \frac{|z|}{2} > 0. \quad \exists K_1 : n \ge K_1 \implies |z_n - z| < \frac{|z|}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By reverse triangle inequality, $|z_n| \ge |z| - |z_n - z| > |z| - \frac{|z|}{2} = \frac{|z|}{2}$ for all $n \ge K_1$.

solution_steps.title: Convergence of Reciprocals $1/z_n \to 1/z$
solution_steps.math: \left|\frac{1}{z_n} - \frac{1}{z}\right| = \frac{|z - z_n|}{|z_n||z|} \le \frac{|z_n - z|}{\frac{|z|}{2}|z|} = \frac{2}{|z|^2} |z_n - z|
solution_steps.explanation: Given $\epsilon > 0$, choose $K_2$ such that $n \ge K_2 \implies |z_n - z| < \frac{|z|^2 \epsilon}{2}$. For $n \ge \max(K_1, K_2)$, $|1/z_n - 1/z| < \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Product Limit Law
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{x_n}{z_n} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(x_n \cdot \frac{1}{z_n}\right) = x \cdot \frac{1}{z} = \frac{x}{z}
solution_steps.explanation: Applying the theorem that the limit of a product of convergent sequences is the product of their limits.

m3.final_answer: $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{x_n}{z_n} = \frac{x}{z}$.
m3.exam_tip: The step establishing $|z_n| > |z|/2$ is where most students lose marks if omitted.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded increasing sequence. Prove that $\lim(x_n) = \sup \{x_n \mid n \in \mathbb{N}\}$.
m3.approach: Let $u = \sup\{x_n\}$, use $\epsilon$-definition of supremum, then monotonicity.

solution_steps.title: Existence of Supremum
solution_steps.math: S = \{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}. \quad S \ne \emptyset, \, S \text{ bounded above} \implies u = \sup S \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Axiom of $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Finding Index $K$
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; u - \epsilon < u \implies \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } u - \epsilon < x_K \le u
solution_steps.explanation: Since $u - \epsilon$ is not an upper bound of $S$.

solution_steps.title: Monotonicity Inequality
solution_steps.math: n \ge K \implies u - \epsilon < x_K \le x_n \le u < u + \epsilon \implies |x_n - u| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since $(x_n)$ is increasing, $x_n \ge x_K$. Since $u$ is an upper bound, $x_n \le u$.

m3.final_answer: $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = \sup\{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$.
m3.exam_tip: State clearly that every term is bounded between $u - \epsilon$ and $u + \epsilon$ for all $n \ge K$.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Show that the sequence of functions $f_n(x) = \frac{x^n}{1+x^n}$ converges pointwise but not uniformly on the interval $[0, 2]$.
m3.approach: Find pointwise limit $f(x)$ on $[0, 2]$, note discontinuity at $x=1$, which rules out uniform convergence.

solution_steps.title: Pointwise Limit Calculation
solution_steps.math: f(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{x^n}{1+x^n} = \begin{cases} 0, & 0 \le x < 1 \\ 1/2, & x = 1 \\ 1, & 1 < x \le 2 \end{cases}

solution_steps.title: Continuity of Individual Functions
solution_steps.math: f_n(x) = \frac{x^n}{1+x^n} \text{ is continuous on } [0, 2] \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $1 + x^n \ge 1 \ne 0$ on $[0, 2]$, $f_n$ is a rational function with non-vanishing denominator, hence continuous.

solution_steps.title: Discontinuity of Limit Function
solution_steps.explanation: $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x = 1$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion on Uniform Convergence
solution_steps.math: (f_n \text{ continuous} \land f_n \rightrightarrows f) \implies f \text{ continuous}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Uniform Limit Theorem, uniform convergence preserves continuity. Since $f$ is discontinuous, $(f_n)$ cannot converge uniformly on $[0, 2]$.

m3.final_answer: $f_n \to f$ pointwise, but NOT uniformly on $[0, 2]$ because the limit function $f$ is discontinuous at $x = 1$.
m3.exam_tip: Using the Uniform Limit Theorem contrapositive is much faster than computing the supremum norm.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Show that every uniformly convergent sequence of bounded functions is uniformly bounded.
m3.concept_tested: Uniform Boundedness of Uniformly Convergent Sequences
m3.approach: Use uniform convergence to bound $|f_n(x) - f(x)| < 1$, then bound $f(x)$, then take maximum over initial functions.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Convergence for $\epsilon = 1$
solution_steps.math: f_n \rightrightarrows f \text{ on } A \implies \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } \forall n \ge H, \; \sup_{x \in A} |f_n(x) - f(x)| < 1
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of uniform convergence with $\epsilon = 1$.

solution_steps.title: Boundedness of Limit Function $f$
solution_steps.math: f_H \text{ is bounded by } M_H \implies |f(x)| \le |f(x) - f_H(x)| + |f_H(x)| < 1 + M_H \; (\forall x \in A)
solution_steps.explanation: Thus the limit function $f$ is bounded on $A$ by $M_f = 1 + M_H$.

solution_steps.title: Bound for $n \ge H$
solution_steps.math: n \ge H \implies |f_n(x)| \le |f_n(x) - f(x)| + |f(x)| < 1 + M_f \; (\forall x \in A)
solution_steps.explanation: All functions beyond index $H$ are uniformly bounded by $1 + M_f$.

solution_steps.title: Global Uniform Bound $M$
solution_steps.math: M = \max\{M_1, M_2, \dots, M_{H-1}, 1 + M_f\} \implies |f_n(x)| \le M \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \; \forall x \in A
solution_steps.explanation: Since each of the first $H-1$ functions is bounded by some $M_k$, taking the maximum over this finite set gives a uniform bound valid for all $n$ and all $x \in A$.

m3.final_answer: There exists $M > 0$ such that $|f_n(x)| \le M$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $x \in A$.
m3.exam_tip: Emphasize that the finite collection $\{f_1, \dots, f_{H-1}\}$ has a maximum bound, which ensures a single global bound $M$.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Let $f_n(x) = \frac{\sin(nx)}{\sqrt{n}}$ for $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Show that $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to 0, but the sequence of derivatives $(f_n')$ does not converge pointwise to 0 on $\mathbb{R}$.
m3.concept_tested: Uniform Convergence vs Differentiation of Sequences
m3.approach: Show $\sup |f_n(x)| \to 0$, compute $f_n'(x) = \sqrt{n}\cos(nx)$, and evaluate at $x = 0$.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Convergence of $(f_n)$
solution_steps.math: |f_n(x)| = \left|\frac{\sin(nx)}{\sqrt{n}}\right| \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $|\sin(u)| \le 1$ for all $u$.

solution_steps.title: Supremum Norm Limit
solution_steps.math: \|f_n - 0\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |f_n(x)| \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \to 0 \text{ as } n \to \infty \implies f_n \rightrightarrows 0 \text{ on } \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to the zero function on $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Compute Derivative $f_n'(x)$
solution_steps.math: f_n'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{\sin(nx)}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = \frac{n\cos(nx)}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{n}\cos(nx)
solution_steps.explanation: By standard differentiation.

solution_steps.title: Evaluate at $x = 0$
solution_steps.math: f_n'(0) = \sqrt{n} \cos(0) = \sqrt{n} \to +\infty \ne 0
solution_steps.explanation: At $x = 0$, $f_n'(0) \to +\infty$, so $(f_n')$ does not converge to $0$ (it diverges).

m3.final_answer: $f_n \rightrightarrows 0$ uniformly, but $f_n'(0) = \sqrt{n} \to \infty$, so $(f_n')$ does not converge pointwise to $(0)' = 0$.
m3.exam_tip: This is the classic example demonstrating why differentiation does not commute with uniform limits without additional conditions on $f_n'$.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Show that every convergent sequence in a metric space is a Cauchy sequence.
m3.concept_tested: Convergent Sequences are Cauchy in Metric Spaces
m3.approach: Use the metric triangle inequality $d(x_n, x_m) \le d(x_n, x) + d(x, x_m)$ with tolerance $\epsilon/2$.

solution_steps.title: Convergence Hypothesis
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x \text{ in } (M, d) \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } n \ge H \implies d(x_n, x) < \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of metric convergence.

solution_steps.title: Metric Triangle Inequality
solution_steps.math: d(x_n, x_m) \le d(x_n, x) + d(x, x_m) = d(x_n, x) + d(x_m, x)
solution_steps.explanation: Using triangle inequality and symmetry $d(x, x_m) = d(x_m, x)$.

solution_steps.title: Cauchy Condition
solution_steps.math: n, m \ge H \implies d(x_n, x_m) < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Hence $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $(M, d)$.

m3.final_answer: Every convergent sequence in any metric space is Cauchy.
m3.exam_tip: Always mention the use of both the triangle inequality and symmetry axioms of the metric.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Prove that every convergent sequence of real numbers is a Cauchy sequence.
m3.approach: Apply triangle inequality $|x_n - x_m| \le |x_n - x| + |x_m - x|$ with $\epsilon/2$.

solution_steps.title: Convergence Definition & Setup with $\epsilon/2$
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x \implies \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n \ge H \implies |x_n - x| < \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of sequence convergence, for any chosen tolerance $\epsilon > 0$, the sequence terms eventually lie within $\epsilon/2$ of the limit $x$.

solution_steps.title: Pairing Indices $n, m \ge H$
solution_steps.math: n \ge H \implies |x_n - x| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} \quad \text{and} \quad m \ge H \implies |x_m - x| < \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: Both indices $n$ and $m$ are greater than or equal to $H$, so both $x_n$ and $x_m$ are within distance $\epsilon/2$ of the target limit $x$.

solution_steps.title: Triangle Inequality & Cauchy Conclusion
solution_steps.math: n, m \ge H \implies |x_n - x_m| = |(x_n - x) + (x - x_m)| \le |x_n - x| + |x_m - x| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: By the Triangle Inequality, the distance between any two terms past index $H$ satisfies $|x_n - x_m| < \epsilon$. Therefore, $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence.

m3.final_answer: Every convergent sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
m3.exam_tip: State that the converse also holds in $\mathbb{R}$ (Cauchy Convergence Criterion / Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$).

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: State and prove the Monotone Convergence Theorem for sequences.
m3.approach: Prove both directions: bounded monotone implies convergent; convergent implies bounded.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \text{A monotone sequence of real numbers is convergent } \iff \text{it is bounded.}
solution_steps.explanation: Convergence implies boundedness (for all sequences). For monotone sequences, boundedness also implies convergence.

solution_steps.title: Convergence $\implies$ Boundedness
solution_steps.math: x_n \to x \implies (x_n) \text{ is bounded}
solution_steps.explanation: Every convergent sequence is bounded (choose $\epsilon=1$, $M = \max\{|x_1|, \dots, |x_{K-1}|, |x|+1\}$).

solution_steps.title: Boundedness $\implies$ Convergence (Increasing case)
solution_steps.math: x_n \le x_{n+1}, \, x_n \le M \implies u = \sup\{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, the supremum $u$ exists.

solution_steps.title: Verification of Limit
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K : u - \epsilon < x_K \le x_n \le u < u + \epsilon \; (\forall n \ge K) \implies \lim x_n = u
solution_steps.explanation: This shows $x_n \to u$.

m3.final_answer: A monotone sequence converges if and only if it is bounded. If $(x_n)$ is increasing and bounded, $\lim x_n = \sup\{x_n\}$; if decreasing and bounded, $\lim x_n = \inf\{x_n\}$.
m3.exam_tip: Remember to address the $(\implies)$ direction as well since the theorem is an 'if and only if' statement.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Prove that a sequence of real numbers is convergent if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence.
m3.approach: Prove both: $(\implies)$ convergent is Cauchy; $(\impliedby)$ Cauchy is bounded, has convergent subsequence by Bolzano-Weierstrass, then converges to same limit.

solution_steps.title: Direction 1 ($\implies$): Convergent $\implies$ Cauchy
solution_steps.math: |x_n - x_m| \le |x_n - x| + |x_m - x| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon \quad (n, m \ge H)
solution_steps.explanation: Proved using the triangle inequality.

solution_steps.title: Direction 2 ($\impliedby$): Step 2a — Cauchy is Bounded
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \text{ is Cauchy} \implies (x_n) \text{ is bounded}
solution_steps.explanation: Fix $\epsilon = 1$, all terms beyond $H$ lie in $(x_H - 1, x_H + 1)$.

solution_steps.title: Step 2b — Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \text{ bounded} \implies \exists \text{ subsequence } (x_{n_k}) \text{ converging to some } x^* \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ contains a convergent subsequence.

solution_steps.title: Step 2c — Parent Sequence Converges to $x^*$
solution_steps.math: |x_n - x^*| \le |x_n - x_{n_k}| + |x_{n_k} - x^*| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon \quad \text{for large } n, k
solution_steps.explanation: Since $n_k \ge k \ge H$ and $n \ge H$, the Cauchy property traps $x_n$ close to $x_{n_k}$, which is close to $x^*$.

m3.final_answer: A sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ converges if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence.
m3.exam_tip: The chain of logic for completeness: Cauchy $\implies$ bounded $\implies$ Bolzano-Weierstrass gives convergent subsequence $\implies$ entire Cauchy sequence converges.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Show that the sequence $(x_n)$ defined by $x_1 = 1$ and $x_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + x_n}$ is convergent and find its limit.
m3.approach: Use mathematical induction to show bounded and increasing, apply Monotone Convergence Theorem, then solve the algebraic limit equation.

solution_steps.title: Induction: Bounded above by 2
solution_steps.math: x_1 = 1 < 2. \quad \text{Assume } x_k < 2 \implies x_{k+1} = \sqrt{2 + x_k} < \sqrt{2 + 2} = 2
solution_steps.explanation: By induction, $x_n < 2$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

solution_steps.title: Induction: Monotonically Increasing
solution_steps.math: x_1 = 1 < x_2 = \sqrt{3}. \quad x_k < x_{k+1} \implies 2 + x_k < 2 + x_{k+1} \implies \sqrt{2 + x_k} < \sqrt{2 + x_{k+1}} \implies x_{k+1} < x_{k+2}
solution_steps.explanation: By induction, $x_n < x_{n+1}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

solution_steps.title: Monotone Convergence Theorem
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \text{ is increasing and bounded above} \implies L = \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n \text{ exists}
solution_steps.explanation: The limit $L$ exists and $L > 0$ since $x_n \ge 1$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate Limit
solution_steps.math: L = \sqrt{2 + L} \implies L^2 = 2 + L \implies L^2 - L - 2 = 0 \implies (L - 2)(L + 1) = 0
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x_n > 0$, $L \ge 1 > 0$, discarding $L = -1$ gives $L = 2$.

m3.final_answer: $(x_n)$ is convergent and $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = 2$.
m3.exam_tip: You must prove convergence BEFORE writing $L = \sqrt{2+L}$; writing the equation first assumes the limit exists.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Let $X = (x_n)$ be a sequence of real numbers and let $m \in \mathbb{N}$. Prove that the $m$-tail $X_m = (x_{n+m})$ of $X$ converges if and only if $X$ converges, and $\lim X = \lim X_m$.
m3.approach: Use the definition of limit and index shift $k = n + m$.

solution_steps.title: Definition of $m$-tail
solution_steps.explanation: The sequence obtained by discarding the first $m$ terms.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction: $X \to x \implies X_m \to x$
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists K : n \ge K \implies |x_n - x| < \epsilon. \quad \text{For } X_m, \text{ if } n \ge K, \text{ then } n + m > n \ge K \implies |x_{n+m} - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: So $X_m$ converges to $x$ (with cutoff index $K_m = \max(1, K - m)$).

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction: $X_m \to x \implies X \to x$
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists K_m : n \ge K_m \implies |x_{n+m} - x| < \epsilon. \quad \text{Set } K = K_m + m. \text{ For } p \ge K, p - m \ge K_m \implies |x_p - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $X$ converges to $x$.

m3.final_answer: The $m$-tail $X_m$ converges if and only if $X$ converges, and $\lim X_m = \lim X$.
m3.exam_tip: This theorem formally justifies why finitely many initial terms never affect convergence or the value of the limit.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Construct a sequence $(s_n)$ of real numbers that converges to $\sqrt{5}$ and is correct to within 4 decimal places.
m3.concept_tested: Construction of Sequence Converging to $\sqrt{5}$ (Newton's Method)
m3.approach: Use the Babylonian recurrence $s_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}(s_n + 5/s_n)$ with $s_1 = 2$.

solution_steps.title: Recurrence Formula
solution_steps.math: s_1 = 2, \quad s_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2} \left(s_n + \frac{5}{s_n}\right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 1
solution_steps.explanation: Newton-Raphson iteration for solving $f(x) = x^2 - 5 = 0$.

solution_steps.title: Computing Iterates
solution_steps.explanation: First iteration.

solution_steps.title: Second and Third Iterates
solution_steps.math: s_3 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{9}{4} + \frac{20}{9}\right) = \frac{161}{72} \approx 2.236111\dots, \quad s_4 = \frac{1}{2}\left(s_3 + \frac{5}{s_3}\right) \approx 2.236067977
solution_steps.explanation: Evaluating successive terms.

solution_steps.title: Error Bound
solution_steps.explanation: $s_3 = 161/72$ is already accurate to 4 decimal places ($2.2361$). $s_4$ is accurate to 8 decimal places.

m3.final_answer: The sequence is defined by $s_1 = 2, s_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}(s_n + 5/s_n)$. The term $s_3 = \frac{161}{72} \approx 2.2361$ approximates $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236068$ correct to 4 decimal places.
m3.exam_tip: Show the fraction $161/72$ and its decimal value to prove accuracy within $0.0001$.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: State and prove the Monotone Subsequence Theorem.
m3.approach: Define peak points: $x_m$ is a peak if $x_m \ge x_n$ for all $n > m$. Case 1: infinitely many peaks; Case 2: finitely many peaks.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \text{Every sequence of real numbers } (x_n) \text{ has a monotonic subsequence.}
solution_steps.explanation: Either a monotonically increasing or monotonically decreasing subsequence always exists.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Peak
solution_steps.math: x_m \text{ is a peak if } x_m \ge x_n \quad \forall n > m
solution_steps.explanation: A term is a peak if no subsequent term strictly exceeds it.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: Infinitely Many Peaks
solution_steps.math: m_1 < m_2 < m_3 < \dots \text{ (peak indices)} \implies x_{m_1} \ge x_{m_2} \ge x_{m_3} \ge \dots
solution_steps.explanation: The subsequence of peaks $(x_{m_k})$ is a decreasing sequence.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: Finitely Many Peaks (or No Peaks)
solution_steps.math: s_1 > \text{last peak} \implies \exists s_2 > s_1 \text{ s.t. } x_{s_2} > x_{s_1}; \quad \exists s_3 > s_2 \text{ s.t. } x_{s_3} > x_{s_2}, \dots
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x_{s_1}$ is not a peak, there exists $s_2 > s_1$ with $x_{s_2} > x_{s_1}$. Continuing inductively produces a strictly increasing subsequence $x_{s_1} < x_{s_2} < x_{s_3} < \dots$.

m3.final_answer: Every sequence has a monotonic subsequence (decreasing if infinitely many peaks, increasing if finitely many peaks).
m3.exam_tip: This theorem is the fastest and most elegant way to prove the Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Let $x_1 = 2$ and $x_{n+1} = 2 + \frac{1}{x_n}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Show that $(x_n)$ is a contractive sequence, and find its limit.
m3.concept_tested: Contractive Sequences and Fixed Point Limits
m3.approach: Show $|x_{n+2} - x_{n+1}| \le C |x_{n+1} - x_n|$ with $C < 1$, then solve $L = 2 + 1/L$.

solution_steps.title: Terms and Bounds
solution_steps.math: x_1 = 2, \quad x_2 = 2 + 1/2 = 2.5, \quad x_n \ge 2 \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x_1 = 2$ and $x_{n+1} = 2 + 1/x_n > 2$ by induction.

solution_steps.title: Contractive Verification
solution_steps.math: |x_{n+2} - x_{n+1}| = \left|\left(2 + \frac{1}{x_{n+1}}\right) - \left(2 + \frac{1}{x_n}\right)\right| = \frac{|x_n - x_{n+1}|}{x_n x_{n+1}}
solution_steps.explanation: Compute the difference between successive terms.

solution_steps.title: Contractive Constant $C$
solution_steps.math: x_n \ge 2, \, x_{n+1} \ge 2 \implies x_n x_{n+1} \ge 4 \implies |x_{n+2} - x_{n+1}| \le \frac{1}{4} |x_{n+1} - x_n|
solution_steps.explanation: Since $C = 1/4 < 1$, the sequence is contractive.

solution_steps.title: Convergence and Limit
solution_steps.math: L = 2 + \frac{1}{L} \implies L^2 - 2L - 1 = 0 \implies L = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 4}}{2} = 1 \pm \sqrt{2}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x_n \ge 2 > 0$, $L > 0$, so $L = 1 + \sqrt{2}$.

m3.final_answer: $(x_n)$ is contractive with constant $C = 1/4 < 1$, hence it converges to $L = 1 + \sqrt{2}$.
m3.exam_tip: Note that every contractive sequence is Cauchy, and hence convergent in $\mathbb{R}$.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: State and prove the Monotone Convergence Theorem. Let $s_1 = 1$ and $s_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}(s_n + \frac{a}{s_n})$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, where $a > 0$. Prove that $(s_n)$ converges to $\sqrt{a}$.
m3.concept_tested: Monotone Convergence Theorem and Heron's Algorithm for $\sqrt{a}$
m3.approach: Prove the general MCT for bounded increasing sequences. Then show $s_n^2 \ge a$ for $n \ge 2$, $(s_n)$ is decreasing for $n \ge 2$ and bounded below, apply MCT, and find $L = \sqrt{a}$.

solution_steps.title: Statement of Monotone Convergence Theorem
solution_steps.math: \text{A monotone sequence of real numbers is convergent } \iff \text{it is bounded.} \quad \text{If bounded increasing, } \lim x_n = \sup\{x_n\}; \text{ if bounded decreasing, } \lim x_n = \inf\{x_n\}.
solution_steps.explanation: A sequence that is both monotone and bounded always converges to its supremum (if increasing) or infimum (if decreasing).

solution_steps.title: Proof of Monotone Convergence Theorem
solution_steps.math: S = \{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \ne \emptyset, \, S \text{ bounded above} \implies x = \sup S \in \mathbb{R}. \quad \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } x - \epsilon < x_K \le x. \quad n \ge K \implies x - \epsilon < x_K \le x_n \le x < x + \epsilon \implies |x_n - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Axiom of $\mathbb{R}$, $S$ has a supremum $x$. Since $x - \epsilon$ is not an upper bound, some $x_K > x - \epsilon$. Since $(x_n)$ is increasing, $x_n \ge x_K > x - \epsilon$ for all $n \ge K$, while $x_n \le x < x + \epsilon$. Thus $|x_n - x| < \epsilon$, proving $\lim x_n = \sup S$.

solution_steps.title: Part 2: Boundedness of $(s_n)$ for $n \ge 2$
solution_steps.math: s_{n+1}^2 - a = \frac{1}{4}\left(s_n + \frac{a}{s_n}\right)^2 - a = \frac{1}{4}\left(s_n - \frac{a}{s_n}\right)^2 \ge 0 \implies s_{n+1} \ge \sqrt{a} \quad (\forall n \ge 1)
solution_steps.explanation: Completing the square proves $s_n \ge \sqrt{a} > 0$ for all $n \ge 2$, so the sequence is bounded below by $\sqrt{a}$.

solution_steps.title: Monotonicity of $(s_n)$ for $n \ge 2$
solution_steps.math: s_n - s_{n+1} = s_n - \frac{1}{2}\left(s_n + \frac{a}{s_n}\right) = \frac{s_n^2 - a}{2s_n} \ge 0 \quad (\forall n \ge 2) \implies s_{n+1} \le s_n
solution_steps.explanation: Since $s_n^2 \ge a$ and $s_n > 0$ for $n \ge 2$, the difference is non-negative, proving $(s_n)_{n=2}^\infty$ is monotonically decreasing.

solution_steps.title: Apply MCT and Solve for Limit
solution_steps.math: (s_n)_{n=2}^\infty \text{ bounded below and decreasing} \implies L = \lim s_n \text{ exists with } L \ge \sqrt{a}. \quad L = \frac{1}{2}\left(L + \frac{a}{L}\right) \implies 2L^2 = L^2 + a \implies L = \sqrt{a}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Monotone Convergence Theorem, $(s_n)$ converges to a real limit $L \ge \sqrt{a} > 0$. Taking limits on both sides of the recurrence equation gives $L = \sqrt{a}$.

m3.final_answer: By the Monotone Convergence Theorem, $(s_n)$ converges to $L = \sqrt{a}$.
m3.exam_tip: Notice that $s_1 = 1$ may not be $\ge \sqrt{a}$; monotonicity begins at $n = 2$.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Prove that every contractive sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ is a Cauchy sequence. Let $f_1=1, f_2=1$ and $f_{n+1}=f_n+f_{n-1}$. Define $x_n = \frac{f_n}{f_{n+1}}$. Prove that $\lim x_n = \frac{-1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
m3.concept_tested: Contractive Sequences, Cauchy Property, and Fibonacci Ratio Limit
m3.approach: Prove contractive implies Cauchy via geometric series bound. Then show $x_{n+1} = 1/(1 + x_n)$ and solve $L = 1/(1+L)$ for golden ratio conjugate.

solution_steps.title: Part 1: Contractive $\implies$ Cauchy
solution_steps.explanation: By repeated application of the contractive definition.

solution_steps.title: Telescoping Sum and Bound for $m > n$
solution_steps.explanation: Since $0 < C < 1$, $C^{n-1} \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. For any $\epsilon > 0$, choosing $H$ large enough makes this bound $< \epsilon$. Thus $(x_n)$ is Cauchy.

solution_steps.title: Part 2: Fibonacci Ratio Recurrence
solution_steps.explanation: Express $x_n$ in terms of $x_{n-1}$.

solution_steps.title: Convergence and Evaluation of Limit
solution_steps.explanation: Since $1/2 \le x_n \le 1$ for all $n \ge 1$, $C = 4/9 < 1$, so $(x_n)$ is contractive and converges to $L$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate Value of Limit
solution_steps.math: L = \frac{1}{1 + L} \implies L^2 + L - 1 = 0 \implies L = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 4}}{2} = \frac{-1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x_n > 0$, we take the positive root $L = \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2} = \frac{1}{\phi}$.

m3.final_answer: Every contractive sequence is Cauchy and hence convergent in $\mathbb{R}$. The Fibonacci ratio sequence converges to $L = \frac{-1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
m3.exam_tip: Note that $L = (\sqrt{5}-1)/2 = 1/\phi \approx 0.6180339$, the reciprocal of the golden ratio.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: State and prove the Nested Intervals Property of real numbers.
m3.approach: State the theorem for closed bounded nested intervals, prove non-empty intersection, and prove uniqueness when length converges to 0.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: I_n = [a_n, b_n], \quad I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N} \implies \exists \xi \in \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } \xi \in I_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Furthermore, if $\inf\{b_n - a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} = 0$, then the common point $\xi$ is unique.

solution_steps.title: Monotonicity of Endpoints
solution_steps.math: a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_n \le \dots \le b_m \le \dots \le b_2 \le b_1 \quad (\forall n, m \in \mathbb{N})
solution_steps.explanation: Since $I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n$, $[a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}] \subseteq [a_n, b_n]$, so $a_n \le a_{n+1}$ and $b_{n+1} \le b_n$. Moreover, for any $n, m$, $a_n \le a_{\max(n,m)} \le b_{\max(n,m)} \le b_m$.

solution_steps.title: Completeness Axiom Application
solution_steps.math: S = \{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \ne \emptyset, \, S \text{ bounded above by } b_1 \implies \xi = \sup S \in \mathbb{R} \text{ exists}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Property of $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Proof that $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n$
solution_steps.math: a_n \le \xi \; (\forall n) \quad \text{and} \quad \xi \le b_n \; (\forall n) \implies a_n \le \xi \le b_n \iff \xi \in [a_n, b_n] = I_n
