solution_steps.explanation: Because $\xi = \sup S$, $a_n \le \xi$. Because each $b_n$ is an upper bound of $S$, $\xi \le b_n$.

solution_steps.title: Uniqueness under $\lim(b_n - a_n) = 0$
solution_steps.math: \xi_1, \xi_2 \in \bigcap I_n \implies a_n \le \xi_1, \xi_2 \le b_n \implies 0 \le |\xi_1 - \xi_2| \le b_n - a_n \to 0 \implies \xi_1 = \xi_2
solution_steps.explanation: If the lengths tend to 0, the intersection contains precisely one point.

m3.final_answer: $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n = \{\xi\}$ when $\lim(b_n - a_n) = 0$.
m3.exam_tip: Give a counterexample to show why closedness is essential: for open intervals $J_n = (0, 1/n)$, $\bigcap J_n = \emptyset$.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: Let $X = (x_n)$ be a sequence of real numbers that converges to $x$ and suppose that $x_n \ge 0$ for all $n$. Prove that the sequence $(\sqrt{x_n})$ of positive square roots converges to $\sqrt{x}$.
m3.concept_tested: Continuity of Square Root / Limit of $(\sqrt{x_n})$
m3.approach: Consider cases $x = 0$ and $x > 0$. For $x > 0$, rationalize numerator using $\sqrt{x_n} - \sqrt{x} = \frac{x_n - x}{\sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x}}$.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: $x = 0$
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = 0, \, x_n \ge 0. \quad \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } n \ge K \implies 0 \le x_n < \epsilon^2
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\epsilon^2 > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Case 1 Conclusion
solution_steps.math: 0 \le x_n < \epsilon^2 \implies 0 \le \sqrt{x_n} < \epsilon \implies |\sqrt{x_n} - 0| < \epsilon \; (\forall n \ge K)
solution_steps.explanation: Taking square roots preserves order for non-negative numbers, so $\lim \sqrt{x_n} = 0 = \sqrt{0}$.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: $x > 0$ — Rationalizing the Difference
solution_steps.math: |\sqrt{x_n} - \sqrt{x}| = \left|\frac{(\sqrt{x_n} - \sqrt{x})(\sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x})}{\sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x}}\right| = \frac{|x_n - x|}{\sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x}}
solution_steps.explanation: Multiply and divide by conjugate $\sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x}$.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: Bounding the Denominator
solution_steps.math: \sqrt{x_n} \ge 0 \implies \sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x} \ge \sqrt{x} \implies |\sqrt{x_n} - \sqrt{x}| \le \frac{|x_n - x|}{\sqrt{x}}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\sqrt{x_n} \ge 0$, the denominator is at least $\sqrt{x} > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K : n \ge K \implies |x_n - x| < \epsilon\sqrt{x} \implies |\sqrt{x_n} - \sqrt{x}| < \frac{\epsilon\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}} = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $\lim_{n \to \infty} \sqrt{x_n} = \sqrt{x}$.

m3.final_answer: In both cases ($x = 0$ and $x > 0$), $\lim_{n \to \infty} \sqrt{x_n} = \sqrt{x}$.
m3.exam_tip: Do NOT forget to treat $x = 0$ separately, because dividing by $\sqrt{x}$ is undefined when $x = 0$!

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: State and prove Cauchy's criterion for uniform convergence of sequences of functions.
m3.concept_tested: Cauchy Criterion for Uniform Convergence of Sequences of Functions
m3.approach: Prove both directions: $f_n \rightrightarrows f \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists H, \forall n, m \ge H, \forall x \in A, |f_n(x) - f_m(x)| < \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: (f_n) \text{ converges uniformly on } A \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } \forall n, m \ge H, \; \sup_{x \in A} |f_n(x) - f_m(x)| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: A sequence of functions converges uniformly if and only if it satisfies the uniform Cauchy criterion.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction ($\implies$)
solution_steps.math: f_n \rightrightarrows f \implies \exists H : n \ge H \implies |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} \; (\forall x \in A)
solution_steps.explanation: For $n, m \ge H$: $|f_n(x) - f_m(x)| \le |f_n(x) - f(x)| + |f(x) - f_m(x)| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon$ for all $x \in A$.

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction ($\impliedby$): Pointwise Limit
solution_steps.math: \forall x_0 \in A, \; |f_n(x_0) - f_m(x_0)| < \epsilon \implies (f_n(x_0)) \text{ is Cauchy in } \mathbb{R} \implies f(x_0) = \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(x_0) \text{ exists}
solution_steps.explanation: By Cauchy completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, $(f_n)$ converges pointwise to some limit function $f: A \to \mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction: Uniformity of the Limit
solution_steps.math: n, m \ge H \implies |f_n(x) - f_m(x)| < \epsilon. \quad \text{Take } m \to \infty: \quad |f_n(x) - f(x)| \le \epsilon \quad \forall n \ge H, \; \forall x \in A
solution_steps.explanation: Passing to the limit as $m \to \infty$ with $n \ge H$ fixed preserves the weak inequality $\le \epsilon < 2\epsilon$, establishing uniform convergence.

m3.final_answer: $(f_n)$ converges uniformly on $A$ if and only if it satisfies the Cauchy criterion on $A$.
m3.exam_tip: The power of this criterion is that it establishes uniform convergence WITHOUT needing to know the limit function $f$ in advance.

m3.topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
m3.question: State and prove the Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem for sequences of real numbers.
m3.approach: State the theorem and prove using the Monotone Subsequence Theorem + Monotone Convergence Theorem, or by bisection of intervals.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \text{Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence.}
solution_steps.explanation: If $(x_n)$ is bounded, there exists a subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ that converges in $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Step 1: Existence of Monotonic Subsequence (Peak Points)
solution_steps.math: x_m \text{ is a peak if } x_m \ge x_n \; \forall n \ge m. \quad \text{Case 1: } \infty \text{ peaks } \implies x_{m_1} \ge x_{m_2} \ge \dots \text{ (decreasing)}. \quad \text{Case 2: finitely many peaks } \implies \text{chase strictly larger elements (increasing)}.
solution_steps.explanation: By the Monotone Subsequence Theorem, every sequence has a monotonic subsequence: either infinitely many peak points exist (producing a decreasing subsequence), or past the last peak every term is exceeded by a later term (producing a strictly increasing subsequence).

solution_steps.title: Step 2: Subsequence Inherits Boundedness
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \text{ is bounded} \implies \exists M > 0 \text{ s.t. } -M \le x_n \le M \; (\forall n) \implies -M \le x_{n_k} \le M \; (\forall k)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $(x_{n_k})$ is a subsequence of $(x_n)$, every term $x_{n_k}$ satisfies the same bounds.

solution_steps.title: Step 3: Application of Monotone Convergence Theorem
solution_steps.math: (x_{n_k}) \text{ is bounded and monotone} \implies (x_{n_k}) \text{ converges to a real limit } x^*
solution_steps.explanation: If $(x_{n_k})$ is increasing, $x^* = \sup\{x_{n_k}\}$; if decreasing, $x^* = \inf\{x_{n_k}\}$.

m3.final_answer: Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ contains a convergent subsequence.
m3.exam_tip: The two-step proof (Monotone Subsequence Theorem + Monotone Convergence Theorem) is the cleanest and fastest method in Bartle & Sherbert.

m4.question: Define a partition of a closed interval $[a, b]$.
m4.concept_tested: Definition of Partition of an Interval
m4.approach: Give the formal definition of a partition $P$ as an ordered finite set of points starting at $a$ and ending at $b$.

solution_steps.title: Formal Definition
solution_steps.math: P = \{x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\} \quad \text{where } a = x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_{n-1} < x_n = b
solution_steps.explanation: A partition $P$ of $[a, b]$ is a finite ordered subset of $[a, b]$ dividing the interval into $n$ non-overlapping subintervals $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$ for $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$.

m4.final_answer: A partition of $[a, b]$ is a finite ordered set of points $P = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ such that $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$.
m4.exam_tip: Always mention the subintervals $I_i = [x_{i-1}, x_i]$ and that their union is $[a, b]$.

m4.question: State the Riemann integrability criterion for a bounded function $f$ on $[a, b]$.
m4.approach: State the necessary and sufficient condition $U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Criterion Statement
solution_steps.math: f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b] \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists \text{ partition } P_\epsilon \text{ of } [a, b] \text{ such that } U(P_\epsilon, f) - L(P_\epsilon, f) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: A bounded function $f$ on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable if and only if the difference between its upper and lower Darboux sums can be made arbitrarily small by choosing a suitable partition.

m4.final_answer: $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$ iff for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a partition $P$ such that $U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon$.
m4.exam_tip: State clearly that $f$ must be bounded on $[a, b]$ for this criterion to be applicable.

m4.question: Define the upper and lower Darboux sums of a function $f$ on $[a, b]$.
m4.approach: Define $M_i = \sup_{x \in I_i} f(x)$, $m_i = \inf_{x \in I_i} f(x)$, and the corresponding sum formulas.

solution_steps.title: Subinterval Extrema
solution_steps.math: M_i = \sup\{f(x) : x \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]\}, \quad m_i = \inf\{f(x) : x \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]\}, \quad \Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}
solution_steps.explanation: For each subinterval $I_i$ formed by partition $P$.

solution_steps.title: Definitions of Darboux Sums
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n M_i \Delta x_i \quad (\text{Upper Darboux Sum}), \qquad L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \Delta x_i \quad (\text{Lower Darboux Sum})
solution_steps.explanation: The upper sum is the sum of circumscribed rectangle areas; the lower sum is the sum of inscribed rectangle areas.

m4.final_answer: Upper sum: $U(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n M_i \Delta x_i$; Lower sum: $L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \Delta x_i$.
m4.exam_tip: Always note that $L(P, f) \le U(P, f)$ for any partition $P$.

m4.question: State the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (First Part).
m4.concept_tested: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (First Part / Differentiation Theorem)
m4.approach: State the differentiation property of the indefinite integral function $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)dt$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: F(x) = \int_a^x f(t) dt \quad \text{for } x \in [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: If $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$, then $F$ is continuous on $[a, b]$.

solution_steps.title: Differentiability at Continuity Points
solution_steps.math: \text{If } f \text{ is continuous at } c \in [a, b], \text{ then } F'(c) = f(c)
solution_steps.explanation: The derivative of the accumulation function equals the original function wherever the integrand is continuous.

m4.final_answer: If $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$ and $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)dt$, then $F$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, and if $f$ is continuous at $c \in [a, b]$, then $F'(c) = f(c)$.
m4.exam_tip: Differentiate clearly between FTC-1 (derivative of indefinite integral) and FTC-2 (evaluation of integral via antiderivative).

m4.question: State the Mean Value Theorem for integrals.
m4.concept_tested: Mean Value Theorem for Integrals (First MVT)
m4.approach: State that for continuous $f$, the integral equals $f(c)(b-a)$ for some $c \in [a, b]$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R} \text{ continuous} \implies \exists c \in [a, b] \text{ such that } \int_a^b f(x) dx = f(c)(b - a)
solution_steps.explanation: The average value of a continuous function on $[a, b]$ is attained at some point $c$ in the interval.

m4.final_answer: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, then there exists $c \in [a, b]$ such that $\int_a^b f(x)dx = f(c)(b-a)$.
m4.exam_tip: Note that this is the integral counterpart to Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem applied to $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)dt$.

m4.question: Give an example of a bounded function on $[0, 1]$ which is not Riemann integrable.
m4.approach: State Dirichlet's indicator function of the rationals and compute its upper and lower integrals.

solution_steps.title: Dirichlet's Function
solution_steps.math: f(x) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } x \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0, 1] \\ 0, & \text{if } x \in [0, 1] \setminus \mathbb{Q} \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $|f(x)| \le 1$, $f$ is bounded on $[0, 1]$.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Sums Calculation
solution_steps.math: M_i = \sup_{x \in I_i} f(x) = 1, \quad m_i = \inf_{x \in I_i} f(x) = 0 \implies U(P, f) = 1, \quad L(P, f) = 0
solution_steps.explanation: Because every interval of positive length contains both rationals and irrationals.

solution_steps.title: Non-Integrability
solution_steps.math: \overline{\int_0^1} f = 1 \ne 0 = \underline{\int_0^1} f \implies f \notin \mathcal{R}[0, 1]
solution_steps.explanation: The upper and lower Darboux integrals do not match.

m4.final_answer: Dirichlet's function $f(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)$ on $[0, 1]$ is bounded ($0 \le f \le 1$) but not Riemann integrable because $\overline{\int} f = 1 \ne 0 = \underline{\int} f$.
m4.exam_tip: Always mention the density of rationals and irrationals as the mathematical justification for $M_i = 1$ and $m_i = 0$.

m4.question: Define a refinement of a partition in Riemann integration.
m4.approach: Define refinement $P^* \supseteq P$ and explain that it adds additional division points.

solution_steps.title: Formal Definition
solution_steps.math: P^* \text{ is a refinement of } P \iff P \subseteq P^*
solution_steps.explanation: A partition $P^*$ of $[a, b]$ is said to be a refinement of partition $P$ if every partition point of $P$ is also a partition point of $P^*$.

solution_steps.title: Common Refinement
solution_steps.math: P_1 \cup P_2 \text{ is the common refinement of } P_1 \text{ and } P_2
solution_steps.explanation: The union of two partitions is a refinement of both.

m4.final_answer: A partition $P^*$ is a refinement of $P$ if $P \subseteq P^*$.
m4.exam_tip: Key consequence: $L(P, f) \le L(P^*, f) \le U(P^*, f) \le U(P, f)$.

m4.question: State the properties of Riemann integral for scalar multiplication.
m4.concept_tested: Properties of Riemann Integral: Scalar Multiplication
m4.approach: State linearity with respect to scalar multiplication $\int_a^b (cf) = c \int_a^b f$ for any $c \in \mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b], \, c \in \mathbb{R} \implies cf \in \mathcal{R}[a, b] \quad \text{and} \quad \int_a^b c f(x) dx = c \int_a^b f(x) dx
solution_steps.explanation: The Riemann integral is a linear operator on the space of integrable functions.

m4.final_answer: If $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, then $cf$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$ and $\int_a^b cf(x)dx = c \int_a^b f(x)dx$.
m4.exam_tip: State that for $c = -1$, this implies $\int_a^b (-f) = -\int_a^b f$.

m4.question: Define a partition of a closed interval $[a, b]$.
m4.approach: Formal set-theoretic definition of partition $P$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: P = \{a = x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{n-1}, x_n = b\} \quad \text{with } x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n
solution_steps.explanation: A partition of $[a, b]$ is a finite collection of points dividing $[a, b]$ into $n$ subintervals $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$.

m4.final_answer: A partition $P = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ with $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$.
m4.exam_tip: Mention the length of each subinterval is $\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1} > 0$.

m4.question: Define upper and lower Riemann integrals of a bounded function $f$ on $[a, b]$.
m4.approach: Define $\overline{\int} f = \inf\{U(P, f)\}$ and $\underline{\int} f = \sup\{L(P, f)\}$.

solution_steps.title: Upper Riemann Integral
solution_steps.math: U(f) = \overline{\int_a^b} f(x) dx = \inf \{U(P, f) : P \text{ is a partition of } [a, b]\}
solution_steps.explanation: The infimum of all upper Darboux sums over all possible partitions of $[a, b]$.

solution_steps.title: Lower Riemann Integral
solution_steps.math: L(f) = \underline{\int_a^b} f(x) dx = \sup \{L(P, f) : P \text{ is a partition of } [a, b]\}
solution_steps.explanation: The supremum of all lower Darboux sums over all possible partitions of $[a, b]$.

m4.final_answer: Upper integral: $\overline{\int_a^b} f = \inf_P U(P, f)$; Lower integral: $\underline{\int_a^b} f = \sup_P L(P, f)$. $f$ is integrable iff $\underline{\int_a^b} f = \overline{\int_a^b} f$.
m4.exam_tip: Upper integral is the INFIMUM of upper sums, and lower integral is the SUPREMUM of lower sums (do not swap them!).

m4.question: State the Mean Value Theorem for integrals.
m4.approach: State the theorem for continuous $f$ on $[a, b]$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R} \text{ is continuous} \implies \exists c \in (a, b) \text{ such that } \int_a^b f(x) dx = f(c)(b - a)
solution_steps.explanation: There exists a point $c$ in the interval where the function attains its average value over $[a, b]$.

m4.final_answer: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, there exists $c \in [a, b]$ such that $\int_a^b f(x)dx = f(c)(b-a)$.
m4.exam_tip: Also mention the generalized MVT: if $g \ge 0$ is integrable, $\int_a^b f g = f(c) \int_a^b g$.

m4.question: Give an example of a bounded function on $[0, 1]$ that is not Riemann integrable.
m4.concept_tested: Example of Bounded Non-Riemann Integrable Function
m4.approach: Provide Dirichlet's function or Riemann's non-integrable example.

solution_steps.title: Dirichlet Function
solution_steps.math: f(x) = \begin{cases} 1, & x \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0, 1] \\ 0, & x \in [0, 1] \setminus \mathbb{Q} \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: Clearly $|f(x)| \le 1$, so $f$ is bounded.

solution_steps.title: Justification
solution_steps.math: L(P, f) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad U(P, f) = 1 \quad \forall P \implies \underline{\int} f = 0 \ne 1 = \overline{\int} f
solution_steps.explanation: Since every non-degenerate subinterval contains both rational and irrational points.

m4.final_answer: The Dirichlet function $f(x) = 1$ if $x \in \mathbb{Q}$ and $0$ if $x \notin \mathbb{Q}$ on $[0, 1]$ is bounded but not Riemann integrable.
m4.exam_tip: Contrast this with Thomae's function (popcorn function), which is Riemann integrable with integral 0.

m4.question: Define the mesh (or norm) of a partition $P$.
m4.approach: Define $\|P\|$ as the maximum subinterval length.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: \|P\| = \max_{1 \le i \le n} \Delta x_i = \max_{1 \le i \le n} (x_i - x_{i-1})
solution_steps.explanation: The mesh (or norm) of partition $P = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ is the length of the longest subinterval in $P$.

m4.final_answer: The mesh (or norm) of partition $P$ is $\|P\| = \max\{x_i - x_{i-1} : 1 \le i \le n\}$.
m4.exam_tip: In Riemann's original definition, $f$ is integrable iff the Riemann sums converge as $\|P\| \to 0$.

m4.question: State the integration by parts formula for Riemann integrals.
m4.concept_tested: Integration by Parts Formula for Riemann Integrals
m4.approach: State the formula with hypotheses: $f, g$ differentiable and $f', g'$ integrable.

solution_steps.title: Hypotheses and Formula
solution_steps.math: f, g \in C^1[a, b] \implies \int_a^b f(x) g'(x) dx = [f(x)g(x)]_a^b - \int_a^b f'(x) g(x) dx
solution_steps.explanation: Derived from the product rule of differentiation: $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$.

m4.final_answer: $\int_a^b f(x) g'(x) dx = f(b)g(b) - f(a)g(a) - \int_a^b f'(x) g(x) dx$.
m4.exam_tip: State that $f$ and $g$ must have continuous (or integrable) derivatives on $[a, b]$.

m4.question: State the change of variable theorem for Riemann integration.
m4.concept_tested: Change of Variable (Substitution) Theorem for Integrals
m4.approach: State the theorem: $\phi: [\alpha, \beta] \to [a, b]$ continuously differentiable.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \int_{\phi(\alpha)}^{\phi(\beta)} f(x) dx = \int_\alpha^\beta f(\phi(t)) \phi'(t) dt
solution_steps.explanation: If $\phi: [\alpha, \beta] \to [a, b]$ has continuous derivative $\phi'$ and $f$ is continuous on the range of $\phi$.

m4.final_answer: $\int_a^b f(x)dx = \int_\alpha^\beta f(\phi(t))\phi'(t)dt$ where $a = \phi(\alpha)$ and $b = \phi(\beta)$.
m4.exam_tip: State clearly that $\phi'$ must be continuous on $[\alpha, \beta]$.

m4.question: Define refinement of a partition $P$.
m4.approach: Define $P \subseteq P^*$ and state its effect on Darboux sums.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: P^* \text{ is a refinement of } P \iff P \subset P^*
solution_steps.explanation: A partition $P^*$ is a refinement of $P$ if $P^*$ contains all the partition points of $P$ plus one or more additional points.

m4.final_answer: $P^*$ is a refinement of $P$ if $P \subseteq P^*$.
m4.exam_tip: Refining a partition increases (or preserves) the lower sum and decreases (or preserves) the upper sum.

m4.question: Define step function on $[a, b]$.
m4.approach: Define step function as piecewise constant on open subintervals of a partition.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: \phi: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R} \text{ is a step function} \iff \exists \text{ partition } P = \{x_0, \dots, x_n\} \text{ s.t. } \phi(x) = c_i \; \forall x \in (x_{i-1}, x_i)
solution_steps.explanation: A step function takes a constant value on each open subinterval of some partition $P$.

m4.final_answer: A function $\phi: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is a step function if there exists a partition $P$ such that $\phi$ is constant on each open subinterval $(x_{i-1}, x_i)$.
m4.exam_tip: Every step function is Riemann integrable with $\int_a^b \phi = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i (x_i - x_{i-1})$.

m4.question: Define a tagged partition of $[a, b]$.
m4.approach: Define partition $P$ with tags $t_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.explanation: A tagged partition $\dot{P}$ consists of a partition $P = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ together with a choice of sample point (tag) $t_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]$ in each subinterval.

m4.final_answer: A tagged partition is a pair $(P, \{t_i\}_{i=1}^n)$ where $P$ partitions $[a, b]$ and $t_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]$ for each $i$.
m4.exam_tip: The Riemann sum for a tagged partition is $S(f, \dot{P}) = \sum_{i=1}^n f(t_i)(x_i - x_{i-1})$.

m4.question: State the Leibniz Rule for differentiating under the integral sign.
m4.concept_tested: Leibniz Rule for Differentiation under the Integral Sign
m4.approach: State the formula for $\frac{d}{dx} \int_{u(x)}^{v(x)} f(x, t) dt$.

solution_steps.title: General Leibniz Formula
solution_steps.math: \frac{d}{dx} \left( \int_{u(x)}^{v(x)} f(x, t) dt \right) = f(x, v(x)) v'(x) - f(x, u(x)) u'(x) + \int_{u(x)}^{v(x)} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, t) dt
solution_steps.explanation: Assuming $f(x, t)$ and $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, t)$ are continuous on the region, and $u(x), v(x)$ are differentiable.

m4.final_answer: $\frac{d}{dx} \int_{u(x)}^{v(x)} f(x, t) dt = f(x, v(x)) v'(x) - f(x, u(x)) u'(x) + \int_{u(x)}^{v(x)} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, t) dt$.
m4.exam_tip: If limits $u, v$ are constant, the formula simplifies to $\frac{d}{dx} \int_a^b f(x, t)dt = \int_a^b \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, t)dt$.

m4.question: Prove that if a function $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, then it is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.
m4.approach: Use Heine-Cantor theorem (continuous on compact $[a, b]$ is uniformly continuous) and Riemann's criterion.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Continuity on Compact Interval
solution_steps.math: f \in C[a, b] \implies f \text{ is uniformly continuous on } [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Since $[a, b]$ is closed and bounded, continuity implies uniform continuity.

solution_steps.title: Choosing Partition Mesh
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists \delta > 0 : |x - y| < \delta \implies |f(x) - f(y)| < \frac{\epsilon}{b - a}
solution_steps.explanation: By uniform continuity.

solution_steps.title: Oscillation on Subintervals
solution_steps.math: \|P\| < \delta \implies M_i - m_i = f(u_i) - f(v_i) < \frac{\epsilon}{b - a}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ attains its supremum $M_i$ and infimum $m_i$ on $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$ at some points $u_i, v_i$.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Sum Difference
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) - L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n (M_i - m_i)\Delta x_i < \frac{\epsilon}{b-a} \sum_{i=1}^n \Delta x_i = \frac{\epsilon}{b-a}(b - a) = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: By Riemann's Criterion, $f$ is Riemann integrable.

m4.final_answer: Every continuous function on a closed bounded interval $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
m4.exam_tip: Explicitly invoke the Heine-Cantor Theorem: continuity on a compact interval implies uniform continuity.

m4.question: State and prove the Integration by Parts formula for Riemann integrals.
m4.approach: Integrate the product rule derivative $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$ using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: f, g \in C^1[a, b] \implies \int_a^b f(x) g'(x) dx = [f(x)g(x)]_a^b - \int_a^b f'(x) g(x) dx
solution_steps.explanation: Integration by parts formula for Riemann integrals.

solution_steps.title: Product Rule of Differentiation
solution_steps.math: (fg)'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x) \quad \forall x \in [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ and $g$ are differentiable.

solution_steps.title: Integration and Linearity
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b (fg)'(x) dx = \int_a^b f'(x)g(x) dx + \int_a^b f(x)g'(x) dx
solution_steps.explanation: Integrating both sides from $a$ to $b$.

solution_steps.title: Application of Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b (fg)'(x) dx = [f(x)g(x)]_a^b = f(b)g(b) - f(a)g(a)
solution_steps.explanation: Rearranging gives the desired formula.

m4.final_answer: $\int_a^b f g' = f(b)g(b) - f(a)g(a) - \int_a^b f' g$.
m4.exam_tip: Make sure to state that both $f'$ and $g'$ must be Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.

m4.question: State and prove the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
m4.concept_tested: Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Evaluation Theorem)
m4.approach: Let $F$ be an antiderivative ($F' = f$), use Mean Value Theorem on each subinterval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$, and squeeze between Darboux sums.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b] \land F'(x) = f(x) \; \forall x \in [a, b] \implies \int_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)
solution_steps.explanation: If $f$ is Riemann integrable and has an antiderivative $F$, then the integral equals the total change in $F$.

solution_steps.title: Telescoping Sum & Mean Value Theorem
solution_steps.math: F(b) - F(a) = \sum_{i=1}^n [F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1})] = \sum_{i=1}^n F'(t_i)\Delta x_i = \sum_{i=1}^n f(t_i)\Delta x_i
solution_steps.explanation: By Lagrange's MVT on each subinterval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$, there exists $t_i \in (x_{i-1}, x_i)$ such that $F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) = F'(t_i)\Delta x_i$.

solution_steps.title: Trapping between Darboux Sums
solution_steps.math: m_i \le f(t_i) \le M_i \implies L(P, f) \le F(b) - F(a) \le U(P, f) \quad \forall P
solution_steps.explanation: Since $F(b) - F(a)$ is trapped between $L(P, f)$ and $U(P, f)$ for every partition $P$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \sup_P L(P, f) \le F(b) - F(a) \le \inf_P U(P, f) \implies \int_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$, the upper and lower integrals coincide and equal $\int_a^b f$.

m4.final_answer: $\int_a^b f(x)dx = F(b) - F(a)$.
m4.exam_tip: The telescoping MVT argument is the standard rigorous proof in Bartle & Sherbert Theorem 7.3.1.

m4.question: If $f$ is monotonic on $[a, b]$, show that $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.
m4.approach: Partition into $n$ equal subintervals; telescoping sum cancels internal terms.

solution_steps.title: Partition Setup
solution_steps.math: \Delta x_i = \frac{b - a}{n} \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, n
solution_steps.explanation: Choose a uniform partition $P_n$ of $[a, b]$ into $n$ equal parts.

solution_steps.title: Subinterval Extrema for Increasing Function
solution_steps.math: m_i = f(x_{i-1}), \quad M_i = f(x_i) \implies M_i - m_i = f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})
solution_steps.explanation: Because $f$ is monotonically increasing.

solution_steps.title: Telescoping Darboux Difference
solution_steps.math: U(P_n, f) - L(P_n, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n [f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})] \frac{b - a}{n} = \frac{b - a}{n} [f(b) - f(a)]
solution_steps.explanation: The sum telescopes to $f(b) - f(a)$.

solution_steps.title: Riemann Criterion Verification
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \text{ choose } n > \frac{(b-a)[f(b)-f(a)]}{\epsilon} \implies U(P_n, f) - L(P_n, f) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: By the Archimedean Property, such $n$ exists. Hence $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$.

m4.final_answer: Every monotonic function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
m4.exam_tip: Note that monotonic functions may have countably many discontinuities and are still Riemann integrable!

m4.question: State and prove the Riemann Criterion for integrability of a bounded function.
m4.approach: Prove both directions: $(\implies)$ integrability implies $U - L < \epsilon$; $(\impliedby)$ $U - L < \epsilon$ implies $\overline{\int} = \underline{\int}$.

solution_steps.title: Direction 1 ($\implies$): Integrability $\implies$ Criterion
solution_steps.math: \underline{\int_a^b} f = \overline{\int_a^b} f = I. \quad \exists P_1 : L(P_1, f) > I - \frac{\epsilon}{2}, \quad \exists P_2 : U(P_2, f) < I + \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By definitions of supremum and infimum.

solution_steps.title: Common Refinement $P = P_1 \cup P_2$
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) - L(P, f) \le U(P_2, f) - L(P_1, f) < \left(I + \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right) - \left(I - \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right) = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Refinement decreases upper sums and increases lower sums.

solution_steps.title: Direction 2 ($\impliedby$): Criterion $\implies$ Integrability
solution_steps.math: L(P, f) \le \underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f \le U(P, f) \implies 0 \le \overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since this holds for every $\epsilon > 0$, the non-negative quantity $\overline{\int} f - \underline{\int} f$ must equal 0.

m4.final_answer: $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b] \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists P_\epsilon \text{ s.t. } U(P_\epsilon, f) - L(P_\epsilon, f) < \epsilon$.
m4.exam_tip: The common refinement $P = P_1 \cup P_2$ is essential in the forward direction.

m4.question: Prove that every continuous function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
m4.approach: Use uniform continuity on $[a, b]$: $\forall \epsilon > 0, \exists \delta > 0: |x-y| < \delta \implies |f(x) - f(y)| < \frac{\epsilon}{b-a}$.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Continuity
solution_steps.math: f \in C[a, b] \implies f \text{ is uniformly continuous on } [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Continuous function on a closed bounded interval is uniformly continuous.

solution_steps.title: Partition with $\|P\| < \delta$
solution_steps.math: x, y \in [x_{i-1}, x_i] \implies |x - y| \le \|P\| < \delta \implies |f(x) - f(y)| < \frac{\epsilon}{b - a}
solution_steps.explanation: Given $\epsilon > 0$, choose partition $P$ with $\|P\| < \delta$.

solution_steps.title: Sum Difference
solution_steps.math: M_i - m_i = f(u_i) - f(v_i) \le \frac{\epsilon}{b-a} \implies U(P, f) - L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n (M_i - m_i)\Delta x_i < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ attains extreme values at $u_i, v_i$.

m4.final_answer: By Riemann's criterion, $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.
m4.exam_tip: Uniform continuity is the key ingredient that lets us choose a single $\delta$ across the whole interval.

m4.question: Prove that every monotonic function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
m4.approach: Telescoping sum with uniform partition of $n$ subintervals.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Partition
solution_steps.math: P_n = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\}, \quad \Delta x_i = \frac{b - a}{n}
solution_steps.explanation: Divide $[a, b]$ into $n$ equal segments.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Sum Difference
solution_steps.math: U(P_n, f) - L(P_n, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n (f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})) \frac{b-a}{n} = \frac{b-a}{n}(f(b) - f(a))
solution_steps.explanation: Sum telescopes completely.

solution_steps.title: Choosing $n$
solution_steps.math: n > \frac{(b-a)(f(b)-f(a))}{\epsilon} \implies U(P_n, f) - L(P_n, f) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $f$ satisfies Riemann's criterion.

m4.final_answer: Every monotonic function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
m4.exam_tip: If $f(a) = f(b)$, $f$ is constant and the result is trivial.

m4.question: Let $f(x) = x$ on $[0, 1]$. Using partitions into equal subintervals, find the Riemann integral $\int_0^1 x dx$.
m4.concept_tested: Direct Computation of Riemann Integral via Upper/Lower Sums
m4.approach: Use uniform partition of $[0, 1]$ into $n$ parts for $f(x) = x$, compute $U(P_n)$ and $L(P_n)$, and take limit as $n \to \infty$.

solution_steps.title: Partition Setup
solution_steps.math: P_n = \left\{0, \frac{1}{n}, \frac{2}{n}, \dots, \frac{n}{n} = 1\right\}, \quad \Delta x_i = \frac{1}{n}
solution_steps.explanation: Subintervals are $[\frac{i-1}{n}, \frac{i}{n}]$.

solution_steps.title: Upper Sum $U(P_n, f)$
solution_steps.math: M_i = f\left(\frac{i}{n}\right) = \frac{i}{n} \implies U(P_n, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1}{n^2} \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac{n+1}{2n} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2n}
solution_steps.explanation: Using the formula $\sum_{i=1}^n i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

solution_steps.title: Lower Sum $L(P_n, f)$
solution_steps.math: m_i = f\left(\frac{i-1}{n}\right) = \frac{i-1}{n} \implies L(P_n, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i-1}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1}{n^2} \frac{(n-1)n}{2} = \frac{n-1}{2n} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2n}
solution_steps.explanation: Using $\sum_{i=1}^n (i-1) = \frac{(n-1)n}{2}$.

solution_steps.title: Limit as $n \to \infty$
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} U(P_n, f) = \lim_{n \to \infty} L(P_n, f) = \frac{1}{2} \implies \int_0^1 x dx = \frac{1}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: Both upper and lower sums converge to $1/2$.

m4.exam_tip: Explicitly state the summation identities used: $\sum_{i=1}^n i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

m4.question: Show that Dirichlet's function $f(x) = 1$ if $x \in \mathbb{Q}$ and $f(x) = 0$ if $x \notin \mathbb{Q}$ is not Riemann integrable on $[0, 1]$.
m4.approach: Compute upper and lower integrals using density of $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$.

solution_steps.title: Subinterval Sup and Inf
solution_steps.math: f(x) = \begin{cases} 1, & x \in \mathbb{Q} \\ 0, & x \notin \mathbb{Q} \end{cases} \implies M_i = \sup_{I_i} f = 1, \quad m_i = \inf_{I_i} f = 0
solution_steps.explanation: Every non-empty open subinterval contains both rational and irrational numbers.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Sums for Any Partition $P$
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n 1 \cdot \Delta x_i = 1(1 - 0) = 1, \qquad L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n 0 \cdot \Delta x_i = 0
solution_steps.explanation: These hold identically for every partition $P$.

solution_steps.title: Comparison of Integrals
solution_steps.math: \overline{\int_0^1} f = \inf_P U(P, f) = 1 \ne 0 = \sup_P L(P, f) = \underline{\int_0^1} f
solution_steps.explanation: Since the upper and lower integrals are not equal, $f$ is not Riemann integrable.

m4.final_answer: Dirichlet's function is not Riemann integrable on $[0, 1]$ because $\underline{\int} f = 0 \ne 1 = \overline{\int} f$.
m4.exam_tip: Cite the Density Theorems for $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ as the rigorous justification.

m4.question: Prove that if $f$ and $g$ are Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$, then $f + g$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$ and $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$.
m4.approach: Use tagged Riemann sums or Darboux sums and the inequality $m_i(f) + m_i(g) \le m_i(f+g) \le M_i(f+g) \le M_i(f) + M_i(g)$.

solution_steps.title: Subinterval Bounds
solution_steps.math: m_i(f) + m_i(g) \le m_i(f+g) \le M_i(f+g) \le M_i(f) + M_i(g)
solution_steps.explanation: By properties of supremum and infimum.

solution_steps.title: Sum Inequalities
solution_steps.math: L(P, f) + L(P, g) \le L(P, f+g) \le U(P, f+g) \le U(P, f) + U(P, g)
solution_steps.explanation: Multiplying by $\Delta x_i$ and summing over $i$.

solution_steps.title: Riemann Criterion for $f+g$
solution_steps.math: U(P, f+g) - L(P, f+g) \le [U(P, f) - L(P, f)] + [U(P, g) - L(P, g)] < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Choosing common partition where both $f$ and $g$ have Darboux differences $< \epsilon/2$.

solution_steps.title: Integral Value
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g
solution_steps.explanation: Since the integral is squeezed between $L(P, f) + L(P, g)$ and $U(P, f) + U(P, g)$.

m4.final_answer: $f+g \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$ and $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$.
m4.exam_tip: Note that $U(P, f+g) \le U(P, f) + U(P, g)$ follows from subadditivity of the supremum.

m4.question: Show that if $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$, then $|f|$ is Riemann integrable and $|\int_a^b f| \le \int_a^b |f|$.
m4.approach: Use reverse triangle inequality $||f(x)| - |f(y)|| \le |f(x) - f(y)|$ to bound oscillations, then $-|f| \le f \le |f|$.

solution_steps.title: Oscillation Bound
solution_steps.math: M_i(|f|) - m_i(|f|) = \sup_{x, y \in I_i} ||f(x)| - |f(y)|| \le \sup_{x, y \in I_i} |f(x) - f(y)| = M_i(f) - m_i(f)
solution_steps.explanation: The oscillation of $|f|$ on any interval never exceeds the oscillation of $f$.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Difference
solution_steps.math: U(P, |f|) - L(P, |f|) \le U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Hence $|f|$ satisfies the Riemann Criterion and is integrable.

solution_steps.title: Integral Inequality
solution_steps.math: -|f(x)| \le f(x) \le |f(x)| \implies -\int_a^b |f| \le \int_a^b f \le \int_a^b |f| \iff \left|\int_a^b f\right| \le \int_a^b |f|
solution_steps.explanation: By monotonicity of the Riemann integral.

m4.final_answer: $|f| \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$ and $|\int_a^b f| \le \int_a^b |f|$.
m4.exam_tip: Mention that the converse is false: Dirichlet's function modified to take values $\pm 1$ has $|f|=1$ integrable, but $f$ is not integrable.

m4.question: Let $f(x) = c$ be a constant function on $[a, b]$. Show that $f$ is Riemann integrable and $\int_a^b c dx = c(b-a)$.
m4.approach: Compute $U(P, c)$ and $L(P, c)$ for an arbitrary partition $P$.

solution_steps.title: Extrema on Subintervals
solution_steps.math: f(x) = c \; \forall x \in [a, b] \implies M_i = c, \quad m_i = c \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, n
solution_steps.explanation: A constant function attains the same value everywhere.

solution_steps.title: Upper and Lower Sums
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n c \Delta x_i = c \sum_{i=1}^n \Delta x_i = c(b - a), \qquad L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n c \Delta x_i = c(b - a)
solution_steps.explanation: The sum of the lengths of the subintervals is $\sum \Delta x_i = b - a$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: L(P, f) = U(P, f) = c(b - a) \implies \underline{\int_a^b} c dx = \overline{\int_a^b} c dx = c(b - a)
solution_steps.explanation: Since upper and lower sums are equal to $c(b-a)$ for every partition $P$, $f$ is integrable with integral $c(b-a)$.

m4.final_answer: $f(x) = c$ is Riemann integrable and $\int_a^b c dx = c(b-a)$.
m4.exam_tip: Notice this works for any constant $c$, whether positive, negative, or zero.

m4.question: Show that if $P^*$ is a refinement of a partition $P$, then $L(P, f) \le L(P^*, f)$ and $U(P^*, f) \le U(P, f)$.
m4.approach: Prove for adding a single partition point $x^*$, then use induction for any refinement $P^* \supseteq P$.

solution_steps.title: Single Point Refinement
solution_steps.math: P^* = P \cup \{x^*\}, \quad x^* \in (x_{k-1}, x_k)
solution_steps.explanation: The subinterval $[x_{k-1}, x_k]$ is split into $[x_{k-1}, x^*]$ and $[x^*, x_k]$.

solution_steps.title: Lower Sum Comparison
solution_steps.math: m_k' = \inf_{[x_{k-1}, x^*]} f \ge m_k, \quad m_k'' = \inf_{[x^*, x_k]} f \ge m_k
solution_steps.explanation: Since infimum over a subset is greater than or equal to infimum over the whole set.

solution_steps.title: Contribution Difference
solution_steps.explanation: Summing across all intervals gives $L(P^*, f) \ge L(P, f)$.

solution_steps.title: Upper Sum Comparison
solution_steps.math: M_k' \le M_k, \, M_k'' \le M_k \implies U(P^*, f) \le U(P, f)
solution_steps.explanation: Supremum over a subset is less than or equal to supremum over the whole set.

m4.final_answer: $L(P, f) \le L(P^*, f)$ and $U(P^*, f) \le U(P, f)$ for any refinement $P^* \supseteq P$.
m4.exam_tip: Mention the geometric intuition: refining adds more rectangles, filling gaps for lower sums and cutting corners for upper sums.

m4.question: Show that every step function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
m4.approach: Use the fact that a step function is constant on open subintervals, which can be modified at finitely many endpoints without affecting integrability.

solution_steps.title: Step Function Definition
solution_steps.math: \phi(x) = c_i \quad \forall x \in (x_{i-1}, x_i), \quad i = 1, \dots, n
solution_steps.explanation: Where $P = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ is the defining partition.

solution_steps.title: Linear Combination of Characteristic Functions
solution_steps.math: \phi(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \mathbf{1}_{(x_{i-1}, x_i)}(x) + \sum_{i=0}^n \phi(x_i) \mathbf{1}_{\{x_i\}}(x)
solution_steps.explanation: Characteristic functions of open intervals are Riemann integrable, and finite points of jump do not affect integrability.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Criterion / Evaluation
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b \phi(x) dx = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i (x_i - x_{i-1})
solution_steps.explanation: By additivity over subintervals, each interval contributes $c_i \Delta x_i$.

m4.final_answer: Every step function is Riemann integrable with $\int_a^b \phi = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \Delta x_i$.
m4.exam_tip: Step functions form a dense subspace of $\mathcal{R}[a, b]$ in the $L^1$ norm.

m4.question: Prove that if $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$ and $c \in (a, b)$, then $f$ is integrable on $[a, c]$ and $[c, b]$ and $\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$.
m4.approach: Include $c$ in partitions of $[a, b]$, splitting $P = P_1 \cup P_2$ with $P_1$ partitioning $[a, c]$ and $P_2$ partitioning $[c, b]$.

solution_steps.title: Partition Splitting
solution_steps.math: P_1 \text{ partition of } [a, c], \; P_2 \text{ partition of } [c, b] \implies P = P_1 \cup P_2 \text{ partition of } [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: The point $c$ serves as the right endpoint of $P_1$ and left endpoint of $P_2$.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Sum Additivity
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) = U(P_1, f) + U(P_2, f) \quad \text{and} \quad L(P, f) = L(P_1, f) + L(P_2, f)
solution_steps.explanation: The sum splits cleanly across the junction $c$.

solution_steps.title: Integrability Squeeze
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) - L(P, f) = [U(P_1, f) - L(P_1, f)] + [U(P_2, f) - L(P_2, f)] < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since each term is non-negative, $U(P_1, f) - L(P_1, f) < \epsilon$ and $U(P_2, f) - L(P_2, f) < \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Integral Equality
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f
solution_steps.explanation: Taking infima/suprema proves the identity.

m4.final_answer: If $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$ and $c \in (a, b)$, then $f$ is integrable on $[a, c]$ and $[c, b]$, and $\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$.
m4.exam_tip: Note this identity extends to any ordering of $a, b, c$ using the convention $\int_b^a f = -\int_a^b f$.

m4.question: Show that if $f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is Riemann integrable, then $f$ is bounded on $[a, b]$.
m4.approach: Proof by contradiction: if $f$ is unbounded, then in any partition at least one subinterval has $f$ unbounded, making Riemann sums diverge.

solution_steps.title: Assumption for Contradiction
solution_steps.math: f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b] \text{ with integral } L, \quad \text{suppose } f \text{ is unbounded on } [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Assume $f$ is Riemann integrable in the Riemann-sum sense, yet unbounded.

solution_steps.title: Riemann Sum Bound
solution_steps.math: \exists P = \{x_0, \dots, x_n\} : |S(\dot{P}, f) - L| < 1 \implies |S(\dot{P}, f)| < |L| + 1
solution_steps.explanation: For any choice of tags $t_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]$.

solution_steps.title: Unbounded Subinterval
solution_steps.math: \exists k \in \{1, \dots, n\} \text{ such that } f \text{ is unbounded on } [x_{k-1}, x_k]
solution_steps.explanation: If every subinterval were bounded, the entire interval $[a, b]$ would be bounded.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction via Tag Choice
solution_steps.math: S(\dot{P}, f) = f(t_k)\Delta x_k + \sum_{i \ne k} f(t_i)\Delta x_i \implies |f(t_k)|\Delta x_k \le |L| + 1 + \left|\sum_{i \ne k} f(t_i)\Delta x_i\right|
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ is unbounded on $[x_{k-1}, x_k]$, we can pick $t_k$ to make $|f(t_k)|$ arbitrarily large, violating the bound.

m4.final_answer: If $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$, then $f$ must be bounded on $[a, b]$.
m4.exam_tip: This fundamental result explains why the Riemann integral cannot handle unbounded functions (which require improper integrals).

m4.question: Evaluate $\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{n}{n^2 + i^2}$ by expressing it as a Riemann sum.
m4.concept_tested: Evaluation of Limit of a Sum via Riemann Integral
m4.approach: Rewrite $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{n}{n^2 + i^2} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{1 + (i/n)^2}$, recognize as Riemann sum of $f(x) = \frac{1}{1+x^2}$ on $[0, 1]$.

solution_steps.title: Algebraic Transformation
solution_steps.math: \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{n}{n^2 + i^2} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{n}{n^2\left(1 + \frac{i^2}{n^2}\right)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{1 + \left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^2}
solution_steps.explanation: Factor out $n^2$ from the denominator.

solution_steps.title: Identification as Riemann Sum
solution_steps.math: f(x) = \frac{1}{1+x^2}, \quad x_i = \frac{i}{n}, \quad \Delta x = \frac{1}{n} \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f\left(\frac{i}{n}\right) = \int_0^1 \frac{1}{1+x^2} dx
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f(x) = \frac{1}{1+x^2}$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$, the Riemann sums converge to the definite integral.

solution_steps.title: Evaluate the Integral
solution_steps.math: \int_0^1 \frac{1}{1+x^2} dx = [\arctan(x)]_0^1 = \arctan(1) - \arctan(0) = \frac{\pi}{4} - 0 = \frac{\pi}{4}
solution_steps.explanation: Standard antiderivative of $\frac{1}{1+x^2}$ is $\arctan(x)$.

m4.final_answer: $\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{n}{n^2 + i^2} = \frac{\pi}{4}$.
m4.exam_tip: Always write down the general formula: $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f(i/n) = \int_0^1 f(x) dx$.

m4.question: State and prove the First Mean Value Theorem for Integrals.
m4.concept_tested: First Mean Value Theorem for Integrals (Past Paper Model)
m4.approach: State and prove that for continuous $f$ on $[a, b]$, $\exists c \in [a, b]$ such that $\int_a^b f(x)dx = f(c)(b-a)$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R} \text{ is continuous} \implies \exists c \in [a, b] \text{ such that } \int_a^b f(x) dx = f(c)(b - a)
solution_steps.explanation: The average value of a continuous function on $[a, b]$ is attained at least once.

solution_steps.title: Extreme Value Theorem
solution_steps.math: m = \min_{x \in [a, b]} f(x), \quad M = \max_{x \in [a, b]} f(x) \implies m \le f(x) \le M \; (\forall x \in [a, b])
solution_steps.explanation: Continuous function on compact interval attains its minimum $m$ and maximum $M$.

solution_steps.title: Integrating the Inequalities
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b m dx \le \int_a^b f(x) dx \le \int_a^b M dx \implies m(b - a) \le \int_a^b f(x) dx \le M(b - a)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $b - a > 0$, divide by $b - a$.

solution_steps.title: Intermediate Value Theorem Application
solution_steps.math: m \le \frac{1}{b - a} \int_a^b f(x) dx \le M \implies \exists c \in [a, b] \text{ s.t. } f(c) = \frac{1}{b - a} \int_a^b f(x) dx
solution_steps.explanation: By IVT, $f$ takes on every value between its minimum $m$ and maximum $M$.

m4.final_answer: $\int_a^b f(x)dx = f(c)(b-a)$ for some $c \in [a, b]$.
m4.exam_tip: Combining EVT (Extreme Value Theorem) and IVT (Intermediate Value Theorem) is the classic proof.

m4.question: Define Riemann integration using Darboux sums. Prove that a bounded function $f:[a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is Riemann integrable if and only if for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ such that $U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon$.
m4.concept_tested: Darboux Definition of Riemann Integral and Integrability Criterion (Complete Essay)
m4.approach: Define partitions, subintervals, $M_i, m_i$, Darboux sums $U(P, f), L(P, f)$, upper and lower integrals. State and prove the refinement lemma, then establish $U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon$ biconditional.

solution_steps.title: Part 1: Definitions of Darboux Sums & Integrals
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n M_i \Delta x_i, \quad L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \Delta x_i \quad \text{where } M_i = \sup_{I_i} f, \, m_i = \inf_{I_i} f
solution_steps.explanation: The upper integral is $\overline{\int_a^b} f = \inf_P U(P, f)$ and lower integral is $\underline{\int_a^b} f = \sup_P L(P, f)$. A bounded function is Riemann integrable if $\underline{\int_a^b} f = \overline{\int_a^b} f = \int_a^b f$.

solution_steps.title: Part 2: Refinement Property
solution_steps.math: P \subseteq P^* \implies L(P, f) \le L(P^*, f) \le U(P^*, f) \le U(P, f)
solution_steps.explanation: Refining a partition cannot decrease lower sums nor increase upper sums. Furthermore, for any two partitions $P_1, P_2$, $L(P_1, f) \le U(P_2, f)$ by taking the common refinement $P^* = P_1 \cup P_2$.

solution_steps.title: Part 3: Forward Direction ($\implies$)
solution_steps.math: \underline{\int} f = \overline{\int} f = I. \quad \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists P_1 : L(P_1, f) > I - \frac{\epsilon}{2}, \quad \exists P_2 : U(P_2, f) < I + \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of supremum and infimum.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction: Common Refinement
solution_steps.math: P = P_1 \cup P_2 \implies U(P, f) - L(P, f) \le U(P_2, f) - L(P_1, f) < \left(I + \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right) - \left(I - \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right) = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Thus there exists a partition $P$ with $U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Part 4: Backward Direction ($\impliedby$)
solution_steps.math: L(P, f) \le \underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f \le U(P, f) \implies 0 \le \overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since $0 \le \overline{\int} f - \underline{\int} f < \epsilon$ for all $\epsilon > 0$, the non-negative difference must be 0, so $\overline{\int} f = \underline{\int} f$, proving $f$ is Riemann integrable.

m4.final_answer: A bounded function $f$ on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable if and only if for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a partition $P$ such that $U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon$.
m4.exam_tip: In a 10-mark essay, clearly include the definitions, the common refinement lemma $L(P_1) \le U(P_2)$, and both directions of the biconditional.

m4.question: State and prove the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (First and Second Parts).
m4.concept_tested: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (First and Second Parts)
m4.approach: State and prove FTC-1 ($F'(x) = f(x)$ for continuous $f$) using difference quotient, then prove FTC-2 ($\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)$) using MVT and Darboux squeeze.

solution_steps.title: FTC Part 1 Statement
solution_steps.math: f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b], \quad F(x) = \int_a^x f(t) dt \quad (x \in [a, b])
solution_steps.explanation: Then $F$ is continuous on $[a, b]$. Furthermore, if $f$ is continuous at $c \in [a, b]$, then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ and $F'(c) = f(c)$.

solution_steps.title: Proof of FTC Part 1
solution_steps.math: \frac{F(c+h) - F(c)}{h} - f(c) = \frac{1}{h} \int_c^{c+h} [f(t) - f(c)] dt
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ is continuous at $c$, for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $|t - c| < \delta \implies |f(t) - f(c)| < \epsilon$. For $0 < |h| < \delta$:

solution_steps.title: Bounding Difference Quotient
solution_steps.math: \left|\frac{F(c+h) - F(c)}{h} - f(c)\right| \le \frac{1}{|h|} \left|\int_c^{c+h} |f(t) - f(c)| dt\right| < \frac{1}{|h|} \epsilon |h| = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Taking $h \to 0$ gives $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{F(c+h) - F(c)}{h} = f(c)$, hence $F'(c) = f(c)$.

solution_steps.title: FTC Part 2 Statement & Proof
solution_steps.math: f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b], \, F'(x) = f(x) \; \forall x \in [a, b] \implies \int_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)
solution_steps.explanation: For any partition $P = \{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$, by the Mean Value Theorem on $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$, $\exists t_i \in (x_{i-1}, x_i)$ such that $F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) = F'(t_i)\Delta x_i = f(t_i)\Delta x_i$.

solution_steps.title: Summation and Darboux Squeeze
solution_steps.math: F(b) - F(a) = \sum_{i=1}^n [F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1})] = \sum_{i=1}^n f(t_i)\Delta x_i \implies L(P, f) \le F(b) - F(a) \le U(P, f)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$, taking $\sup L(P, f) = \inf U(P, f) = \int_a^b f$ gives $\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)$.

m4.final_answer: FTC-1 establishes that differentiation reverses integration ($F'(c) = f(c)$); FTC-2 establishes that integration can be evaluated by an antiderivative ($\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)$).
m4.exam_tip: Clearly separate the hypotheses: FTC-1 assumes continuity of $f$ at point $c$; FTC-2 assumes $f$ has an antiderivative $F$ on $[a, b]$ and $f$ is integrable.

m4.question: Prove that if a bounded function $f:[a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ has only a finite number of points of discontinuity, then $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.
m4.concept_tested: Riemann Integrability of Functions with Finitely Many Discontinuities / Substitution Theorem
m4.approach: State and prove that if a bounded function $f:[a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous except at a finite number of points, then $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R} \text{ bounded with discontinuities at } c_1 < c_2 < \dots < c_k \implies f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: A bounded function on $[a, b]$ having only a finite number of points of discontinuity is Riemann integrable.

solution_steps.title: Single Discontinuity Case ($k = 1$)
solution_steps.math: c \in (a, b), \quad |f(x)| \le M \; \forall x \in [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Let $c$ be the single point of discontinuity. Enclose $c$ in an interval $[c - \delta, c + \delta]$ with $\delta < \frac{\epsilon}{8M}$.

solution_steps.title: Integrability on Outer Intervals
solution_steps.math: f \text{ continuous on } [a, c - \delta] \text{ and } [c + \delta, b] \implies \exists P_1, P_2 \text{ s.t. } U(P_1) - L(P_1) < \frac{\epsilon}{4}, \; U(P_2) - L(P_2) < \frac{\epsilon}{4}
solution_steps.explanation: Continuous functions on closed bounded intervals are Riemann integrable.

solution_steps.title: Combining Partitions
solution_steps.math: P = P_1 \cup P_2 \implies U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \frac{\epsilon}{4} + 2M(2\delta) + \frac{\epsilon}{4} < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + 4M\left(\frac{\epsilon}{8M}\right) = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: The oscillation on the middle interval is at most $2M$, contributing $2M(2\delta) < \epsilon/2$.

solution_steps.title: General Case by Induction
solution_steps.math: \text{By additivity of integral over } [a, b] = [a, c_1] \cup [c_1, c_2] \cup \dots \cup [c_k, b], \quad f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ is integrable on each subinterval with at most one endpoint discontinuity, it is integrable on $[a, b]$.

m4.final_answer: Every bounded function with finitely many discontinuities on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
m4.exam_tip: This theorem is a key consequence of Lebesgue's Criterion (a bounded function is Riemann integrable iff its set of discontinuities has measure zero).

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Prove that the intersection of any finite collection of open sets in $\mathbb{R}$ is open.
m5.concept_tested: Finite Intersection of Open Sets in $\mathbb{R}$
m5.approach: Let $x \in \bigcap_{k=1}^m G_k$, find open intervals $(x-\epsilon_k, x+\epsilon_k) \subseteq G_k$, and take $\epsilon = \min \epsilon_k > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Setup
solution_steps.math: G = \bigcap_{k=1}^m G_k, \quad x \in G \implies x \in G_k \quad \forall k \in \{1, 2, \dots, m\}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x$ belongs to the intersection, it belongs to each individual open set $G_k$.

solution_steps.title: Openness of Each $G_k$
solution_steps.math: \forall k \in \{1, \dots, m\}, \; \exists \epsilon_k > 0 \text{ such that } V_{\epsilon_k}(x) = (x - \epsilon_k, x + \epsilon_k) \subseteq G_k
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of open sets in $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Taking Minimum Radius
solution_steps.math: \epsilon = \min\{\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2, \dots, \epsilon_m\} > 0 \implies V_\epsilon(x) \subseteq V_{\epsilon_k}(x) \subseteq G_k \; (\forall k) \implies V_\epsilon(x) \subseteq \bigcap_{k=1}^m G_k = G
solution_steps.explanation: The minimum of finitely many strictly positive real numbers is strictly positive. Hence $G$ is open.

m5.final_answer: The intersection of any finite collection of open sets is open because $\epsilon = \min_{1 \le k \le m} \epsilon_k > 0$.
m5.exam_tip: Emphasize why this fails for infinite intersections: the infimum of infinitely many positive numbers can be 0 (e.g. $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty (-1/n, 1/n) = \{0\}$, which is not open).

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: State the definition of uniform convergence of a sequence of functions.
m5.concept_tested: Definition of Uniform Convergence of Sequence of Functions
m5.approach: State the $\epsilon-K$ definition where $K$ depends solely on $\epsilon$, not on $x$.

solution_steps.title: Formal Definition
solution_steps.math: f_n \rightrightarrows f \text{ on } A \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K(\epsilon) \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } \forall n \ge K, \; \forall x \in A, \; |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: A sequence of functions $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to $f$ on a set $A$ if the rate of convergence is uniform across all points $x \in A$.

solution_steps.title: Supremum Norm Equivalent
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} \|f_n - f\|_A = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sup_{x \in A} |f_n(x) - f(x)| = 0
solution_steps.explanation: Uniform convergence is equivalent to convergence in the uniform (supremum) norm.

m5.final_answer: $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to $f$ on $A$ if $\forall \epsilon > 0, \exists K \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \epsilon$ for all $n \ge K$ and all $x \in A$.
m5.exam_tip: Write the quantifiers in order: '$\forall \epsilon > 0, \exists K \in \mathbb{N}, \forall n \ge K, \forall x \in A$'. Placing $\forall x$ before $\exists K$ gives pointwise convergence!

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Write the difference between pointwise convergence and uniform convergence.
m5.concept_tested: Pointwise vs Uniform Convergence
m5.approach: Contrast the quantifier dependencies: $K(\epsilon, x)$ vs $K(\epsilon)$, and preservation of continuity.

solution_steps.title: Quantifier Dependency
solution_steps.math: \text{Pointwise: } K = K(\epsilon, x); \qquad \text{Uniform: } K = K(\epsilon) \text{ (independent of } x)
solution_steps.explanation: In pointwise convergence, different points $x$ can require different numbers of terms to get within $\epsilon$. In uniform convergence, a single $K$ works simultaneously for all points in the domain.

solution_steps.title: Property Preservation
solution_steps.math: \text{Uniform convergence preserves continuity and integrates term-by-term; pointwise convergence does not.}
solution_steps.explanation: Pointwise limits of continuous functions can be discontinuous (e.g., $x^n$ on $[0, 1]$).

m5.final_answer: Pointwise: $K$ depends on both $\epsilon$ and $x$. Uniform: $K$ depends only on $\epsilon$, holding simultaneously for all $x \in A$. Uniform convergence guarantees the limit of continuous functions is continuous.
m5.exam_tip: A two-column comparison table is the cleanest way to present this answer in an exam.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: State the Weierstrass M-test for uniform convergence of infinite series of functions.
m5.concept_tested: Weierstrass M-Test
m5.approach: State hypotheses $|f_n(x)| \le M_n$ and $\sum M_n < \infty$, and the conclusion of uniform and absolute convergence.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: |f_n(x)| \le M_n \quad \forall x \in A, \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \qquad \sum_{n=1}^\infty M_n < \infty
solution_steps.explanation: If each function $f_n$ is bounded on $A$ by a constant $M_n$, and the numerical series $\sum M_n$ converges.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x) \text{ converges absolutely and uniformly on } A
solution_steps.explanation: The series of functions converges uniformly to a function $S(x)$ on $A$.

m5.final_answer: If $|f_n(x)| \le M_n$ for all $x \in A$ and $\sum M_n$ converges, then $\sum f_n$ converges uniformly and absolutely on $A$.
m5.exam_tip: Remember that $M_n$ must be constants independent of $x$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Define the radius of convergence of a power series.
m5.concept_tested: Radius of Convergence of Power Series
m5.approach: Define $R$ via Cauchy-Hadamard formula $1/R = \limsup |a_n|^{1/n}$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: R = \sup\{r \ge 0 : \sum a_n r^n \text{ converges}\} \in [0, \infty]
solution_steps.explanation: The radius of convergence $R$ is the non-negative number (or $\infty$) such that $\sum a_n (x-c)^n$ converges for $|x-c| < R$ and diverges for $|x-c| > R$.

solution_steps.title: Cauchy-Hadamard Formula
solution_steps.math: \frac{1}{R} = \limsup_{n \to \infty} |a_n|^{1/n} \quad (\text{or } \frac{1}{R} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| \text{ when it exists})
solution_steps.explanation: Standard computational formulas.

m5.final_answer: The radius of convergence $R$ is defined by $\frac{1}{R} = \limsup_{n \to \infty} |a_n|^{1/n}$ (with $R=0$ if $\limsup = \infty$, and $R=\infty$ if $\limsup = 0$).
m5.exam_tip: Mention that convergence at the boundary points $|x - c| = R$ must be tested separately.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Find the radius of convergence of the power series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty n! x^n$.
m5.concept_tested: Radius of Convergence Calculation
m5.approach: Apply Ratio Test to coefficients $a_n = n!$.

solution_steps.title: Ratio of Coefficients
solution_steps.math: \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \frac{(n+1)!}{n!} = n + 1
solution_steps.explanation: Compute consecutive coefficient ratio.

solution_steps.title: Take Limit
solution_steps.math: L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \lim_{n \to \infty} (n+1) = +\infty
solution_steps.explanation: The ratio diverges to $+\infty$.

solution_steps.title: Radius of Convergence
solution_steps.math: R = \frac{1}{L} = \frac{1}{\infty} = 0
solution_steps.explanation: The series converges only at $x = 0$.

m5.final_answer: The radius of convergence is $R = 0$.
m5.exam_tip: $R = 0$ means the series converges only at the single point $x = 0$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Define pointwise convergence of a sequence of functions.
m5.concept_tested: Pointwise Convergence of Sequence of Functions
m5.approach: State the definition that for every fixed $x_0 \in A$, the real sequence $(f_n(x_0))$ converges to $f(x_0)$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: f_n \to f \text{ pointwise on } A \iff \forall x \in A, \; \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(x) = f(x)
solution_steps.explanation: Equivalently: $\forall x \in A, \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists K(x, \epsilon) \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n \ge K \implies |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \epsilon$.

m5.final_answer: $(f_n)$ converges pointwise to $f$ on $A$ if for each fixed $x \in A$, $\lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(x) = f(x)$.
m5.exam_tip: Stress that $K$ is allowed to vary with $x$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Write the power series expansion of $e^x$ and find its interval of convergence.
m5.concept_tested: Taylor / Power Series for $e^x$
m5.approach: Write $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}$ and apply Ratio Test to find $R = \infty$.

solution_steps.title: Power Series Expansion
solution_steps.math: e^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!} = 1 + x + \frac{x^2}{2!} + \frac{x^3}{3!} + \dots
solution_steps.explanation: Maclaurin series for $e^x$.

solution_steps.title: Radius of Convergence
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} \left|\frac{x^{n+1}/(n+1)!}{x^n/n!}\right| = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{|x|}{n+1} = 0 < 1 \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Ratio Test, the series converges for every real number $x$, so $R = \infty$.

m5.final_answer: Expansion: $e^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}$. Interval of convergence: $(-\infty, \infty) = \mathbb{R}$.
m5.exam_tip: State both the radius of convergence $R = \infty$ and the interval of convergence $(-\infty, \infty)$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Determine the limit of sequence $f_n(x) = x^n$ on $[0, 1]$ as $n \to \infty$.
m5.concept_tested: Pointwise Limit of $f_n(x) = x^n$ on $[0, 1]$
m5.approach: Analyze cases $x \in [0, 1)$ and $x = 1$.

solution_steps.title: Case $0 \le x < 1$
solution_steps.math: |x| < 1 \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} x^n = 0
solution_steps.explanation: Standard geometric sequence limit.

solution_steps.title: Case $x = 1$
solution_steps.math: x = 1 \implies f_n(1) = 1^n = 1 \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(1) = 1
solution_steps.explanation: Constant sequence of 1s.

m5.final_answer: $f(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} x^n = \begin{cases} 0, & 0 \le x < 1 \\ 1, & x = 1 \end{cases}$.
m5.exam_tip: Note that the limit function is discontinuous at $x = 1$, which proves the convergence is not uniform on $[0, 1]$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: State Abel's limit theorem for power series.
m5.concept_tested: Abel's Limit Theorem for Power Series
m5.approach: State that if a power series converges at an endpoint, the sum function is continuous up to that endpoint.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n R^n \text{ converges} \implies \lim_{x \to R^-} \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n R^n
solution_steps.explanation: If a real power series $\sum a_n x^n$ with radius of convergence $R$ converges at $x = R$, then the sum function $f(x)$ is continuous from the left at $x = R$.

m5.final_answer: If $\sum a_n R^n$ converges, then $f(x) = \sum a_n x^n$ is continuous on $[0, R]$, so $\lim_{x \to R^-} f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n R^n$.
m5.exam_tip: A classic application of Abel's Theorem is evaluating the alternating harmonic series: $\ln(2) = 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - \dots$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: State the Taylor series theorem for real functions.
m5.concept_tested: Taylor's Theorem with Remainder
m5.approach: State Taylor's Theorem with Lagrange form of the remainder.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.explanation: If $f$ has $n+1$ derivatives on an interval containing $x_0$ and $x$.

solution_steps.title: Lagrange Form of Remainder
solution_steps.math: R_n(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!} (x - x_0)^{n+1} \quad \text{for some } c \text{ strictly between } x_0 \text{ and } x
solution_steps.explanation: The error term resembles the next term in the series evaluated at an intermediate point $c$.

m5.final_answer: $f(x) = P_n(x) + R_n(x)$ where $R_n(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(x-x_0)^{n+1}$ for some $c$ between $x_0$ and $x$.
m5.exam_tip: Note that for $n = 0$, Taylor's theorem reduces directly to the Mean Value Theorem.
