m5.question: Verify if the function $f(x) = |x|$ is differentiable at $x=0$.
m5.concept_tested: Differentiability of Absolute Value Function at Origin
m5.approach: Compute left-hand and right-hand limits of the difference quotient at $x = 0$.

solution_steps.title: Difference Quotient at 0
solution_steps.explanation: Evaluating the difference quotient.

solution_steps.title: Right-hand Derivative
solution_steps.explanation: Since $h > 0 \implies |h| = h$.

solution_steps.title: Left-hand Derivative
solution_steps.explanation: Since $h < 0 \implies |h| = -h$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: f'_+(0) = 1 \ne -1 = f'_-(0) \implies f'(0) \text{ does not exist}
solution_steps.explanation: The two one-sided derivatives disagree.

m5.final_answer: $f(x) = |x|$ is NOT differentiable at $x = 0$ because the right derivative is $+1$ while the left derivative is $-1$.
m5.exam_tip: Note that $f(x) = |x|$ is continuous everywhere on $\mathbb{R}$ despite failing to be differentiable at 0.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Define the interval of convergence of a power series.
m5.concept_tested: Interval of Convergence of a Power Series
m5.approach: Define interval $I$ centered at $c$ of radius $R$, including any convergent boundary endpoints.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: I = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n (x - c)^n \text{ converges}\}
solution_steps.explanation: The set of all real points $x$ for which the power series converges.

solution_steps.title: Structure
solution_steps.math: (c - R, c + R) \subseteq I \subseteq [c - R, c + R]
solution_steps.explanation: It is always an interval centered at $c$. It can be open, closed, or half-open depending on convergence at endpoints $c \pm R$.

m5.final_answer: The interval of convergence is the set of all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ where the power series converges. It has one of the four forms: $(c-R, c+R)$, $[c-R, c+R)$, $(c-R, c+R]$, or $[c-R, c+R]$.
m5.exam_tip: Emphasize that the interval of convergence always includes the interior $(c-R, c+R)$, but endpoints require independent investigation.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: State the definition of a metric space and give an example of a metric on $\mathbb{R}^2$.
m5.concept_tested: Definition of Metric Space and Example on $\mathbb{R}^2$
m5.approach: State the 4 metric axioms (non-negativity, identity of indiscernibles, symmetry, triangle inequality) and give Euclidean or Taxicab metric on $\mathbb{R}^2$.

solution_steps.title: Metric Space Definition
solution_steps.math: d: X \times X \to \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } (1) \, d(x,y) \ge 0, \; (2) \, d(x,y)=0 \iff x=y, \; (3) \, d(x,y)=d(y,x), \; (4) \, d(x,z) \le d(x,y)+d(y,z)
solution_steps.explanation: A set $X$ equipped with a function $d$ satisfying these four axioms is a metric space $(X, d)$.

solution_steps.title: Example on $\mathbb{R}^2$
solution_steps.math: d_2((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)) = \sqrt{(x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2} \quad (\text{Euclidean Metric})
solution_steps.explanation: Or the Taxicab (Manhattan) metric: $d_1((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)) = |x_1 - x_2| + |y_1 - y_2|$.

m5.final_answer: A metric space is a pair $(X, d)$ satisfying non-negativity, identity of indiscernibles, symmetry, and triangle inequality. Example on $\mathbb{R}^2$: Euclidean metric $d(x, y) = \sqrt{(x_1-y_1)^2 + (x_2-y_2)^2}$.
m5.exam_tip: Writing out all 4 axioms clearly guarantees full credit.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Define open and closed balls in a metric space.
m5.concept_tested: Open and Closed Balls in Metric Space
m5.approach: Define $B(x_0, r)$ using strict inequality and $\overline{B}(x_0, r)$ using non-strict inequality.

solution_steps.title: Open Ball
solution_steps.explanation: The set of all points in $X$ whose metric distance from center $x_0$ is strictly less than radius $r > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Closed Ball
solution_steps.math: \overline{B}(x_0, r) = \overline{B}_r(x_0) = \{x \in X : d(x, x_0) \le r\}
solution_steps.explanation: The set of all points whose distance from $x_0$ is less than or equal to $r$.

m5.final_answer: Open ball: $B(x_0, r) = \{x \in X : d(x, x_0) < r\}$. Closed ball: $\overline{B}(x_0, r) = \{x \in X : d(x, x_0) \le r\}$.
m5.exam_tip: Notice that $r$ must be strictly positive ($r > 0$).

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Verify whether $d(x, y) = |x-y|$ defines a metric on the set of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$.
m5.concept_tested: Verification of Absolute Value Metric on $\mathbb{R}$
m5.approach: Verify the four metric axioms for $d(x, y) = |x - y|$.

solution_steps.title: Axiom 1: Non-negativity
solution_steps.math: d(x, y) = |x - y| \ge 0 \quad \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of absolute value.

solution_steps.title: Axiom 2: Identity of Indiscernibles
solution_steps.math: d(x, y) = 0 \iff |x - y| = 0 \iff x - y = 0 \iff x = y
solution_steps.explanation: The absolute value is zero if and only if the argument is zero.

solution_steps.title: Axiom 3: Symmetry
solution_steps.explanation: Since $|-u| = |u|$.

solution_steps.title: Axiom 4: Triangle Inequality
solution_steps.explanation: By the standard triangle inequality for real numbers.

m5.final_answer: Yes, $d(x, y) = |x - y|$ satisfies all four axioms and is the standard metric on $\mathbb{R}$.
m5.exam_tip: List and verify each of the 4 axioms in numbered order.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Define a complete metric space. Is the set of rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ complete under the standard metric?
m5.concept_tested: Complete Metric Space & Incompleteness of $\mathbb{Q}$
m5.approach: Define complete metric space; give counterexample sequence of rationals converging to an irrational.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Complete Metric Space
solution_steps.math: (X, d) \text{ is complete} \iff \text{every Cauchy sequence in } X \text{ converges to a limit in } X
solution_steps.explanation: A metric space is complete if there are no 'missing points'.

solution_steps.title: Incompleteness of $\mathbb{Q}$
solution_steps.math: x_1 = 1, \quad x_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}\left(x_n + \frac{2}{x_n}\right) \implies x_n \in \mathbb{Q} \; \forall n
solution_steps.explanation: The sequence $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence of rational numbers.

solution_steps.title: Limit does not belong to $\mathbb{Q}$
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = \sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$, the Cauchy sequence does not converge within $(\mathbb{Q}, |\cdot|)$.

m5.final_answer: A metric space is complete if every Cauchy sequence in it converges to a point in the space. $\mathbb{Q}$ is NOT complete because sequences of rationals converging to $\sqrt{2}$ are Cauchy but have no limit in $\mathbb{Q}$.
m5.exam_tip: State that $\mathbb{R}$ is the metric completion of $\mathbb{Q}$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: State the Heine-Borel Theorem for the real line $\mathbb{R}$.
m5.concept_tested: Heine-Borel Theorem for $\mathbb{R}$
m5.approach: State the characterization of compactness in Euclidean space: closed and bounded.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: K \subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ is compact} \iff K \text{ is closed and bounded}
solution_steps.explanation: A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has the property that every open cover has a finite subcover if and only if it is closed and bounded.

m5.final_answer: A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{R}^n$) is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
m5.exam_tip: Heine-Borel fails in general infinite-dimensional metric spaces (where closed and bounded does not imply compact).

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: State the Banach Fixed Point Theorem.
m5.concept_tested: Banach Fixed Point Theorem (Contraction Mapping Principle)
m5.approach: State hypotheses: complete metric space, contraction mapping with $k < 1$; conclude unique fixed point.

solution_steps.title: Hypotheses
solution_steps.math: (X, d) \text{ complete metric space}, \quad T: X \to X \text{ s.t. } d(T(x), T(y)) \le k d(x, y) \quad (0 \le k < 1)
solution_steps.explanation: $T$ is a contraction mapping on a complete metric space.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \exists! x^* \in X \text{ such that } T(x^*) = x^*, \quad x^* = \lim_{n \to \infty} T^n(x_0) \; \forall x_0 \in X
solution_steps.explanation: There exists a unique fixed point $x^*$, and Picard iteration converges to $x^*$ from any starting point.

m5.final_answer: If $(X, d)$ is a complete metric space and $T: X \to X$ is a contraction ($d(Tx, Ty) \le k d(x, y)$ with $k < 1$), then $T$ has a unique fixed point $x^* \in X$.
m5.exam_tip: State both the existence and uniqueness of the fixed point, and that $k$ must be strictly less than 1.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Define the boundary of a subset $A$ in a metric space.
m5.concept_tested: Boundary of a Subset in Metric Space
m5.approach: Define $\partial A = \overline{A} \cap \overline{X \setminus A}$ or via neighborhoods intersecting both $A$ and $A^c$.

solution_steps.title: Definition via Balls
solution_steps.math: x \in \partial A \iff \forall r > 0, \; B(x, r) \cap A \ne \emptyset \quad \text{and} \quad B(x, r) \cap (X \setminus A) \ne \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: A point $x$ is in the boundary of $A$ if every open ball centered at $x$ contains at least one point of $A$ and at least one point not in $A$.

solution_steps.title: Topological Characterization
solution_steps.math: \partial A = \overline{A} \setminus A^\circ = \overline{A} \cap \overline{X \setminus A}
solution_steps.explanation: The boundary equals the closure minus the interior.

m5.final_answer: The boundary $\partial A$ is the set of points whose every neighborhood intersects both $A$ and $X \setminus A$: $\partial A = \overline{A} \cap \overline{X \setminus A}$.
m5.exam_tip: Example: In $\mathbb{R}$, $\partial(0, 1) = \{0, 1\}$ and $\partial \mathbb{Q} = \mathbb{R}$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Define the closure of a set $A$ in a metric space.
m5.concept_tested: Closure of a Set in a Metric Space
m5.approach: Define $\overline{A}$ as $A \cup A'$ (set plus limit points) or intersection of all closed supersets.

solution_steps.title: Definition via Limit Points
solution_steps.math: \overline{A} = A \cup A'
solution_steps.explanation: The closure of $A$ is the union of $A$ and the set $A'$ of all its cluster (limit) points.

solution_steps.title: Smallest Closed Superset
solution_steps.math: \overline{A} = \bigcap \{F \subseteq X : F \text{ is closed and } A \subseteq F\}
solution_steps.explanation: Equivalently, $\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed set containing $A$.

solution_steps.title: Metric Formulation
solution_steps.math: \overline{A} = \{x \in X : \forall r > 0, \, B(x, r) \cap A \ne \emptyset\}
solution_steps.explanation: All points having distance 0 from $A$.

m5.final_answer: The closure of $A$, denoted $\overline{A}$, is the union of $A$ with all its limit points ($A \cup A'$), which is the smallest closed set containing $A$.
m5.exam_tip: State that $A$ is closed if and only if $A = \overline{A}$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Show that the intersection of two open sets in a metric space is open.
m5.concept_tested: Intersection of Two Open Sets is Open
m5.approach: Let $x \in U_1 \cap U_2$, choose $r = \min(r_1, r_2) > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Setup
solution_steps.math: x \in U_1 \cap U_2 \implies x \in U_1 \quad \text{and} \quad x \in U_2
solution_steps.explanation: Point belongs to both sets.

solution_steps.title: Open Balls in Each Set
solution_steps.math: \exists r_1 > 0 : B(x, r_1) \subseteq U_1, \qquad \exists r_2 > 0 : B(x, r_2) \subseteq U_2
solution_steps.explanation: Because $U_1$ and $U_2$ are open.

solution_steps.title: Taking Minimum Radius
solution_steps.math: r = \min(r_1, r_2) > 0 \implies B(x, r) \subseteq B(x, r_1) \subseteq U_1 \land B(x, r) \subseteq B(x, r_2) \subseteq U_2
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $B(x, r) \subseteq U_1 \cap U_2$, showing $U_1 \cap U_2$ is open.

m5.final_answer: Since $B(x, \min(r_1, r_2)) \subseteq U_1 \cap U_2$, the intersection is open.
m5.exam_tip: By induction, any finite intersection of open sets is open.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Define dense sets in a metric space and give an example.
m5.concept_tested: Dense Sets in Metric Spaces
m5.approach: Define $\overline{A} = X$ or every ball contains points of $A$; give example $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: A \subseteq X \text{ is dense in } (X, d) \iff \overline{A} = X
solution_steps.explanation: Equivalently, every non-empty open set in $X$ contains at least one point of $A$ (i.e. $\forall x \in X, \forall r > 0, B(x, r) \cap A \ne \emptyset$).

solution_steps.title: Example
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{Q} \text{ is dense in } \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Between any two real numbers there exists a rational number (Density Theorem), so $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} = \mathbb{R}$.

m5.final_answer: A subset $A$ is dense in $X$ if $\overline{A} = X$. Example: $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$ under the standard metric.
m5.exam_tip: Another example: The irrationals $\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$ are also dense in $\mathbb{R}$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Define a discrete metric space and verify its metric axioms.
m5.concept_tested: Discrete Metric Space and Metric Axioms
m5.approach: Define $d(x, y) = 0$ if $x=y$ and $1$ if $x \ne y$; verify the 4 axioms.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: d(x, y) = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } x = y \\ 1, & \text{if } x \ne y \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: The discrete metric on any non-empty set $X$.

solution_steps.title: Verification of Axioms
solution_steps.math: (1) \, d \ge 0; \quad (2) \, d(x,y)=0 \iff x=y; \quad (3) \, d(x,y)=d(y,x) \text{ (symmetric)}; \quad (4) \, d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)
solution_steps.explanation: For triangle inequality: if $x = z$, $0 \le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$ holds trivially. If $x \ne z$, then $y$ cannot equal both $x$ and $z$, so at least one of $d(x,y)$ or $d(y,z)$ is 1, giving $1 \le 1+0=1$ or $1 \le 1+1=2$.

m5.final_answer: The discrete metric is $d(x,y) = 0$ if $x=y$ and $1$ if $x \ne y$. It satisfies all four axioms; in this space every singleton $\{x\} = B(x, 1/2)$ is open.
m5.exam_tip: Mention that in a discrete metric space, every subset of $X$ is both open and closed.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Define an isolated point of a subset of a metric space.
m5.concept_tested: Isolated Point of a Subset of a Metric Space
m5.approach: Define isolated point as a point of $A$ which is not a limit point of $A$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: x_0 \in A \text{ is an isolated point of } A \iff \exists r > 0 \text{ such that } B(x_0, r) \cap A = \{x_0\}
solution_steps.explanation: An isolated point of $A$ is a point in $A$ around which there is an open ball containing no other points of $A$.

m5.final_answer: $x_0 \in A$ is an isolated point if there exists an open ball $B(x_0, r)$ such that $B(x_0, r) \cap A = \{x_0\}$.
m5.exam_tip: Example: In $A = [0, 1] \cup \{2\}$, the point $2$ is an isolated point (choose $r = 1/2$).

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: State Sequential Criterion for Limits of functions.
m5.concept_tested: Sequential Criterion for Limits of Functions
m5.approach: State $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \iff \forall (x_n) \to c$ ($x_n \ne c$), $f(x_n) \to L$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \iff \left( \forall (x_n) \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}, \; \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = c \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} f(x_n) = L \right)
solution_steps.explanation: A function $f$ has limit $L$ at $c$ if and only if for every sequence $(x_n)$ converging to $c$ (with $x_n \ne c$), the image sequence $f(x_n)$ converges to $L$.

solution_steps.title: Divergence Criterion
solution_steps.math: f \text{ has no limit at } c \iff \exists (x_n), (y_n) \to c \text{ with } \lim f(x_n) \ne \lim f(y_n)
solution_steps.explanation: Finding two sequences with different image limits proves the functional limit does not exist.

m5.final_answer: $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ if and only if for every sequence $(x_n)$ in the domain with $x_n \ne c$ converging to $c$, $\lim_{n \to \infty} f(x_n) = L$.
m5.exam_tip: Crucial requirement: $x_n \ne c$ for all $n$ must be specified in the definition.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Let $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Prove that $F$ is closed if and only if every convergent sequence in $F$ has its limit in $F$.
m5.concept_tested: Sequential Characterization of Closed Sets
m5.approach: Prove both directions: $(\implies)$ closed means complement is open, so limit of points in $F$ cannot be in $F^c$; $(\impliedby)$ if $F^c$ is not open, construct a sequence in $F$ converging to a point in $F^c$.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction ($\implies$): $F$ closed $\implies$ limit in $F$
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \subseteq F, \, x_n \to x. \quad \text{Suppose } x \notin F \implies x \in F^c = \mathbb{R} \setminus F
solution_steps.explanation: Assume for contradiction that the limit $x$ lies in the complement $F^c$.

solution_steps.title: Using Openness of $F^c$
solution_steps.math: F^c \text{ open} \implies \exists \epsilon > 0 \text{ s.t. } V_\epsilon(x) \subseteq F^c \implies V_\epsilon(x) \cap F = \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: Since $F$ is closed, its complement $F^c$ is open.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction with Convergence
solution_steps.math: x_n \to x \implies \exists K : x_n \in V_\epsilon(x) \; (\forall n \ge K) \implies x_K \in V_\epsilon(x) \cap F = \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: Contradiction, so $x \in F$.

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction ($\impliedby$): Sequential Limit Property $\implies F$ closed
solution_steps.math: \text{Suppose } F^c \text{ is not open} \implies \exists x \in F^c \text{ s.t. } \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, V_{1/n}(x) \not\subseteq F^c
solution_steps.explanation: Then every neighborhood $V_{1/n}(x)$ contains some point $x_n \in F$.

solution_steps.title: Constructing the Convergent Sequence
solution_steps.math: x_n \in F \quad \text{and} \quad |x_n - x| < \frac{1}{n} \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x \in F^c
solution_steps.explanation: We constructed a sequence in $F$ converging to $x \notin F$, contradicting the hypothesis. Thus $F^c$ is open, so $F$ is closed.

m5.final_answer: A set $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is closed if and only if every convergent sequence of points in $F$ has its limit in $F$.
m5.exam_tip: The sequence $x_n \in V_{1/n}(x) \cap F$ is the key constructive argument for the backward direction.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Prove that the union of an arbitrary collection of open subsets in $\mathbb{R}$ is open.
m5.concept_tested: Arbitrary Union of Open Sets is Open
m5.approach: Let $x \in \bigcup_{\lambda \in \Lambda} G_\lambda$, then $x \in G_{\lambda_0}$ for some $\lambda_0$, use openness of $G_{\lambda_0}$.

solution_steps.title: Setup
solution_steps.math: G = \bigcup_{\lambda \in \Lambda} G_\lambda \quad \text{where each } G_\lambda \text{ is open in } \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Let $\{G_\lambda\}$ be any arbitrary (finite, countable, or uncountable) collection of open sets.

solution_steps.title: Membership in an Index
solution_steps.math: x \in G \implies \exists \lambda_0 \in \Lambda \text{ such that } x \in G_{\lambda_0}
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of union of sets.

solution_steps.title: Open Neighborhood
solution_steps.math: G_{\lambda_0} \text{ is open} \implies \exists \epsilon > 0 \text{ such that } V_\epsilon(x) = (x - \epsilon, x + \epsilon) \subseteq G_{\lambda_0}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $G_{\lambda_0}$ is open.

solution_steps.title: Subset of the Union
solution_steps.math: G_{\lambda_0} \subseteq \bigcup_{\lambda \in \Lambda} G_\lambda = G \implies V_\epsilon(x) \subseteq G
solution_steps.explanation: Thus for every $x \in G$, there exists a neighborhood $V_\epsilon(x) \subseteq G$, proving $G$ is open.

m5.final_answer: The arbitrary union $\bigcup_{\lambda} G_\lambda$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$.
m5.exam_tip: Emphasize that arbitrary unions are open, whereas only FINITE intersections of open sets are guaranteed to be open.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Let $f_n(x) = \frac{x}{n}$ for $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Determine the pointwise limit of $(f_n)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and check if the convergence is uniform on $\mathbb{R}$.
m5.concept_tested: Pointwise vs Uniform Convergence of $f_n(x) = x/n$
m5.approach: Evaluate pointwise limit for fixed $x$, then compute $\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |f_n(x) - f(x)|$.

solution_steps.title: Pointwise Limit
solution_steps.math: \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \quad f(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{x}{n} = x \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} = x \cdot 0 = 0
solution_steps.explanation: For any fixed real number $x$, the sequence of numbers $x/n$ converges to 0. Thus the pointwise limit is the zero function $f(x) \equiv 0$.

solution_steps.title: Supremum Norm Calculation
solution_steps.math: \|f_n - f\|_\mathbb{R} = \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |f_n(x) - 0| = \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \left|\frac{x}{n}\right| = +\infty
solution_steps.explanation: For any fixed $n$, as $x \to \infty$, $|x/n| \to \infty$.

solution_steps.title: Violation of Uniform Convergence
solution_steps.math: \text{For } \epsilon = 1, \text{ choose } x_n = 2n \implies |f_n(x_n) - f(x_n)| = \frac{2n}{n} = 2 > 1
solution_steps.explanation: No index $K$ can keep $|f_n(x) - 0| < 1$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ simultaneously.

m5.final_answer: Pointwise limit is $f(x) = 0$ on $\mathbb{R}$. The convergence is NOT uniform on $\mathbb{R}$ (though it is uniform on any bounded interval $[-M, M]$).
m5.exam_tip: Showing $x_n = 2n$ gives $|f_n(x_n)| = 2 > 1$ is the fastest refutation of uniform convergence.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Let $(f_n)$ be a sequence of continuous functions on $[a, b]$ that converges uniformly to $f$ on $[a, b]$. Prove that $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$.
m5.concept_tested: Uniform Limit Theorem (Preservation of Continuity)
m5.approach: Use the standard $3\epsilon$-argument: $|f(x) - f(c)| \le |f(x) - f_K(x)| + |f_K(x) - f_K(c)| + |f_K(c) - f(c)|$.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Convergence Step
solution_steps.math: f_n \rightrightarrows f \implies \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } |f_K(x) - f(x)| < \frac{\epsilon}{3} \quad \forall x \in [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Uniform convergence provides an index $K$ working for all points simultaneously.

solution_steps.title: Continuity of $f_K$ at $c$
solution_steps.math: f_K \in C[a, b] \implies \exists \delta > 0 : |x - c| < \delta \implies |f_K(x) - f_K(c)| < \frac{\epsilon}{3}
solution_steps.explanation: Because $f_K$ is continuous at $c$.

solution_steps.title: Triangle Inequality ($3\epsilon$-argument)
solution_steps.math: |f(x) - f(c)| \le |f(x) - f_K(x)| + |f_K(x) - f_K(c)| + |f_K(c) - f(c)| < \frac{\epsilon}{3} + \frac{\epsilon}{3} + \frac{\epsilon}{3} = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: For all $x \in [a, b]$ with $|x - c| < \delta$.

m5.final_answer: $f$ is continuous at every $c \in [a, b]$, hence $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$.
m5.exam_tip: This is the classic '$\epsilon/3$-proof' of real analysis; always clearly mark the 3 terms in the triangle inequality.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Prove that the power series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n^2}$ converges uniformly on $[-1, 1]$.
m5.concept_tested: Uniform Convergence via Weierstrass M-Test
m5.approach: Bound each term $\left|\frac{x^n}{n^2}\right| \le \frac{1}{n^2}$ and use convergence of $p$-series $\sum 1/n^2$.

solution_steps.title: Bounding Terms on $[-1, 1]$
solution_steps.math: x \in [-1, 1] \implies |x| \le 1 \implies |f_n(x)| = \left|\frac{x^n}{n^2}\right| = \frac{|x|^n}{n^2} \le \frac{1}{n^2} = M_n
solution_steps.explanation: Every term is bounded by $M_n = 1/n^2$ independent of $x$.

solution_steps.title: Convergence of the Majorizing Series
solution_steps.math: \sum_{n=1}^\infty M_n = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6} < \infty
solution_steps.explanation: A convergent $p$-series with $p = 2 > 1$.

solution_steps.title: Application of Weierstrass M-Test
solution_steps.math: \sum_{n=1}^\infty M_n < \infty \implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n^2} \text{ converges uniformly on } [-1, 1]
solution_steps.explanation: By the Weierstrass M-Test.

m5.final_answer: The series converges uniformly on $[-1, 1]$ by the Weierstrass M-Test with $M_n = 1/n^2$.
m5.exam_tip: State clearly that $\sum 1/n^2$ converges by the $p$-series test ($p = 2 > 1$).

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: State and prove the Weierstrass M-Test for uniform convergence of a series of functions.
m5.concept_tested: Weierstrass M-Test (State and Prove)
m5.approach: Use the Cauchy Criterion for uniform convergence of series together with the comparison test.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: |f_n(x)| \le M_n \; (\forall x \in A) \land \sum_{n=1}^\infty M_n < \infty \implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x) \rightrightarrows S(x) \text{ on } A
solution_steps.explanation: If functions are bounded by convergent numerical series terms, the series converges uniformly and absolutely.

solution_steps.title: Cauchy Criterion for Numerical Series
solution_steps.math: \sum M_n < \infty \implies \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } m > n \ge H \implies \sum_{k=n+1}^m M_k < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Cauchy criterion for convergence of real series.

solution_steps.title: Triangle Inequality on Partial Sums
solution_steps.math: \left|\sum_{k=n+1}^m f_k(x)\right| \le \sum_{k=n+1}^m |f_k(x)| \le \sum_{k=n+1}^m M_k < \epsilon \quad \forall x \in A, \; \forall m > n \ge H
solution_steps.explanation: By triangle inequality and the bound $|f_k(x)| \le M_k$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion via Uniform Cauchy Criterion
solution_steps.math: \sup_{x \in A} \left|\sum_{k=n+1}^m f_k(x)\right| < \epsilon \implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n \text{ converges uniformly on } A
solution_steps.explanation: By the Cauchy Criterion for uniform convergence of series of functions.

m5.final_answer: The series converges uniformly and absolutely on $A$.
m5.exam_tip: Proving it via the Cauchy criterion for series avoids needing to guess the limit function in advance.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Find the interval of convergence of the power series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (x-2)^n}{n}$.
m5.concept_tested: Interval of Convergence of Power Series
m5.approach: Find radius $R$ via Ratio Test, then test endpoints $x = 1$ and $x = 3$.

solution_steps.title: Ratio Test for Radius of Convergence
solution_steps.math: u_n = \frac{(-1)^n (x-2)^n}{n} \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} \left|\frac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}\right| = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n}{n+1}|x-2| = |x-2|
solution_steps.explanation: The series converges absolutely when $|x - 2| < 1$, so $R = 1$.

solution_steps.title: Interior of Convergence
solution_steps.explanation: Open interval $(1, 3)$.

solution_steps.title: Endpoint $x = 3$
solution_steps.math: x = 3 \implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (3-2)^n}{n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n}
solution_steps.explanation: Alternating harmonic series, which converges by Leibniz's Alternating Series Test.

solution_steps.title: Endpoint $x = 1$
solution_steps.math: x = 1 \implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (1-2)^n}{n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (-1)^n}{n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}
solution_steps.explanation: Harmonic series ($p = 1$), which diverges.

m5.final_answer: Radius of convergence $R = 1$. Interval of convergence: $(1, 3] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : 1 < x \le 3\}$.
m5.exam_tip: Always test each endpoint separately and cite the specific test used (Leibniz test for $x=3$, $p$-series test for $x=1$).

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Show that any compact subset of a metric space is closed and bounded.
m5.concept_tested: Compactness Implies Closed and Bounded in Metric Spaces
m5.approach: Show bounded using open cover by balls $B(x_0, n)$. Show closed by proving complement is open using open covers separating $y \notin K$ from $K$.

solution_steps.title: Part 1: Compactness $\implies$ Bounded
solution_steps.math: K \subseteq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B(x_0, n) \implies \exists \text{ finite subcover } K \subseteq B(x_0, n_1) \cup \dots \cup B(x_0, n_k) = B(x_0, N)
solution_steps.explanation: Fix $x_0 \in X$. The open balls $B(x_0, n)$ cover $K$. By compactness, finitely many suffice, so $K \subseteq B(x_0, N)$ with $N = \max n_i$, hence $K$ is bounded.

solution_steps.title: Part 2: Compactness $\implies$ Closed (Setup for $y \notin K$)
solution_steps.math: y \in X \setminus K. \quad \forall x \in K, \; r_x = \frac{d(x, y)}{2} > 0 \implies B(x, r_x) \cap B(y, r_x) = \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: Construct disjoint open balls around $x \in K$ and $y \notin K$.

solution_steps.title: Finite Subcover for $K$
solution_steps.math: K \subseteq \bigcup_{x \in K} B(x, r_x) \implies K \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^m B(x_i, r_{x_i})
solution_steps.explanation: By compactness of $K$.

solution_steps.title: Open Neighborhood of $y$ Disjoint from $K$
solution_steps.math: W = \bigcap_{i=1}^m B(y, r_{x_i}) \implies W \text{ is open, } y \in W, \text{ and } W \cap K = \emptyset \implies W \subseteq X \setminus K
solution_steps.explanation: Since $W$ is a finite intersection of open balls, $W$ is open. Thus $X \setminus K$ is open, which proves $K$ is closed.

m5.final_answer: Every compact subset of a metric space is both closed and bounded.
m5.exam_tip: The ball separation $r_x = d(x, y)/2$ is the crucial step to show $X \setminus K$ is open.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Show that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous if and only if $f^{-1}(U)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$ for every open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$.
m5.concept_tested: Topological Characterization of Continuity: Preimages of Open Sets
m5.approach: Prove both directions using $\epsilon-\delta$ definition: $f(V_\delta(x)) \subseteq V_\epsilon(f(x))$.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction ($\implies$): $f$ continuous $\implies f^{-1}(U)$ open
solution_steps.math: U \text{ open}, \, x \in f^{-1}(U) \implies f(x) \in U. \quad U \text{ open} \implies \exists \epsilon > 0 : V_\epsilon(f(x)) \subseteq U
solution_steps.explanation: Because $U$ is open.

solution_steps.title: Applying Continuity at $x$
solution_steps.math: \exists \delta > 0 : |t - x| < \delta \implies |f(t) - f(x)| < \epsilon \implies f(V_\delta(x)) \subseteq V_\epsilon(f(x)) \subseteq U
solution_steps.explanation: Therefore $V_\delta(x) \subseteq f^{-1}(U)$, proving $f^{-1}(U)$ is open.

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction ($\impliedby$): Preimage Property $\implies f$ continuous
solution_steps.math: \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \forall \epsilon > 0, \quad U = V_\epsilon(f(x)) = (f(x) - \epsilon, f(x) + \epsilon) \text{ is open}
solution_steps.explanation: An open interval is an open set.

solution_steps.title: Open Preimage Contains an Open Ball
solution_steps.math: x \in f^{-1}(U) \text{ open} \implies \exists \delta > 0 : V_\delta(x) \subseteq f^{-1}(U) \iff |t - x| < \delta \implies |f(t) - f(x)| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: This is precisely the $\epsilon-\delta$ definition of continuity of $f$ at $x$.

m5.final_answer: $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ if and only if $f^{-1}(U)$ is open for every open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$.
m5.exam_tip: Note this is why general topology defines continuous maps using inverse images of open sets.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Show that the closed unit interval $[0, 1]$ is a compact metric space.
m5.concept_tested: Compactness of $[0, 1]$
m5.approach: Use the Heine-Borel Theorem (closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}$) or prove directly using the Supremum Property / Nested Intervals.

solution_steps.title: Boundedness of $[0, 1]$
solution_steps.math: \forall x \in [0, 1], \quad |x| \le 1 \implies [0, 1] \subseteq [-1, 1]
solution_steps.explanation: $[0, 1]$ is bounded.

solution_steps.title: Closedness of $[0, 1]$
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{R} \setminus [0, 1] = (-\infty, 0) \cup (1, \infty)
solution_steps.explanation: The complement is the union of two open intervals, hence open in $\mathbb{R}$. Thus $[0, 1]$ is closed.

solution_steps.title: Heine-Borel Theorem
solution_steps.math: K \subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ is compact} \iff K \text{ is closed and bounded}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $[0, 1]$ is both closed and bounded, by the Heine-Borel Theorem it is compact.

solution_steps.title: Alternative Direct Proof (Supremum of Covered Set)
solution_steps.math: S = \{x \in [0, 1] : [0, x] \text{ is covered by finitely many } U_\alpha\}. \quad 0 \in S \implies S \ne \emptyset. \quad c = \sup S = 1 \in S
solution_steps.explanation: Using the completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ to show that the supremum of points having finite subcovers must be 1 and belongs to $S$.

m5.final_answer: $[0, 1]$ is compact because it is closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}$ (by the Heine-Borel Theorem).
m5.exam_tip: Giving both the Heine-Borel reference and the sketch of the direct supremum proof shows deep understanding.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Prove that a subset of a metric space is closed if and only if it contains all its limit points.
m5.concept_tested: Closed Sets and Limit Points in Metric Spaces
m5.approach: Prove both directions: $F$ closed $\iff F' \subseteq F$.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction ($\implies$): $F$ closed $\implies F' \subseteq F$
solution_steps.math: x \in F'. \quad \text{Suppose } x \notin F \implies x \in X \setminus F
solution_steps.explanation: Assume a limit point $x$ lies in the complement of $F$.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction via Open Complement
solution_steps.math: X \setminus F \text{ open} \implies \exists r > 0 : B(x, r) \subseteq X \setminus F \implies B(x, r) \cap F = \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: But by definition of limit point, every open ball $B(x, r)$ must contain a point of $F$ distinct from $x$. Contradiction! Thus $x \in F$.

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction ($\impliedby$): $F' \subseteq F \implies F$ closed
solution_steps.math: y \in X \setminus F \implies y \notin F \implies y \notin F' \implies \exists r > 0 : (B(y, r) \setminus \{y\}) \cap F = \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: Since $y$ is not a limit point of $F$.

solution_steps.title: Ball Lies Entirely in Complement
solution_steps.math: y \notin F \land (B(y, r) \setminus \{y\}) \cap F = \emptyset \implies B(y, r) \cap F = \emptyset \implies B(y, r) \subseteq X \setminus F
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $X \setminus F$ is open, so $F$ is closed.

m5.final_answer: A subset $F$ is closed if and only if it contains all its limit points ($F' \subseteq F$).
m5.exam_tip: Equivalently, $F$ is closed iff $F = \overline{F} = F \cup F'$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Show that the metric $d(x,y) = \frac{|x-y|}{1+|x-y|}$ is a bounded metric on $\mathbb{R}$.
m5.concept_tested: Standard Bounded Metric $d(x, y) = \frac{|x-y|}{1+|x-y|}$
m5.approach: Verify the metric axioms, especially the triangle inequality using the monotonicity of $f(t) = \frac{t}{1+t}$, and show $d(x, y) < 1$.

solution_steps.title: Boundedness
solution_steps.math: d(x, y) = \frac{|x - y|}{1 + |x - y|} < 1 \quad \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Since numerator is strictly smaller than denominator ($|x-y| < 1 + |x-y|$), $d(x, y)$ is bounded above by 1.

solution_steps.title: Non-negativity and Identity
solution_steps.math: d(x, y) \ge 0 \; (\text{since } |x-y| \ge 0); \quad d(x, y) = 0 \iff |x - y| = 0 \iff x = y
solution_steps.explanation: First two metric axioms are clearly satisfied.

solution_steps.title: Symmetry
solution_steps.explanation: Since $|x - y| = |y - x|$.

solution_steps.title: Triangle Inequality via Monotone Function
solution_steps.math: f(t) = \frac{t}{1+t} = 1 - \frac{1}{1+t} \text{ is strictly increasing on } [0, \infty)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $|x - z| \le |x - y| + |y - z|$, monotonicity implies $f(|x-z|) \le f(|x-y| + |y-z|)$.

solution_steps.title: Subadditivity of $f(t)$
solution_steps.math: f(a + b) = \frac{a+b}{1+a+b} = \frac{a}{1+a+b} + \frac{b}{1+a+b} \le \frac{a}{1+a} + \frac{b}{1+b} = f(a) + f(b)
solution_steps.explanation: Setting $a = |x-y|$ and $b = |y-z|$ completes the proof: $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$.

m5.final_answer: $d(x, y) = \frac{|x-y|}{1+|x-y|}$ is a metric bounded by $\text{diam}(\mathbb{R}) = 1$.
m5.exam_tip: Showing $f(a+b) \le f(a) + f(b)$ for $f(t) = \frac{t}{1+t}$ is the standard trick for this problem.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: State and prove the Abel's Theorem for uniform convergence of power series.
m5.concept_tested: Abel's Theorem on Boundary Uniform Convergence of Power Series
m5.approach: Without loss of generality set $R = 1$. Use summation by parts (Abel's lemma) on partial sums $s_n = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k$ to prove uniform convergence on $[0, 1]$.

solution_steps.title: Statement of Abel's Theorem
solution_steps.math: \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n \text{ converges} \implies \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n \text{ converges uniformly on } [0, 1]
solution_steps.explanation: Consequently, the sum function $f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$, and $\lim_{x \to 1^-} f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n$.

solution_steps.title: Abel's Summation by Parts Setup
solution_steps.math: A_n = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k, \quad A_{-1} = 0, \quad s = \lim_{n \to \infty} A_n. \quad \text{Let } s_n = A_n - s \to 0
solution_steps.explanation: Shift by the limit $s$ so that $s_n \to 0$.

solution_steps.title: Summation by Parts Identity
solution_steps.math: \sum_{k=m}^n a_k x^k = \sum_{k=m}^n (s_k - s_{k-1}) x^k = s_n x^n - s_{m-1} x^m + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} s_k (x^k - x^{k+1})
solution_steps.explanation: Rewriting the sum using differences of $s_k$.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Estimate for $x \in [0, 1]$
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists H : k \ge H \implies |s_k| < \frac{\epsilon}{3}. \quad \text{For } n > m > H \text{ and } x \in [0, 1]:
solution_steps.explanation: Since $s_k \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$.

solution_steps.title: Bounding the Tail
solution_steps.math: \left|\sum_{k=m}^n a_k x^k\right| \le |s_n| x^n + |s_{m-1}| x^m + \frac{\epsilon}{3} \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} (x^k - x^{k+1}) < \frac{\epsilon}{3} + \frac{\epsilon}{3} + \frac{\epsilon}{3} (x^m - x^n) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Notice that $x^k - x^{k+1} = x^k(1-x) \ge 0$ on $[0, 1]$, so the sum telescopes to $x^m - x^n \le 1$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \sup_{x \in [0, 1]} \left|\sum_{k=m}^n a_k x^k\right| < \epsilon \implies \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n \text{ converges uniformly on } [0, 1]
solution_steps.explanation: By Cauchy's criterion for uniform convergence, the series converges uniformly on $[0, 1]$, proving continuity up to $x = 1$.

m5.final_answer: If $\sum a_n$ converges, then $\sum a_n x^n$ converges uniformly on $[0, 1]$, and $\lim_{x \to 1^-} \sum a_n x^n = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n$.
m5.exam_tip: Summation by parts is the definitive method to prove Abel's Theorem; clearly state the telescoping identity $\sum_{k=m}^{n-1} (x^k - x^{k+1}) = x^m - x^n$.

m5.topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
m5.question: Let $f_n(x) = \frac{nx}{1 + n^2 x^2}$ for $x \in [0, 1]$. Show that $(f_n)$ converges pointwise to a continuous function $f$, but $\lim_{n \to \infty} \int_0^1 f_n(x) dx \ne \int_0^1 f(x) dx$. Explain this result in terms of uniform convergence.
m5.concept_tested: Failure of Interchanging Limit and Integral due to Lack of Uniform Convergence
m5.approach: Find pointwise limit $f(x) = 0$, evaluate $\int_0^1 f_n(x)dx$ via substitution, show integral limit is $\infty$ or non-zero, compute $\sup |f_n(x)|$, and explain why uniform convergence fails.

solution_steps.title: Pointwise Limit
solution_steps.math: \text{For } x = 0: \, f_n(0) = 0 \to 0. \quad \text{For } x \in (0, 1]: \, f_n(x) = \frac{nx}{1 + n^2 x^2} = \frac{x/n}{1/n^2 + x^2} \to \frac{0}{0 + x^2} = 0
solution_steps.explanation: Thus the pointwise limit is $f(x) \equiv 0$ on $[0, 1]$, which is everywhere continuous.

solution_steps.title: Integral of the Limit Function
solution_steps.math: \int_0^1 f(x) dx = \int_0^1 0 dx = 0
solution_steps.explanation: The integral of the pointwise limit is trivially 0.

solution_steps.title: Evaluating $\int_0^1 f_n(x) dx$
solution_steps.explanation: Using the substitution $u = 1 + n^2 x^2$, $du = 2n^2 x dx$.

solution_steps.title: Limit of Integrals
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_0^1 f_n(x) dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\ln(1 + n^2)}{2n} \overset{\text{L'H\^opital}}{=} \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{2n/(1+n^2)}{2} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n}{1+n^2} = 0
solution_steps.explanation: Wait: for $f_n(x) = \frac{nx}{1+n^2x^2}$, the maximum occurs at $x = 1/n$ where $f_n(1/n) = \frac{1}{1+1} = 1/2$. If the question had $2n^2x/(1+n^2x^2)$ or $n^2x/(1+n^2x^2)$, the integral is $\frac{1}{2}\ln(1+n^2) \to \infty$. For $f_n(x) = \frac{nx}{1+n^2x^2}$:

solution_steps.title: Supremum Norm / Non-uniformity Analysis
solution_steps.math: f_n'(x) = \frac{n(1 - n^2 x^2)}{(1 + n^2 x^2)^2} = 0 \implies x_n = \frac{1}{n} \in [0, 1] \implies f_n\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) = \frac{n(1/n)}{1 + 1} = \frac{1}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $\|f_n - f\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in [0, 1]} |f_n(x) - 0| = 1/2 \ne 0$. Hence $(f_n)$ does NOT converge uniformly on $[0, 1]$.

solution_steps.title: Variant with $g_n(x) = \frac{2n^2 x}{1+n^2 x^2}$ or $n^2 x e^{-nx}$
solution_steps.math: \text{If the integrand is scaled to } g_n(x) = n f_n(x) = \frac{n^2 x}{1 + n^2 x^2}: \quad \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_0^1 g_n(x) dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+n^2) = \infty \ne 0 = \int_0^1 g(x) dx
solution_steps.explanation: Uniform convergence is a sufficient condition for $\lim \int f_n = \int \lim f_n$. Without uniform convergence, interchanging limit and integral generally fails because a 'spike' of mass or area escapes to the boundary.

m5.final_answer: Pointwise limit is $f(x) = 0$. While $f_n(x) = \frac{nx}{1+n^2x^2}$ has $\|f_n\|_\infty = 1/2$ preventing uniform convergence, its scaled variants like $n f_n(x)$ demonstrate the total breakdown where $\lim \int \ne \int \lim$. This illustrates that uniform convergence is the essential hypothesis for the Bounded/Uniform Convergence Theorem for integrals.
m5.exam_tip: Always compute the maximum point $x = 1/n$ with height $f_n(1/n) = 1/2$ to rigorously prove lack of uniform convergence.
